abstract: An alternative to the typical technique of selecting training examples independently from a fixed distribution is fonnulated and analyzed, in which the current example is presented repeatedly until the error for that item is reduced to some criterion value, ~; then, another item is ran(cid:173) domly selected. The convergence time can be dramatically increased or decreased by this heuristic, depending on the task, and is very sensitive to the value of ~.

The convergence time can be dramatically increased or decreased by this heuristic, depending on the task, and is very sensitive to the value of ~.

paragraphs: This paper studies a training schedule that repeatedly presents the same example until its error falls to a chosen criterion. Only then does the system randomly select another example. The decision about when to move on is therefore tied to the learner's current performance on the item being practiced.

This changes the usual arrangement in which each example is selected independently from a fixed distribution. Under the proposed schedule, a selected item can occupy several successive training presentations. The error criterion controls when that repetition ends, making it a central part of the learning procedure rather than merely a way of reporting progress.

The analysis finds that the strategy can dramatically shorten or lengthen convergence time, depending on the task. Its effect is also highly sensitive to the selected criterion. Repetition is therefore a consequential training choice whose benefit depends on how it is configured. The paper's finding draws attention to example scheduling as a factor that can substantially change learning speed.
summary.tldr: Repeating an example until its error meets a threshold can greatly speed up or slow down learning, depending on the task and threshold.

title: Repeat Until Bored: A Pattern Selection Strategy

abstract: During waking and sleep, the brain and mind undergo a tightly linked and precisely specified set of changes in state. At the level of neurons, this process has been modeled by variations of Volterra-Lotka equations for cyclic fluctuations of brainstem cell populations. However, neural network models based upon rapidly developing knowledge ofthe specific population connectivities and their differential responses to drugs have not yet been developed. Furthermore, only the most preliminary attempts have been made to model across states. Some of our own attempts to link rapid eye movement (REM) sleep neurophysiology and dream cognition using neural network approaches are summarized in this paper.

paragraphs: This paper considers how computational models might explain the linked changes in brain activity and mental experience across waking and sleep. Its starting point is that these state changes have a specific organization. A model must therefore address relationships among states as well as neural activity within an individual state.

Existing work represents cyclic changes in brainstem cell populations using variants of Volterra–Lotka equations. The authors identify a further modeling need: neural networks that incorporate knowledge of the populations' particular connections and their differing responses to drugs. These biological details provide concrete structure that models of sleep and waking should account for.

The paper summarizes preliminary attempts to connect the neurophysiology of rapid eye movement sleep with the cognitive characteristics of dreaming through neural-network approaches. It also describes modeling across states as being at an early stage. Its contribution is an account of this modeling direction and its biological requirements, together with initial efforts to link neural mechanisms to dream cognition.
summary.tldr: The paper outlines biological requirements and preliminary neural-network efforts for connecting sleep physiology with dreaming.

title: Models Wanted: Must Fit Dimensions of Sleep and Dreaming

abstract: Visualizing and structuring pairwise dissimilarity data are difficult combinatorial op(cid:173) timization problems known as multidimensional scaling or pairwise data clustering. Algorithms for embedding dissimilarity data set in a Euclidian space, for clustering these data and for actively selecting data to support the clustering process are discussed in the maximum entropy framework. Active data selection provides a strategy to discover structure in a data set efficiently with partially unknown data.

Active data selection provides a strategy to discover structure in a data set efficiently with partially unknown data.

paragraphs: The paper considers data expressed as pairwise dissimilarities: information about how different items are from one another. Two goals are to visualize those relationships and to organize the items into groups. The authors treat these as difficult combinatorial optimization problems associated with multidimensional scaling and pairwise clustering.

Their discussion places several algorithms within a maximum entropy framework. One task embeds the dissimilarity data in Euclidean space, giving the items a geometric representation. Another clusters them to reveal group structure. A third actively selects data that will help the clustering process. These tasks address different parts of understanding the same relational information.

Active selection is especially relevant when some of the data remains unknown. Instead of requiring all relationships to be available before seeking structure, the approach chooses information to support the clustering process as it proceeds. The stated contribution is a framework covering representation, grouping, and information selection, with active selection offering a strategy for efficiently discovering structure from partially known data.
summary.tldr: The paper connects dissimilarity visualization, clustering, and active data selection within a maximum entropy framework.

title: Multidimensional Scaling and Data Clustering

abstract: We address statistical classifier design given a mixed training set con(cid:173) sisting of a small labelled feature set and a (generally larger) set of unlabelled features. This situation arises, e.g., for medical images, where although training features may be plentiful, expensive expertise is re(cid:173) quired to extract their class labels. We propose a classifier structure and learning algorithm that make effective use of unlabelled data to im(cid:173) prove performance. The learning is based on maximization of the total data likelihood, i.e. over both the labelled and unlabelled data sub(cid:173) sets. Two distinct EM learning algorithms are proposed, differing in the EM formalism applied for unlabelled data. The classifier, based on a joint probability model for features and labels, is a "mixture of experts" structure that is equivalent to the radial basis function (RBF) classifier, but unlike RBFs, is amenable to likelihood-based training. The scope of application for the new method is greatly extended by the observation that test data, or any new data to classify, is in fact additional, unlabelled data - thus, a combined learning/classification operation - much akin to what is done in image segmentation - can be invoked whenever there is new data to classify. Experiments with data sets from the UC Irvine database demonstrate that the new learning algorithms and structure achieve substantial performance gains over alternative approaches.

paragraphs: The paper addresses classification when examples are plentiful but labels are scarce or expensive. Medical images illustrate the problem: collecting features can be easier than obtaining expert judgments about their classes. The aim is to let unlabelled observations contribute to learning alongside a smaller labelled collection.

The proposed classifier models features and labels jointly through a mixture of experts. Its structure is equivalent to a radial basis function classifier, but its probabilistic formulation supports training by maximizing the likelihood of all available data. The authors develop two expectation-maximization algorithms that differ in how they handle the unlabelled portion of the training set.

A further implication is that incoming test examples can themselves supply additional unlabelled information. Learning and classification can therefore be combined when new data arrive, rather than treating training as permanently finished. Experiments on UC Irvine datasets report substantial performance gains over alternative approaches. The central contribution is a structure and training procedure that make unlabelled examples useful within the classification process.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic mixture of experts improves classification by learning jointly from labelled examples and unlabelled data, including incoming test examples.

title: A Mixture of Experts Classifier with Learning Based on Both Labelled and Unlabelled Data

abstract: Neocortical circuits are dominated by massive excitatory feedback: more than eighty percent of the synapses made by excitatory cortical neurons are onto other excitatory cortical neurons. Why is there such massive re(cid:173) current excitation in the neocortex and what is its role in cortical compu(cid:173) tation? Recent neurophysiological experiments have shown that the plas(cid:173) ticity of recurrent neocortical synapses is governed by a temporally asym(cid:173) metric Hebbian learning rule. We describe how such a rule may allow the cortex to modify recurrent synapses for prediction of input sequences. The goal is to predict the next cortical input from the recent past based on previous experience of similar input sequences. We show that a temporal difference learning rule for prediction used in conjunction with dendritic back-propagating action potentials reproduces the temporally asymmet(cid:173) ric Hebbian plasticity observed physiologically. Biophysical simulations demonstrate that a network of cortical neurons can learn to predict mov(cid:173) ing stimuli and develop direction selective responses as a consequence of learning. The space-time response properties of model neurons are shown to be similar to those of direction selective cells in alert monkey VI.

The space-time response properties of model neurons are shown to be similar to those of direction selective cells in alert monkey VI.

paragraphs: The paper explores a possible computational role for the extensive recurrent excitation in neocortical circuits: predicting the next input from recent experience. Its starting point is physiological evidence that changes in recurrent synapses depend asymmetrically on event timing. The authors ask how this timing-dependent learning could support prediction of familiar input sequences.

They show that a temporal-difference learning rule for prediction, combined with action potentials that propagate back into dendrites, reproduces the observed temporally asymmetric Hebbian plasticity. This connects a learning objective with a physiological learning pattern. Recurrent connections could thereby be modified so that recent inputs help anticipate what is likely to arrive next.

Biophysical simulations show a cortical network learning to predict moving stimuli and developing direction-selective responses through learning. Model neurons also exhibit space-time response properties similar to those of direction-selective cells in alert monkey visual cortex. These findings support the proposed predictive role of recurrent circuitry through a combination of learning-rule correspondence and simulated response properties.
summary.tldr: A predictive learning mechanism reproduces timing-dependent cortical plasticity and produces direction-selective responses in biophysical simulations.

title: Predictive Sequence Learning in Recurrent Neocortical Circuits

abstract: When trying to recover 3D structure from a set of images, the most difficult problem is establishing the correspondence between the measurements. Most existing approaches assume that features can be tracked across frames, whereas methods that exploit rigidity constraints to facilitate matching do so only under restricted cam(cid:173) era motion. In this paper we propose a Bayesian approach that avoids the brittleness associated with singling out one "best" cor(cid:173) respondence, and instead consider the distribution over all possible correspondences. We treat both a fully Bayesian approach that yields a posterior distribution, and a MAP approach that makes use of EM to maximize this posterior. We show how Markov chain Monte Carlo methods can be used to implement these techniques in practice, and present experimental results on real data.

Most existing approaches assume that features can be tracked across frames, whereas methods that exploit rigidity constraints to facilitate matching do so only under restricted cam(cid:173) era motion. In this paper we propose a Bayesian approach that avoids the brittleness associated with singling out one "best" cor(cid:173) respondence, and instead consider the distribution over all possible correspondences. We treat both a fully Bayesian approach that yields a posterior distribution, and a MAP approach that makes use of EM to maximize this posterior. We show how Markov chain Monte Carlo methods can be used to implement these techniques in practice, and present experimental results on real data.

paragraphs: Recovering three-dimensional structure from images requires deciding which measurements in different images refer to the same features. The paper identifies this correspondence problem as a major obstacle. Tracking-based approaches assume features remain traceable across frames, while the rigidity-based matching methods discussed in the abstract work only under restricted camera motion.

The proposed Bayesian approach considers a distribution over possible correspondences. This preserves uncertainty about ambiguous matches instead of making an early commitment to a single preferred assignment. The paper develops both a fully Bayesian treatment, which produces a posterior distribution, and a maximum a posteriori treatment, which uses expectation–maximization to maximize that posterior.

Markov chain Monte Carlo provides a practical way to implement these treatments, and the authors present experiments on real data. The contribution is both representational and computational: correspondence uncertainty becomes part of the inference problem, and sampling makes the proposed inference procedures usable. The two treatments offer different ways to work with the same underlying uncertainty.
summary.tldr: Bayesian correspondence inference uses Monte Carlo methods to account for uncertain image matches during 3D reconstruction.

title: Feature Correspondence: A Markov Chain Monte Carlo Approach

abstract: The application of latent/hidden variable Dynamic Bayesian Net- works is constrained by the complexity of marginalising over latent variables. For this reason either small latent dimensions or Gaus- sian latent conditional tables linearly dependent on past states are typically considered in order that inference is tractable. We suggest an alternative approach in which the latent variables are modelled using deterministic conditional probability tables. This specialisa- tion has the advantage of tractable inference even for highly com- plex non-linear/non-Gaussian visible conditional probability tables. This approach enables the consideration of highly complex latent dynamics whilst retaining the bene(cid:12)ts of a tractable probabilistic model.
originalAbstract: The application of latent/hidden variable Dynamic Bayesian Net- works is constrained by the complexity of marginalising over latent variables. For this reason either small latent dimensions or Gaus- sian latent conditional tables linearly dependent on past states are typically considered in order that inference is tractable. We suggest an alternative approach in which the latent variables are modelled using deterministic conditional probability tables. This specialisa- tion has the advantage of tractable inference even for highly com- plex non-linear/non-Gaussian visible conditional probability tables. This approach enables the consideration of highly complex latent dynamics whilst retaining the bene(cid:12)ts of a tractable probabilistic model.

paragraphs: Dynamic Bayesian networks describe systems that evolve over time using observed and hidden variables. A major computational difficulty is averaging over the possible hidden variables. To keep this manageable, models commonly restrict the hidden representation to a small size or use Gaussian conditional distributions with linear dependence on previous states.

This paper proposes a different restriction: deterministic conditional probability tables for the hidden variables. These tables make the latent relationships deterministic within the model. That specialization changes which parts of the network need to carry complexity and permits tractable inference even when the observed-variable conditional distributions are highly nonlinear and non-Gaussian.

The result is a way to represent complex latent dynamics while retaining a manageable probabilistic model. Its significance lies in the particular modeling tradeoff: deterministic hidden relationships permit greater flexibility in the visible distributions. The tractability claim is tied to this specialization, so it should be understood as a property of the proposed model class rather than of unrestricted dynamic Bayesian networks.
summary.tldr: Deterministic hidden-variable tables make inference tractable while allowing complex dynamics and nonlinear, non-Gaussian observation models.

title: Dynamic Bayesian Networks with Deterministic Latent Tables

abstract: Simon Haykin Dept. of Electrical Engineering McMaster University haykin@mcmaster.ca A major issue in evaluating speech enhancement and hearing compensation algorithms is to come up with a suitable metric that predicts intelligibility as judged by a human listener. Previous methods such as the widely used Speech Transmission Index (STI) fail to account for masking effects that arise from the highly nonlinear cochlear transfer function. We therefore propose a Neural Articulation speech intelligibility from the instantaneous neural spike rate over time, produced when a signal is processed by an auditory neural model. By using a well developed model of the auditory periphery and detection theory we show that human perceptual discrimination closely matches the modeled distortion in the instantaneous spike rates of the auditory nerve. In highly rippled frequency transfer conditions the NAI’s prediction error is 8% versus the STI’s prediction error of 10.8%.

Previous methods such as the widely used Speech Transmission Index (STI) fail to account for masking effects that arise from the highly nonlinear cochlear transfer function. We therefore propose a Neural Articulation speech intelligibility from the instantaneous neural spike rate over time, produced when a signal is processed by an auditory neural model. By using a well developed model of the auditory periphery and detection theory we show that human perceptual discrimination closely matches the modeled distortion in the instantaneous spike rates of the auditory nerve. paragraphs: Evaluating speech enhancement and hearing compensation requires a measure that predicts how understandable speech will be to a listener. The paper argues that the widely used Speech Transmission Index misses masking effects arising from the cochlea’s strongly nonlinear response. It therefore seeks an intelligibility measure grounded in a model of auditory processing.

The proposed NAI measure uses the instantaneous neural spike rate over time produced by an auditory neural model. Combining a developed model of the auditory periphery with detection theory, the authors show a close match between human perceptual discrimination and modeled distortion in auditory-nerve spike rates. The comparison is therefore made through the modeled neural response to sound.

Under highly rippled frequency-transfer conditions, the reported prediction error is 8% for NAI and 10.8% for STI. This supports the neural-response approach in that stated setting. The broader significance is that modeling nonlinear auditory processing can improve an intelligibility prediction where a conventional measure fails to account for relevant masking effects.
summary.tldr: An intelligibility measure based on modeled auditory-nerve spike rates improves prediction over STI under highly rippled frequency-transfer conditions.

title: Predicting Speech Intelligibility from a Population of Neurons

abstract: We provide a principle for semi-supervised learning based on optimizing the rate of communicating labels for unlabeled points with side informa- tion. The side information is expressed in terms of identities of sets of points or regions with the purpose of biasing the labels in each region to be the same. The resulting regularization objective is convex, has a unique solution, and the solution can be found with a pair of local prop- agation operations on graphs induced by the regions. We analyze the properties of the algorithm and demonstrate its performance on docu- ment classification tasks.
originalAbstract: We provide a principle for semi-supervised learning based on optimizing the rate of communicating labels for unlabeled points with side informa- tion. The side information is expressed in terms of identities of sets of points or regions with the purpose of biasing the labels in each region to be the same. The resulting regularization objective is convex, has a unique solution, and the solution can be found with a pair of local prop- agation operations on graphs induced by the regions. We analyze the properties of the algorithm and demonstrate its performance on docu- ment classification tasks.

paragraphs: The paper develops a principle for semi-supervised learning based on the rate needed to communicate labels for unlabeled points when side information is available. That side information identifies sets of points or regions. Its role is to encourage points within a region to receive the same label, making the grouping information part of the learning objective.

The resulting regularization objective is convex and has a unique solution. These properties give the optimization a well-defined target. The solution can be computed through two local propagation operations on graphs constructed from the regions, linking the information-based objective to a procedure that operates through local relationships.

This combination matters because the paper supplies both a reason for encouraging regional label agreement and a way to calculate the resulting solution. The authors analyze the algorithm's properties and demonstrate it on document classification tasks. The stated contribution is therefore an information-based learning principle with a uniquely determined solution and a graph-based implementation, supported by application results.
summary.tldr: An information-based objective encourages regional label agreement and yields a unique solution computable by local graph propagation.

title: Distributed Information Regularization on Graphs

abstract: We propose a gossip-based distributed algorithm for Gaussian mixture learning, Newscast EM. The algorithm operates on network topologies where each node observes a local quantity and can communicate with other nodes in an arbitrary point-to-point fashion. The main difference between Newscast EM and the standard EM algorithm is that the M-step in our case is implemented in a decentralized manner: (random) pairs of nodes repeatedly exchange their local parameter estimates and com- bine them by (weighted) averaging. We provide theoretical evidence and demonstrate experimentally that, under this protocol, nodes converge ex- ponentially fast to the correct estimates in each M-step of the EM algo- rithm.
originalAbstract: We propose a gossip-based distributed algorithm for Gaussian mixture learning, Newscast EM. The algorithm operates on network topologies where each node observes a local quantity and can communicate with other nodes in an arbitrary point-to-point fashion. The main difference between Newscast EM and the standard EM algorithm is that the M-step in our case is implemented in a decentralized manner: (random) pairs of nodes repeatedly exchange their local parameter estimates and com- bine them by (weighted) averaging. We provide theoretical evidence and demonstrate experimentally that, under this protocol, nodes converge ex- ponentially fast to the correct estimates in each M-step of the EM algo- rithm.

paragraphs: Newscast EM distributes Gaussian-mixture learning across a network whose nodes each observe a local quantity. Nodes can communicate through arbitrary point-to-point exchanges. The paper focuses on carrying out expectation-maximization in this setting, where information is spread among participants and the parameter update must be coordinated through their communication.

The main modification concerns the maximization step. Random pairs of nodes repeatedly exchange their current local parameter estimates and combine them using weighted averaging. This gossip protocol implements the update in a decentralized way, allowing the network to build agreement through repeated local interactions rather than requiring a single participant to perform the whole maximization step.

The authors provide theoretical evidence and experimental demonstrations that nodes converge exponentially quickly to the correct estimates within each maximization step under this protocol. The scope of that statement matters: it describes the decentralized update's convergence, not a guarantee that mixture-model learning reaches a global optimum. The contribution shows how local averaging can support a central operation of distributed probabilistic learning.
summary.tldr: Newscast EM uses pairwise gossip and weighted averaging to decentralize Gaussian-mixture updates with exponentially fast convergence within each M-step.

title: Newscast EM

abstract: Many real-world classiﬁcation problems involve the prediction of multiple inter-dependent variables forming some structural depen- dency. Recent progress in machine learning has mainly focused on supervised classiﬁcation of such structured variables. In this paper, we investigate structured classiﬁcation in a semi-supervised setting. We present a discriminative approach that utilizes the intrinsic ge- ometry of input patterns revealed by unlabeled data points and we derive a maximum-margin formulation of semi-supervised learning for structured variables. Unlike transductive algorithms, our for- mulation naturally extends to new test points.
originalAbstract: Many real-world classiﬁcation problems involve the prediction of multiple inter-dependent variables forming some structural depen- dency. Recent progress in machine learning has mainly focused on supervised classiﬁcation of such structured variables. In this paper, we investigate structured classiﬁcation in a semi-supervised setting. We present a discriminative approach that utilizes the intrinsic ge- ometry of input patterns revealed by unlabeled data points and we derive a maximum-margin formulation of semi-supervised learning for structured variables. Unlike transductive algorithms, our for- mulation naturally extends to new test points.

paragraphs: This paper considers classification problems where the output contains several interdependent variables. Predicting such an output requires accounting for relationships among its components. The authors study this structured prediction problem in a semi-supervised setting, where unlabeled input examples are available alongside the information used for supervised learning.

Their discriminative approach uses the intrinsic geometry of the input patterns revealed by unlabeled points. Those points contribute information about how the inputs are organized, even though they do not supply labeled structured outputs. The authors incorporate this geometric information into a maximum-margin formulation for predicting structured variables.

A stated feature of the formulation is that it naturally applies to new test points. This extends its use beyond assigning predictions to a fixed collection of unlabeled examples, as in a transductive formulation. The contribution brings together output dependencies, input geometry, and maximum-margin learning in one framework, making unlabeled data part of the construction of a predictor that can subsequently process new inputs.
summary.tldr: The paper combines unlabeled-data geometry with maximum-margin structured prediction in a formulation that extends to new test points.

title: Maximum Margin Semi-Supervised Learning for Structured Variables

abstract: We address the problem of sub-ordinate class recognition, like the distinction between different types of motorcycles. Our approach is motivated by observations from cognitive psychology, which identify parts as the defining component of basic level categories (like motorcycles), while sub-ordinate categories are more often defined by part properties (like 'jagged wheels'). Accordingly, we suggest a two-stage algorithm: First, a relational part based object model is learnt using unsegmented object images from the inclusive class (e.g., motorcycles in general). The model is then used to build a class-specific vector representation for images, where each entry corresponds to a model's part. In the second stage we train a standard discriminative classifier to classify subclass instances (e.g., cross motorcycles) based on the class-specific vector representation. We describe extensive experimental results with several subclasses. The proposed algorithm typically gives better results than a competing one-step algorithm, or a two stage algorithm where classification is based on a model of the sub-ordinate class.

Accordingly, we suggest a two-stage algorithm: First, a relational part based object model is learnt using unsegmented object images from the inclusive class (e.g., motorcycles in general). The model is then used to build a class-specific vector representation for images, where each entry corresponds to a model's part. In the second stage we train a standard discriminative classifier to classify subclass instances (e.g., cross motorcycles) based on the class-specific vector representation. We describe extensive experimental results with several subclasses. The proposed algorithm typically gives better results than a competing one-step algorithm, or a two stage algorithm where classification is based on a model of the sub-ordinate class.

paragraphs: Recognizing a motorcycle and distinguishing between motorcycle types are related but different tasks. This paper draws on psychological observations that broad categories are often defined by their parts, while finer categories depend more on the properties of those parts. It uses that distinction to organize recognition into two learning stages.

First, the method learns a relational model of parts from unsegmented images belonging to the broader category. That model converts each image into a category-specific vector whose entries correspond to model parts. Second, a standard discriminative classifier learns to distinguish subclasses using those vectors. The broad category therefore provides the representation used for finer distinctions.

Experiments cover several subclasses. The proposed approach typically performs better than a competing one-stage algorithm and a two-stage method based on a model of the narrower subclass. These results support learning shared part structure at the broader category level before classifying subclasses. The reported advantage is typical across the experiments, rather than a claim that the approach wins in every case.
summary.tldr: Learning shared object parts at the broad-category level provides a representation that typically improves recognition of finer subclasses.

title: Subordinate class recognition using relational object models

abstract: Neural spike trains present challenges to analytical efforts due to their noisy, spiking nature. Many studies of neuroscienti(cid:2)c and neural prosthetic importance rely on a smoothed, denoised estimate of the spike train’s underlying (cid:2)ring rate. Current techniques to (cid:2)nd time-varying (cid:2)ring rates require ad hoc choices of parameters, offer no con(cid:2)dence intervals on their estimates, and can obscure potentially important single trial variability. We present a new method, based on a Gaussian Process prior, for inferring probabilistically optimal estimates of (cid:2)ring rate functions underlying single or multiple neural spike trains. We test the performance of the method on simulated data and experimentally gathered neural spike trains, and we demonstrate improvements over conventional estimators.
originalAbstract: Neural spike trains present challenges to analytical efforts due to their noisy, spiking nature. Many studies of neuroscienti(cid:2)c and neural prosthetic importance rely on a smoothed, denoised estimate of the spike train’s underlying (cid:2)ring rate. Current techniques to (cid:2)nd time-varying (cid:2)ring rates require ad hoc choices of parameters, offer no con(cid:2)dence intervals on their estimates, and can obscure potentially important single trial variability. We present a new method, based on a Gaussian Process prior, for inferring probabilistically optimal estimates of (cid:2)ring rate functions underlying single or multiple neural spike trains. paragraphs: Neural recordings contain discrete spikes, while many analyses need an estimate of the underlying firing rate as it changes over time. Noise makes this reconstruction difficult. The paper points out that existing techniques require ad hoc parameter choices, lack confidence intervals, and can obscure potentially meaningful differences between individual trials.

The proposed method places a Gaussian process prior over the firing-rate function. This makes rate estimation a probabilistic inference problem in which candidate functions are considered through a common prior model. The method can work with a single spike train or multiple spike trains, directly addressing the need to analyze individual recordings as well as combined observations.

The authors describe the resulting estimates as probabilistically optimal and evaluate the method on simulated data and experimentally recorded neural spike trains. They demonstrate improvements over conventional estimators in those evaluations. The contribution is a probabilistic approach to recovering time-varying firing rates, motivated by the need for denoising that does not obscure important variation across trials.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian process prior supports probabilistic firing-rate estimation from single or multiple spike trains, improving on conventional estimators in the reported tests.

title: Inferring Neural Firing Rates from Spike Trains Using Gaussian Processes

abstract: The present work aims to model the correspondence between facial motion and speech. The face and sound are modelled separately, with phonemes being the link between both. We propose a sequential model and evaluate its suitability for the generation of the facial animation from a sequence of phonemes, which we obtain from speech. We evaluate the results both by computing the error between generated sequences and real video, as well as with a rigorous double-blind test with human subjects. Experiments show that our model compares favourably to other existing methods and that the sequences generated are comparable to real video sequences.

We propose a sequential model and evaluate its suitability for the generation of the facial animation from a sequence of phonemes, which we obtain from speech. We evaluate the results both by computing the error between generated sequences and real video, as well as with a rigorous double-blind test with human subjects. paragraphs: Generating a talking face requires a model of how facial movements correspond to speech. This paper treats the face and the sound as separate modeling problems, connected through phonemes, the speech units used to link them. This organization gives the animation system an intermediate description of speech from which it can generate movement.

The proposed model is sequential: it generates facial animation from an ordered sequence of phonemes obtained from speech. The central task is therefore to produce a sequence of facial movements corresponding to that speech sequence. The authors evaluate whether this probabilistic approach provides a suitable basis for realistic animation.

Evaluation combines two kinds of evidence. The authors measure differences between generated sequences and real video, and they conduct a double-blind study with human participants. Their experiments report favorable comparisons with existing methods and generated sequences comparable to real video. Together, these assessments support the approach through both measured agreement and human evaluation, without establishing that every generated sequence is indistinguishable from a recording.
summary.tldr: A sequential probabilistic model uses phonemes to connect speech with facial animation, producing favorable measured and human evaluations.

title: A probabilistic model for generating realistic lip movements from speech

abstract: We present a new co-clustering problem of images and visual features. The problem involves a set of non-object images in addition to a set of object images and features to be co-clustered. Co-clustering is performed in a way of maximising discrimination of object images from non-object images, thus emphasizing discriminative features. This provides a way of obtaining perceptual joint-clusters of object images and features. We tackle the problem by simultaneously boosting multiple strong classifiers which compete for images by their expertise. Each boosting classifier is an aggregation of weak-learners, i.e. simple visual features. The obtained classifiers are useful for multi-category and multi-view object detection tasks. Experiments on a set of pedestrian images and a face data set demonstrate that the method yields intuitive image clusters with associated features and is much superior to conventional boosting classifiers in object detection tasks.

The grouping objective is to distinguish object images from non-object images. This makes the resulting clusters emphasize features that help recognition, tying the grouping of images to their usefulness for discrimination.

The method simultaneously boosts multiple strong classifiers that compete for images according to their expertise. Each strong classifier combines weak learners corresponding to simple visual features. As a result, the procedure associates image groups with the features used by their classifiers, producing joint clusters with an interpretable connection between images and recognition cues.

The authors also report substantially better object detection than conventional boosting classifiers in those experiments. The contribution is thus a discrimination-driven co-clustering method whose learned groups and features serve an object-detection task.
summary.tldr: MCBoost jointly groups images and discriminative features by training competing boosted classifiers, improving detection in pedestrian and face experiments.

title: MCBoost: Multiple Classifier Boosting for Perceptual Co-clustering of Images and Visual Features

abstract: While clinicians can accurately identify different types of heartbeats in electrocardiograms (ECGs) from different patients, researchers have had limited success in applying supervised machine learning to the same task. The problem is made challenging by the variety of tasks, inter- and intra-patient differences, an often severe class imbalance, and the high cost of getting cardiologists to label data for individual patients. We address these difficulties using active learning to perform patient-adaptive and task-adaptive heartbeat classification. When tested on a benchmark database of cardiologist annotated ECG recordings, our method had considerably better performance than other recently proposed methods on the two primary classification tasks recommended by the Association for the Advancement of Medical Instrumentation. Additionally, our method required over 90% less patient-specific training data than the methods to which we compared it.

This paper addresses these interacting difficulties through active learning that adapts to both the patient and the classification task.

Active learning makes the choice of labeled training examples part of the learning process. In this application, that choice supports adaptation while reducing the amount of patient-specific training data needed. The approach directly targets a practical bottleneck: a model needs information about an individual patient, but expert annotation of that patient's recordings is expensive.

The authors evaluate the method on a benchmark database of ECG recordings annotated by cardiologists. On the two primary classification tasks recommended by the Association for the Advancement of Medical Instrumentation, it performs considerably better than the compared recent methods. It also uses over 90% less patient-specific training data than those methods, demonstrating both predictive and annotation-efficiency gains in that evaluation.
summary.tldr: Patient- and task-adaptive active learning improves benchmark heartbeat classification while using over 90% less patient-specific training data than the compared methods.

title: Active Learning Applied to Patient-Adaptive Heartbeat Classification

abstract: There are many settings in which we wish to fit a model of the behavior of individuals but where our data consist only of aggregate information (counts or low-dimensional contingency tables). This paper introduces Collective Graphical Models---a framework for modeling and probabilistic inference that operates directly on the sufficient statistics of the individual model. We derive a highly-efficient Gibbs sampling algorithm for sampling from the posterior distribution of the sufficient statistics conditioned on noisy aggregate observations, prove its correctness, and demonstrate its effectiveness experimentally.

paragraphs: Researchers sometimes want to model individual behavior even though their observations contain only totals or small tables of counts. In this setting, the available evidence summarizes a population rather than recording each person separately. The paper develops a framework for carrying out probabilistic modeling and inference directly from this aggregate information.

Collective Graphical Models operate on the sufficient statistics of an individual-level model. These are the summaries that retain the information needed for inference within that model. Making these summaries the objects of inference provides a way to connect a model of individuals with observations that are available only collectively.

The authors derive an efficient Gibbs sampling algorithm for the posterior distribution of these statistics, conditioned on noisy aggregate observations. This means the method represents uncertainty about the underlying summaries while accounting for noise in the observed counts. They prove the sampler’s correctness and demonstrate its effectiveness experimentally. The contribution combines a modeling framework suited to aggregate data with a computational procedure for performing its inference.
summary.tldr: Collective Graphical Models enable inference about individual-level models through sufficient statistics observed only as noisy aggregates.

title: Collective Graphical Models

abstract: Markov logic is a widely used tool in statistical relational learning, which uses a weighted first-order logic knowledge base to specify a Markov random field (MRF) or a conditional random field (CRF). In many applications, a Markov logic network (MLN) is trained in one domain, but used in a different one. This paper focuses on dynamic Markov logic networks, where the domain of time points typically varies between training and testing. It has been previously pointed out that the marginal probabilities of truth assignments to ground atoms can change if one extends or reduces the domains of predicates in an MLN. We show that in addition to this problem, the standard way of unrolling a Markov logic theory into a MRF may result in time-inhomogeneity of the underlying Markov chain. Furthermore, even if these representational problems are not significant for a given domain, we show that the more practical problem of generating samples in a sequential conditional random field for the next slice relying on the samples from the previous slice has high computational cost in the general case, due to the need to estimate a normalization factor for each sample. We propose a new discriminative model, slice normalized dynamic Markov logic networks (SN-DMLN), that suffers from none of these issues. It supports efficient online inference, and can directly model influences between variables within a time slice that do not have a causal direction, in contrast with fully directed models (e.g., DBNs). Experimental results show an improvement in accuracy over previous approaches to online inference in dynamic Markov logic networks.

paragraphs: Dynamic Markov logic networks describe temporal relationships using weighted logical statements, but changing the time domain can affect their behavior. The paper identifies problems beyond the known dependence of marginal probabilities on domain size: standard construction can also make the underlying Markov chain vary with time. Generating samples for the next time slice from previous samples can require estimating a separate normalization factor for each sample, which is expensive in general. Experiments show improved accuracy over earlier approaches to online inference in dynamic Markov logic networks, connecting the revised formulation to a demonstrated predictive benefit.
summary.tldr: Slice normalization addresses identified consistency and sampling problems in dynamic Markov logic while enabling efficient, more accurate online inference in experiments.

title: Slice Normalized Dynamic Markov Logic Networks

abstract: Most current planners assume complete domain models and focus on generating correct plans. Unfortunately, domain modeling is a laborious and error-prone task, thus real world agents have to plan with incomplete domain models. While domain experts cannot guarantee completeness, often they are able to circumscribe the incompleteness of the model by providing annotations as to which parts of the domain model may be incomplete. In such cases, the goal should be to synthesize plans that are robust with respect to any known incompleteness of the domain. In this paper, we first introduce annotations expressing the knowledge of the domain incompleteness and formalize the notion of plan robustness with respect to an incomplete domain model. We then show an approach to compiling the problem of finding robust plans to the conformant probabilistic planning problem, and present experimental results with Probabilistic-FF planner.

paragraphs: Planning systems commonly assume that their domain model is complete, even though constructing such a model can be difficult and error prone. This paper studies the situation in which experts cannot guarantee completeness but can indicate where information may be missing. The aim is to use that partial knowledge when choosing plans.

The authors introduce annotations for describing known incompleteness and formalize plan robustness relative to an incomplete domain model. This makes uncertainty about the model an explicit part of the planning task. The relevant scope is the incompleteness described by the annotations, rather than every possible way the real environment could differ from the model.

They then show how to compile robust-plan synthesis into a conformant probabilistic planning problem and present experiments using Probabilistic-FF. The compilation connects the new formulation to an existing planning approach. The contribution is a concrete path from expert statements about missing knowledge to a formal robustness objective and a planner that can address it, with experimental results illustrating the approach.
summary.tldr: Annotations of known model incompleteness enable robust-plan synthesis through a compilation into conformant probabilistic planning.

title: Synthesizing Robust Plans under Incomplete Domain Models

abstract: Logistic-normal topic models can effectively discover correlation structures among latent topics. However, their inference remains a challenge because of the non-conjugacy between the logistic-normal prior and multinomial topic mixing proportions. Existing algorithms either make restricting mean-field assumptions or are not scalable to large-scale applications. This paper presents a partially collapsed Gibbs sampling algorithm that approaches the provably correct distribution by exploring the ideas of data augmentation. To improve time efficiency, we further present a parallel implementation that can deal with large-scale applications and learn the correlation structures of thousands of topics from millions of documents. Extensive empirical results demonstrate the promise.

paragraphs: Logistic-normal topic models can discover how latent topics are correlated, but fitting them is computationally difficult. The logistic-normal prior and multinomial topic proportions do not form a conjugate pairing, which complicates inference. Existing approaches either impose restrictive mean-field assumptions or struggle to scale to large applications.

The paper develops a partially collapsed Gibbs sampler using data augmentation. This introduces auxiliary quantities into the inference procedure to address the computational difficulty. The sampler approaches the provably correct distribution, giving the method a distributional justification beyond simply producing a convenient approximation for the model.

A parallel implementation improves time efficiency and supports learning correlations among thousands of topics from millions of documents. Extensive empirical results demonstrate the approach's promise. The contribution joins two requirements that are especially relevant here: inference that targets the correct distribution and an implementation that can handle large collections. This enables the correlation structure offered by logistic-normal topic models to be explored at a substantially larger scale.
summary.tldr: An augmented Gibbs sampler with a parallel implementation scales logistic-normal topic inference to millions of documents and thousands of correlated topics.

title: Scalable Inference for Logistic-Normal Topic Models

abstract: The estimation of dependencies between multiple variables is a central problem in the analysis of financial time series. A common approach is to express these dependencies in terms of a copula function. Typically the copula function is assumed to be constant but this may be innacurate when there are covariates that could have a large influence on the dependence structure of the data. To account for this, a Bayesian framework for the estimation of conditional copulas is proposed. In this framework the parameters of a copula are non-linearly related to some arbitrary conditioning variables. We evaluate the ability of our method to predict time-varying dependencies on several equities and currencies and observe consistent performance gains compared to static copula models and other time-varying copula methods.

paragraphs: Financial time-series analysis often depends on estimating how multiple variables move together. Copula functions provide a way to express these dependencies, but treating the copula as constant can be inaccurate when other variables influence the relationship. This paper develops a Bayesian framework for conditional copulas that allows dependence to change with the information being conditioned on.

The framework relates copula parameters nonlinearly to conditioning variables. This makes the dependence model responsive to covariates, rather than fixing one relationship across all observations. The central modeling choice is therefore to estimate how dependencies vary with context, with the paper's Gaussian process formulation providing the conditional approach identified in its title.

The authors evaluate predictions of time-varying dependencies for several equities and currencies. They report consistent performance gains over static copulas and other time-varying copula methods in those evaluations. The findings support modeling nonlinear relationships between conditioning information and dependence parameters when analyzing these financial series, where a constant dependence description may miss relevant variation.
summary.tldr: Bayesian conditional copulas model covariate-dependent relationships and improve dependency predictions in the reported equity and currency evaluations.

title: Gaussian Process Conditional Copulas with Applications to Financial Time Series

abstract: Humans and animals readily utilize active sensing, or the use of self-motion, to focus sensory and cognitive resources on the behaviorally most relevant stimuli and events in the environment. Understanding the computational basis of natural active sensing is important both for advancing brain sciences and for developing more powerful artificial systems. Recently, a goal-directed, context-sensitive, Bayesian control strategy for active sensing, termed C-DAC (Context-Dependent Active Controller), was proposed (Ahmad & Yu, 2013). In contrast to previously proposed algorithms for human active vision, which tend to optimize abstract statistical objectives and therefore cannot adapt to changing behavioral context or task goals, C-DAC directly minimizes behavioral costs and thus, automatically adapts itself to different task conditions. However, C-DAC is limited as a model of human active sensing, given its computational/representational requirements, especially for more complex, real-world situations. Here, we propose a myopic approximation to C-DAC, which also takes behavioral costs into account, but achieves a significant reduction in complexity by looking only one step ahead. We also present data from a human active visual search experiment, and compare the performance of the various models against human behavior. We find that C-DAC and its myopic variant both achieve better fit to human data than Infomax (Butko & Movellan, 2010), which maximizes expected cumulative future information gain. In summary, this work provides novel experimental results that differentiate theoretical models for human active sensing, as well as a novel active sensing algorithm that retains the context-sensitivity of the optimal controller while achieving significant computational savings.

paragraphs: Active sensing means moving to obtain information that matters for the task at hand. This paper investigates how to model that behavior in humans. Its starting point is C-DAC, a Bayesian controller that chooses sensing actions by minimizing behavioral costs, allowing its decisions to change with task goals and conditions.

Although C-DAC captures this dependence on context, its computational and representational demands make it challenging as a model of more complex human behavior. The authors introduce a myopic approximation that considers only one step ahead. It still incorporates behavioral costs, retaining context-sensitive decisions while substantially reducing the complexity of planning.

Both C-DAC and the one-step approximation fit the human data better than Infomax, which optimizes expected cumulative information gain. These findings support the relevance of behavioral costs in the tested task. They also show that a computationally simpler controller can preserve the context sensitivity of the original approach.
summary.tldr: A one-step, cost-sensitive sensing controller reduces computation and, like C-DAC, fits the reported human search data better than Infomax.

title: Context-sensitive active sensing in humans

abstract: Unstructured social group activity recognition in web videos is a challenging task due to 1) the semantic gap between class labels and low-level visual features and 2) the lack of labeled training data. To tackle this problem, we propose a relevance topic model" for jointly learning meaningful mid-level representations upon bag-of-words (BoW) video representations and a classifier with sparse weights. In our approach, sparse Bayesian learning is incorporated into an undirected topic model (i.e., Replicated Softmax) to discover topics which are relevant to video classes and suitable for prediction. Rectified linear units are utilized to increase the expressive power of topics so as to explain better video data containing complex contents and make variational inference tractable for the proposed model. An efficient variational EM algorithm is presented for model parameter estimation and inference. Experimental results on the Unstructured Social Activity Attribute dataset show that our model achieves state of the art performance and outperforms other supervised topic model in terms of classification accuracy, particularly in the case of a very small number of labeled training videos."

paragraphs: Recognizing social group activities in web videos is difficult when low-level visual features poorly express activity labels and labeled videos are scarce. This paper proposes a relevance topic model that learns an intermediate representation together with a classifier. It starts from bag-of-words video representations and seeks topics useful for predicting the activity class.

The model incorporates sparse Bayesian learning into an undirected topic model called Replicated Softmax. This ties topic discovery to classification relevance and produces a classifier with sparse weights. Rectified linear units increase the topics' expressive capacity for complex video content while helping make variational inference tractable. The authors provide a variational expectation-maximization algorithm for estimation and inference.

On the Unstructured Social Activity Attribute dataset, the model achieves state-of-the-art performance and higher classification accuracy than the compared supervised topic models. The advantage is especially apparent when very few labeled training videos are available. These results support jointly learning the representation and classifier so that the discovered topics are useful for the recognition task.
summary.tldr: A jointly trained topic model and sparse classifier improves social-activity recognition, particularly with very few labeled training videos.

title: Relevance Topic Model for Unstructured Social Group Activity Recognition

abstract: We present a method for estimating articulated human pose from a single static image based on a graphical model with novel pairwise relations that make adaptive use of local image measurements. More precisely, we specify a graphical model for human pose which exploits the fact the local image measurements can be used both to detect parts (or joints) and also to predict the spatial relationships between them (Image Dependent Pairwise Relations). These spatial relationships are represented by a mixture model. We use Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) to learn conditional probabilities for the presence of parts and their spatial relationships within image patches. Hence our model combines the representational flexibility of graphical models with the efficiency and statistical power of DCNNs. Our method significantly outperforms the state of the art methods on the LSP and FLIC datasets and also performs very well on the Buffy dataset without any training.

paragraphs: Estimating human pose from a single image requires identifying body parts and determining how they fit together. This paper uses local image evidence for both tasks. Its graphical model allows relationships between pairs of parts to depend on the image, so the evidence informs the expected arrangement as well as the presence of individual joints.

A mixture model represents the possible spatial relationships between parts. Deep convolutional neural networks learn conditional probabilities for part presence and spatial relationships within image patches. These predictions feed into the graphical representation of pose. The combination brings learned local visual information into a model that explicitly represents connections among the body's parts.

The authors report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods on the LSP and FLIC datasets. They also report strong performance on Buffy without training on that dataset. The findings support the usefulness of predicting relationships from image content, alongside detecting parts, within the evaluated pose-estimation tasks.
summary.tldr: A pose-estimation model uses convolutional networks to predict both body parts and image-dependent spatial relationships between them.

title: Articulated Pose Estimation by a Graphical Model with Image Dependent Pairwise Relations

abstract: The ability to automatically discover patterns and perform extrapolation is an essential quality of intelligent systems. Kernel methods, such as Gaussian processes, have great potential for pattern extrapolation, since the kernel flexibly and interpretably controls the generalisation properties of these methods. However, automatically extrapolating large scale multidimensional patterns is in general difficult, and developing Gaussian process models for this purpose involves several challenges. A vast majority of kernels, and kernel learning methods, currently only succeed in smoothing and interpolation. This difficulty is compounded by the fact that Gaussian processes are typically only tractable for small datasets, and scaling an expressive kernel learning approach poses different challenges than scaling a standard Gaussian process model. One faces additional computational constraints, and the need to retain significant model structure for expressing the rich information available in a large dataset. In this paper, we propose a Gaussian process approach for large scale multidimensional pattern extrapolation. We recover sophisticated out of class kernels, perform texture extrapolation, inpainting, and video extrapolation, and long range forecasting of land surface temperatures, all on large multidimensional datasets, including a problem with 383,400 training points. The proposed method significantly outperforms alternative scalable and flexible Gaussian process methods, in speed and accuracy. Moreover, we show that a distinct combination of expressive kernels, a fully non-parametric representation, and scalable inference which exploits existing model structure, are critical for large scale multidimensional pattern extrapolation.

paragraphs: This paper develops a Gaussian process approach for extending multidimensional patterns beyond observed data. The kernel determines how observations inform predictions, making kernel learning central to extrapolation. The authors identify a combined challenge: many kernels mainly support smoothing or interpolation, while expressive Gaussian process models can be difficult to scale.

Their approach combines expressive kernels, a fully non-parametric representation, and scalable inference that exploits model structure. The emphasis is on retaining the structure needed to represent rich patterns while making computation feasible on large datasets. The experiments include a dataset with 383,400 training points and recovery of sophisticated kernels outside the fitted class. The method significantly improves speed and accuracy over the alternative scalable and flexible Gaussian process methods evaluated. These results connect modeling expressiveness with practical computation across several pattern-completion and forecasting tasks.
summary.tldr: A scalable Gaussian process approach combines expressive kernels and structured inference to improve multidimensional pattern extrapolation.

title: Fast Kernel Learning for Multidimensional Pattern Extrapolation

abstract: Nonlinear component analysis such as kernel Principle Component Analysis (KPCA) and kernel Canonical Correlation Analysis (KCCA) are widely used in machine learning, statistics and data analysis, but they can not scale up to big datasets. Recent attempts have employed random feature approximations to convert the problem to the primal form for linear computational complexity. However, to obtain high quality solutions, the number of random features should be the same order of magnitude as the number of data points, making such approach not directly applicable to the regime with millions of data points.We propose a simple, computationally efficient, and memory friendly algorithm based on the ``doubly stochastic gradients'' to scale up a range of kernel nonlinear component analysis, such as kernel PCA, CCA and SVD. Despite the \emph{non-convex} nature of these problems, our method enjoys theoretical guarantees that it converges at the rate $\Otil(1/t)$ to the global optimum, even for the top $k$ eigen subspace. Unlike many alternatives, our algorithm does not require explicit orthogonalization, which is infeasible on big datasets. We demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of our algorithm on large scale synthetic and real world datasets.
originalAbstract: Nonlinear component analysis such as kernel Principle Component Analysis (KPCA) and kernel Canonical Correlation Analysis (KCCA) are widely used in machine learning, statistics and data analysis, but they can not scale up to big datasets. Recent attempts have employed random feature approximations to convert the problem to the primal form for linear computational complexity. However, to obtain high quality solutions, the number of random features should be the same order of magnitude as the number of data points, making such approach not directly applicable to the regime with millions of data points.We propose a simple, computationally efficient, and memory friendly algorithm based on the ``doubly stochastic gradients'' to scale up a range of kernel nonlinear component analysis, such as kernel PCA, CCA and SVD. Despite the \emph{non-convex} nature of these problems, our method enjoys theoretical guarantees that it converges at the rate $\Otil(1/t)$ to the global optimum, even for the top $k$ eigen subspace. Unlike many alternatives, our algorithm does not require explicit orthogonalization, which is infeasible on big datasets. We demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of our algorithm on large scale synthetic and real world datasets.

paragraphs: Kernel component methods uncover nonlinear structure but can become difficult to use on very large datasets. Random-feature approximations offer one route to reducing computation, yet high-quality solutions can require a number of features comparable to the number of observations. At millions of observations, that requirement remains a substantial scaling obstacle.

The paper proposes an efficient, memory-friendly algorithm based on doubly stochastic gradients for kernel PCA, CCA, and SVD. It also avoids explicit orthogonalization, a computational requirement the abstract identifies as infeasible at large scale. The design therefore addresses both the representation burden and a costly operation associated with learning component subspaces.

Despite the nonconvex objectives, the authors establish convergence to the global optimum at a rate of roughly 1/t, up to logarithmic factors, including for the leading k-dimensional eigensubspace. This is a guarantee for the analyzed method and problems. Experiments on large synthetic and real datasets demonstrate effectiveness and scalability, linking the theoretical result to the practical goal of expanding nonlinear component analysis.
summary.tldr: Doubly stochastic gradients scale kernel component analysis while avoiding explicit orthogonalization and providing global-convergence guarantees.

title: Scale Up Nonlinear Component Analysis with Doubly Stochastic Gradients

abstract: Recurrent Neural Networks can be trained to produce sequences of tokens given some input, as exemplified by recent results in machine translation and image captioning. The current approach to training them consists of maximizing the likelihood of each token in the sequence given the current (recurrent) state and the previous token. At inference, the unknown previous token is then replaced by a token generated by the model itself. This discrepancy between training and inference can yield errors that can accumulate quickly along the generated sequence. We propose a curriculum learning strategy to gently change the training process from a fully guided scheme using the true previous token, towards a less guided scheme which mostly uses the generated token instead. Experiments on several sequence prediction tasks show that this approach yields significant improvements. Moreover, it was used successfully in our winning bid to the MSCOCO image captioning challenge, 2015.

paragraphs: A recurrent sequence model is commonly trained to predict the next token while receiving the correct previous token. When it generates a sequence, however, it must use its own previous prediction. The paper focuses on this mismatch: an incorrect prediction can become the input to subsequent decisions, allowing errors to accumulate along the generated sequence.

Scheduled sampling changes the training process gradually. It begins with a fully guided setting that supplies the true previous token, then moves toward a setting that mostly supplies tokens generated by the model. This curriculum changes the inputs the model encounters during learning so that they increasingly resemble the inputs available when it produces a sequence.

Experiments on several sequence prediction tasks report significant improvements from this approach. The method also contributed to the authors' winning entry in the MSCOCO image-captioning challenge. These results support the usefulness of gradually exposing the model to its own generated context during training; they do not assert that the procedure eliminates every form of error accumulation.
summary.tldr: Scheduled sampling gradually replaces correct previous tokens with model-generated ones during training, reducing a mismatch in sequence prediction.

title: Scheduled Sampling for Sequence Prediction with Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: Factorial Hidden Markov Models (FHMMs) are powerful models for sequential data but they do not scale well with long sequences. We propose a scalable inference and learning algorithm for FHMMs that draws on ideas from the stochastic variational inference, neural network and copula literatures. Unlike existing approaches, the proposed algorithm requires no message passing procedure among latent variables and can be distributed to a network of computers to speed up learning. Our experiments corroborate that the proposed algorithm does not introduce further approximation bias compared to the proven structured mean-field algorithm, and achieves better performance with long sequences and large FHMMs.

paragraphs: Factorial hidden Markov models are useful for sequential data, but inference and learning become difficult as sequences grow long. This paper proposes a scalable algorithm to address that computational bottleneck. Its construction combines ideas from stochastic variational inference, neural networks, and copulas within a method for learning these models.

The key procedural change is that the algorithm does not require message passing among latent variables. It can also be distributed across a network of computers to accelerate learning. These properties address two aspects of scalability: the inference operations needed within a model and the ability to share computation across machines.

Experiments support the claim that this procedure introduces no additional approximation bias relative to the established structured mean-field algorithm. That is a comparative empirical result, rather than a claim that inference is exact. The authors also report better performance on long sequences and large factorial hidden Markov models. The findings suggest that removing message passing can improve scaling while retaining the approximation quality of the reference method.
summary.tldr: A message-free, distributable inference algorithm improves factorial hidden Markov model scaling without additional approximation bias observed against structured mean-field.

title: Scaling Factorial Hidden Markov Models: Stochastic Variational Inference without Messages

abstract: The question of how to parallelize the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) method has received much attention in the literature. In this paper, we focus instead on batch methods that use a sizeable fraction of the training set at each iteration to facilitate parallelism, and that employ second-order information. In order to improve the learning process, we follow a multi-batch approach in which the batch changes at each iteration. This can cause difficulties because L-BFGS employs gradient differences to update the Hessian approximations, and when these gradients are computed using different data points the process can be unstable. This paper shows how to perform stable quasi-Newton updating in the multi-batch setting, illustrates the behavior of the algorithm in a distributed computing platform, and studies its convergence properties for both the convex and nonconvex cases.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to train machine learning models using sizeable batches and second-order information in a parallel computing setting. Each iteration uses a substantial fraction of the training data, making the work suitable for distribution across computing resources. The batch changes between iterations as part of the proposed multi-batch approach.

Changing batches creates a particular difficulty for L-BFGS. The method uses differences between gradients to update an approximation of the objective's curvature. When those gradients come from different data points, their difference reflects changes in the sampled data as well as changes in the model parameters. That mixture can make the curvature update unstable.

The authors show how to carry out stable quasi-Newton updates despite these changing batches. They illustrate the algorithm's behavior on a distributed computing platform and study convergence for both convex and nonconvex problems. The contribution addresses a concrete obstacle to combining parallel batch computation with curvature-based optimization: maintaining useful updates when the data used at successive iterations changes.
summary.tldr: The paper makes L-BFGS updates stable across changing training batches and studies the method in distributed, convex, and nonconvex settings.

title: A Multi-Batch L-BFGS Method for Machine Learning

abstract: We study the problem of completing a binary matrix in an online learning setting. On each trial we predict a matrix entry and then receive the true entry. We propose a Matrix Exponentiated Gradient algorithm [1] to solve this problem. We provide a mistake bound for the algorithm, which scales with the margin complexity [2, 3] of the underlying matrix. The bound suggests an interpretation where each row of the matrix is a prediction task over a finite set of objects, the columns. Using this we show that the algorithm makes a number of mistakes which is comparable up to a logarithmic factor to the number of mistakes made by the Kernel Perceptron with an optimal kernel in hindsight. We discuss applications of the algorithm to predicting as well as the best biclustering and to the problem of predicting the labeling of a graph without knowing the graph in advance.

paragraphs: This paper studies binary matrix completion as an online prediction problem. On each trial, the learner predicts a matrix entry and then sees its true value. The goal is to control the number of incorrect predictions accumulated as information about the matrix arrives over time.

The authors propose a Matrix Exponentiated Gradient algorithm and prove a mistake bound that scales with the matrix’s margin complexity. The bound supports an interpretation in which each row is a prediction task and the columns are the objects being predicted. This makes the matrix-completion problem a collection of related prediction tasks within one analytical framework.

Using that interpretation, the authors show that the algorithm’s mistake count is comparable, up to a logarithmic factor, to a Kernel Perceptron using an optimal kernel chosen in hindsight. They also discuss predicting as well as the best biclustering and predicting graph labels without knowing the graph beforehand. These applications illustrate how the guarantee can extend beyond filling an isolated table of binary values.
summary.tldr: An online binary-matrix predictor has a margin-complexity mistake bound comparable to a hindsight-optimal Kernel Perceptron up to a logarithmic factor.

title: Mistake Bounds for Binary Matrix Completion

abstract: Neural codes are inevitably shaped by various kinds of biological constraints, \emph{e.g.} noise and metabolic cost. Here we formulate a coding framework which explicitly deals with noise and the metabolic costs associated with the neural representation of information, and analytically derive the optimal neural code for monotonic response functions and arbitrary stimulus distributions. For a single neuron, the theory predicts a family of optimal response functions depending on the metabolic budget and noise characteristics. Interestingly, the well-known histogram equalization solution can be viewed as a special case when metabolic resources are unlimited. For a pair of neurons, our theory suggests that under more severe metabolic constraints, ON-OFF coding is an increasingly more efficient coding scheme compared to ON-ON or OFF-OFF. The advantage could be as large as one-fold, substantially larger than the previous estimation. Some of these predictions could be generalized to the case of large neural populations. In particular, these analytical results may provide a theoretical basis for the predominant segregation into ON- and OFF-cells in early visual processing areas. Overall, we provide a unified framework for optimal neural codes with monotonic tuning curves in the brain, and makes predictions that can be directly tested with physiology experiments.
