paragraphs: The paper asks how neurons should represent information when both noise and metabolic cost matter. It develops a coding framework that includes these constraints explicitly and derives optimal codes for monotonic response functions with arbitrary stimulus distributions. The monotonicity requirement defines the class of responses covered by the analysis.

For a single neuron, the optimal response changes with the energy budget and the noise characteristics. Histogram equalization appears as a special case when metabolic resources are unlimited. This places that familiar solution inside a broader family, showing how resource constraints can change the theoretically preferred representation.

For two neurons, the theory predicts that pairing ON and OFF responses becomes increasingly efficient relative to two responses of the same type as metabolic constraints tighten. Some predictions may extend to larger populations. The authors suggest that the analysis could help explain the prevalence of separate ON and OFF cells in early vision. These are theoretical predictions proposed for physiological testing, rather than reported experimental confirmation of that biological explanation.
summary.tldr: A theory of neural coding under noise and energy constraints predicts budget-dependent responses and increasing efficiency advantages for ON–OFF pairs.

title: Efficient Neural Codes under Metabolic Constraints

abstract: In this work we develop a fast saliency detection method that can be applied to any differentiable image classifier. We train a masking model to manipulate the scores of the classifier by masking salient parts of the input image. Our model generalises well to unseen images and requires a single forward pass to perform saliency detection, therefore suitable for use in real-time systems. We test our approach on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets and show that the produced saliency maps are easily interpretable, sharp, and free of artifacts. We suggest a new metric for saliency and test our method on the ImageNet object localisation task. We achieve results outperforming other weakly supervised methods.

We test our approach on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets and show that the produced saliency maps are easily interpretable, sharp, and free of artifacts. paragraphs: This paper develops a fast way to identify image regions that matter to a classifier’s scores. The method applies to differentiable image classifiers. It trains a separate masking model that changes the classifier’s scores by hiding salient parts of an input image, using the effect of those masks to learn where relevant image content lies.

Once trained, the masking model produces a saliency map in a single forward pass and generalizes well to unseen images, according to the authors. This is the basis for the proposed use in real-time systems: producing a new explanation requires running the learned model once. The paper reports sharp, interpretable maps without artifacts on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet.

The authors also propose a saliency metric and evaluate the method on ImageNet object localization, where it outperforms other weakly supervised methods. This provides an additional task-based assessment of the regions identified by the model. The contribution combines efficient saliency generation with empirical evidence about map quality and their usefulness for locating objects.
summary.tldr: A learned masking model generates saliency maps for differentiable image classifiers in one forward pass and performs strongly on object localization.

title: Real Time Image Saliency for Black Box Classifiers

abstract: Model interpretability is an increasingly important component of practical machine learning. Some of the most common forms of interpretability systems are example-based, local, and global explanations. One of the main challenges in interpretability is designing explanation systems that can capture aspects of each of these explanation types, in order to develop a more thorough understanding of the model. We address this challenge in a novel model called MAPLE that uses local linear modeling techniques along with a dual interpretation of random forests (both as a supervised neighborhood approach and as a feature selection method). MAPLE has two fundamental advantages over existing interpretability systems. First, while it is effective as a black-box explanation system, MAPLE itself is a highly accurate predictive model that provides faithful self explanations, and thus sidesteps the typical accuracy-interpretability trade-off. Specifically, we demonstrate, on several UCI datasets, that MAPLE is at least as accurate as random forests and that it produces more faithful local explanations than LIME, a popular interpretability system. Second, MAPLE provides both example-based and local explanations and can detect global patterns, which allows it to diagnose limitations in its local explanations.

paragraphs: Different explanations reveal different aspects of a predictive model: examples provide reference cases, local explanations describe individual predictions, and global explanations reveal broader behavior. MAPLE aims to bring these perspectives together. It combines local linear modeling with random forests, interpreting the forests as both a way to define supervised neighborhoods and a way to select features.

MAPLE can explain another model as a black box, but it can also serve as the predictive model itself. In the latter role, its explanations describe its own prediction process faithfully. This matters because the explanation system and the predictor can be integrated, rather than requiring a separate account of how a prediction was made.

On several UCI datasets, MAPLE is reported to be at least as accurate as random forests and to produce more faithful local explanations than LIME. It also supplies example-based explanations and detects global patterns that help diagnose limitations in its local explanations. These results support combining predictive performance with several complementary forms of interpretability in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: MAPLE combines local linear models and random forests to deliver accurate predictions with complementary, faithful explanations.

title: Model Agnostic Supervised Local Explanations

abstract: Information theoretic quantities play an important role in various settings in machine learning, including causality testing, structure inference in graphical models, time-series problems, feature selection as well as in providing privacy guarantees. A key quantity of interest is the mutual information and generalizations thereof, including conditional mutual information, multivariate mutual information, total correlation and directed information. While the aforementioned information quantities are well defined in arbitrary probability spaces, existing estimators employ a $\Sigma H$ method, which can only work in purely discrete space or purely continuous case since entropy (or differential entropy) is well defined only in that regime. In this paper, we define a general graph divergence measure ($\mathbb{GDM}$), generalizing the aforementioned information measures and we construct a novel estimator via a coupling trick that directly estimates these multivariate information measures using the Radon-Nikodym derivative. These estimators are proven to be consistent in a general setting which includes several cases where the existing estimators fail, thus providing the only known estimators for the following settings: (1) the data has some discrete and some continuous valued components (2) some (or all) of the components themselves are discrete-continuous \textit{mixtures} (3) the data is real-valued but does not have a joint density on the entire space, rather is supported on a low-dimensional manifold. We show that our proposed estimators significantly outperform known estimators on synthetic and real datasets.

paragraphs: Information measures quantify statistical relationships and support tasks such as feature selection, graphical structure inference, and causality testing. Although these quantities are defined in general probability spaces, familiar estimators compute them by combining entropy terms. That approach encounters problems when observations do not fit a purely discrete or purely continuous setting.

The paper introduces a graph divergence measure that encompasses mutual information and several multivariate extensions. It then constructs an estimator using a coupling technique and the Radon-Nikodym derivative, directly estimating the relevant relationship instead of assembling separate entropy estimates. This provides a common framework for quantities including conditional mutual information, total correlation, and directed information.

The authors prove consistency in a setting that covers combinations of discrete and continuous variables, variables that themselves mix both types, and real-valued data confined to a lower-dimensional manifold. Consistency means the estimates approach the intended quantity as data increases under the result's conditions. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show substantial improvements over known estimators, complementing the theoretical expansion to cases where existing methods fail.
summary.tldr: Direct graph-divergence estimators consistently estimate information measures in settings that include mixed data types and manifold-supported distributions.

title: Estimators for Multivariate Information Measures in General Probability Spaces

abstract: Adversarially trained generative models (GANs) have recently achieved compelling image synthesis results. But despite early successes in using GANs for unsupervised representation learning, they have since been superseded by approaches based on self-supervision. In this work we show that progress in image generation quality translates to substantially improved representation learning performance. Our approach, BigBiGAN, builds upon the state-of-the-art BigGAN model, extending it to representation learning by adding an encoder and modifying the discriminator. We extensively evaluate the representation learning and generation capabilities of these BigBiGAN models, demonstrating that these generation-based models achieve the state of the art in unsupervised representation learning on ImageNet, as well as compelling results in unconditional image generation.

paragraphs: A model that generates convincing images may also learn useful ways to represent visual information. This paper investigates that connection for adversarial generative models. Although GANs had shown early promise for unsupervised representation learning, self-supervised methods had overtaken them, motivating a fresh look as image-generation quality improved.

The authors introduce BigBiGAN by extending BigGAN with an encoder and changing the discriminator. The encoder adds a way to obtain representations from images, allowing the generative approach to serve a representation-learning purpose. This connects advances in image synthesis with the goal of learning useful visual features without supervised labels.

Extensive evaluations examine both learned representations and image generation. The reported models achieve state-of-the-art unsupervised representation learning on ImageNet while also producing compelling unconditional images. These results show that the generation improvements used in this work translate into substantially better representations. The contribution is evidence that strong generative modeling can support both image synthesis and competitive unsupervised visual learning within the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: BigBiGAN extends a strong image generator with an encoder to achieve leading unsupervised ImageNet representations and compelling image synthesis.

title: Large Scale Adversarial Representation Learning

abstract: In this work, we introduce a new decision tree ensemble representation framework: instead of using a graph model we transform each tree into a well-known polynomial form. We apply the new representation to three tasks: theoretical analysis, model reduction, and interpretation. The polynomial form of a tree ensemble allows a straightforward interpretation of the original model. In our experiments, it shows comparable results with state-of-the-art interpretation techniques. Another application of the framework is the ensemble-wise pruning: we can drop monomials from the polynomial, based on train data statistics. This way we reduce the model size up to 3 times without loss of its quality. It is possible to show the equivalence of tree shape classes that share the same polynomial. This fact gives us the ability to train a model in one tree's shape and exploit it in another, which is easier for computation or interpretation. We formulate a problem statement for optimal tree ensemble translation from one form to another and build a greedy solution to this problem.

paragraphs: Decision tree ensembles are usually represented through their branching structures. MonoForest converts each tree into a polynomial form, giving the same model a different mathematical representation. The paper uses this representation for three purposes: understanding ensemble behavior, reducing model size, and translating between tree forms that may have different practical advantages.

The polynomial form supports a straightforward interpretation of the original ensemble. Experiments report results comparable with leading interpretation techniques. It also enables pruning across the ensemble by removing polynomial terms according to training-data statistics. The authors report reducing model size by as much as a factor of three without a loss of quality in their experiments.

The framework additionally identifies equivalence between classes of tree shapes that share a polynomial representation. This makes it possible to train using one shape and use another that is easier to compute or interpret. The authors formulate optimal translation between forms as a problem and develop a greedy solution, extending the framework from analysis to model transformation.
summary.tldr: MonoForest represents tree ensembles as polynomials to support interpretation, pruning, and translation between equivalent tree shapes.

title: MonoForest framework for tree ensemble analysis

abstract: Feature hashing and other random projection schemes are commonly used to reduce the dimensionality of feature vectors. The goal is to efficiently project a high-dimensional feature vector living in R^n into a much lower-dimensional space R^m, while approximately preserving Euclidean norm. These schemes can be constructed using sparse random projections, for example using a sparse Johnson-Lindenstrauss (JL) transform. A line of work introduced by Weinberger et. al (ICML '09) analyzes the accuracy of sparse JL with sparsity 1 on feature vectors with small l infinity-to-l 2 norm ratio. Recently, Freksen, Kamma, and Larsen (NeurIPS '18) closed this line of work by proving a tight tradeoff between l infinity-to-l 2 norm ratio and accuracy for sparse JL with sparsity 1. In this paper, we demonstrate the benefits of using sparsity s greater than 1 in sparse JL on feature vectors. Our main result is a tight tradeoff between l infinity-to-l 2 norm ratio and accuracy for a general sparsity s, that significantly generalizes the result of Freksen et. al. Our result theoretically demonstrates that sparse JL with s > 1 can have significantly better norm-preservation properties on feature vectors than sparse JL with s = 1; we also empirically demonstrate this finding.

paragraphs: Feature hashing and random projections compress high-dimensional feature vectors while attempting to preserve their Euclidean lengths. Sparse Johnson–Lindenstrauss transforms offer a way to perform this compression using sparse random projections. This paper asks what is gained by allowing the sparsity parameter to exceed one.

Earlier work established a tight relationship between accuracy and the ratio of a vector's largest absolute coordinate to its Euclidean norm when sparsity equals one. That ratio captures how concentrated a vector is in its largest coordinate. The authors generalize the relationship to arbitrary sparsity, producing a tight tradeoff that incorporates this additional design choice.

The result shows theoretically that sparsity greater than one can provide substantially better norm preservation than sparsity one. Experiments also demonstrate this benefit. The claim is a possible improvement characterized by the tradeoff, rather than a universal statement that every denser projection is better. The contribution gives a sharper understanding of how vector concentration and projection sparsity jointly influence compression accuracy.
summary.tldr: A tight tradeoff shows how increasing sparse JL sparsity beyond one can substantially improve feature-vector norm preservation.

title: Understanding Sparse JL for Feature Hashing

abstract: In the context of multi-player, general-sum games, there is a growing interest in solution concepts involving some form of communication among players, since they can lead to socially better outcomes with respect to Nash equilibria and may be reached through learning dynamics in a decentralized fashion. In this paper, we focus on coarse correlated equilibria (CCEs) in sequential games. First, we complete the picture on the complexity of finding social-welfare-maximizing CCEs by proving that the problem is not in Poly-APX, unless P = NP, in games with three or more players (including chance). Then, we provide simple arguments showing that CFR---working with behavioral strategies---may not converge to a CCE in multi-player, general-sum sequential games. In order to amend this issue, we devise two variants of CFR that provably converge to a CCE. The first one (CFR-S) is a simple stochastic adaptation of CFR which employs sampling to build a correlated strategy, whereas the second variant (called CFR-Jr) enhances CFR with a more involved reconstruction procedure to recover correlated strategies from behavioral ones. Experiments on a rich testbed of multi-player, general-sum sequential games show that both CFR-S and CFR-Jr are dramatically faster than the state-of-the-art algorithms to compute CCEs, with CFR-Jr being also a good heuristic to find socially-optimal CCEs.

It separates two questions: how hard it is to find an equilibrium maximizing social welfare, and how learning algorithms can reach an equilibrium.

They also show that counterfactual regret minimization using behavioral strategies may fail to converge to a coarse correlated equilibrium. summary.tldr: Two regret-minimization variants provably reach coarse correlated equilibria and compute them much faster in multiplayer game experiments.

title: Learning to Correlate in Multi-Player General-Sum Sequential Games

abstract: We introduce the Neural Conditioner (NC), a self-supervised machine able to learn about all the conditional distributions of a random vector X. The NC is a function NC(x⋅a,a,r) that leverages adversarial training to match each conditional distribution P(Xr|Xa=xa). After training, the NC generalizes to sample from conditional distributions never seen, including the joint distribution. The NC is also able to auto-encode examples, providing data representations useful for downstream classification tasks. In sum, the NC integrates different self-supervised tasks (each being the estimation of a conditional distribution) and levels of supervision (partially observed data) seamlessly into a single learning experience.

paragraphs: A collection of variables defines many prediction tasks, depending on which variables are observed and which ones must be generated. The Neural Conditioner combines these tasks in one self-supervised model. It receives observed values together with specifications of the observed and requested variables, allowing the same function to handle different conditional distributions.

The model uses adversarial training to match the distribution of requested variables given the available observations. This unifies learning tasks that would otherwise differ in their input and output subsets. It also accommodates partially observed data within the same learning process, connecting different amounts of available supervision to the same conditional modeling objective.

The authors report that the trained model samples from conditional distributions it did not encounter during training, including the joint distribution. It can also auto-encode examples and produce representations useful for downstream classification. These capabilities make the contribution broader than a single prediction task: one model supports conditional generation, joint generation, and representation learning through a shared formulation.
summary.tldr: The Neural Conditioner unifies conditional generation and representation learning, generalizing to conditional distributions not encountered during training.

title: Learning about an exponential amount of conditional distributions

abstract: We consider the core reinforcement-learning problem of on-policy value function approximation from a batch of trajectory data, and focus on various issues of Temporal Difference (TD) learning and Monte Carlo (MC) policy evaluation. The two methods are known to achieve complementary bias-variance trade-off properties, with TD tending to achieve lower variance but potentially higher bias. In this paper, we argue that the larger bias of TD can be a result of the amplification of local approximation errors. We address this by proposing an algorithm that adaptively switches between TD and MC in each state, thus mitigating the propagation of errors. Our method is based on learned confidence intervals that detect biases of TD estimates. We demonstrate in a variety of policy evaluation tasks that this simple adaptive algorithm performs competitively with the best approach in hindsight, suggesting that learned confidence intervals are a powerful technique for adapting policy evaluation to use TD or MC returns in a data-driven way.

paragraphs: Policy evaluation estimates the value of following a policy from observed trajectories. Temporal-difference learning and Monte Carlo evaluation have complementary bias-variance behavior: temporal-difference estimates often reduce variance but can introduce more bias. This paper studies on-policy value approximation from a fixed batch of trajectory data.

The authors argue that local approximation errors can be amplified through temporal-difference updates. Their algorithm learns confidence intervals that detect biased temporal-difference estimates and adaptively chooses between temporal-difference and Monte Carlo returns at each state, limiting the propagation of those errors.

Across several policy-evaluation tasks, this adaptive procedure is competitive with the best approach chosen afterward with hindsight. The evidence supports using estimated uncertainty to make local evaluation choices, rather than selecting one return estimator globally. The abstract does not give numerical error reductions or claim that the confidence intervals eliminate all approximation bias.
summary.tldr: State-specific confidence intervals guide a switch between temporal-difference and Monte Carlo evaluation.

title: Adaptive Temporal-Difference Learning for Policy Evaluation with Per-State Uncertainty Estimates

abstract: We consider the task of estimating the entropy of $k$-ary distributions from samples in the streaming model, where space is limited. Our main contribution is an algorithm that requires $O\left(\frac{k \log (1/\varepsilon)^2}{\varepsilon^3}\right)$ samples and a constant $O(1)$ memory words of space and outputs a $\pm\varepsilon$ estimate of $H(p)$. Without space limitations, the sample complexity has been established as $S(k,\varepsilon)=\Theta\left(\frac k{\varepsilon\log k}+\frac{\log^2 k}{\varepsilon^2}\right)$, which is sub-linear in the domain size $k$, and the current algorithms that achieve optimal sample complexity also require nearly-linear space in $k$. Our algorithm partitions $[0,1]$ into intervals and estimates the entropy contribution of probability values in each interval. The intervals are designed to trade bias and variance. Distribution property estimation and testing with limited memory is a largely unexplored research area. We hope our work will motivate research in this field.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to estimate the entropy of a distribution from a stream of samples when memory is tightly limited. The distribution has k possible outcomes, and the target is an estimate within epsilon of its entropy. The central question is how much sampling is needed when the algorithm cannot keep a large memory state.

The proposed algorithm uses a constant number of memory words and O(k log^2(1/epsilon) / epsilon^3) samples. It divides the probability range from zero to one into intervals and estimates the entropy contribution associated with each interval. The interval design balances bias and variance, organizing the estimation around ranges of probability values.

Without memory limits, the established optimal sample complexity is sublinear in k, but existing algorithms achieving it require nearly linear space in k. The paper therefore establishes a different resource tradeoff: entropy estimation with constant-word memory at the stated sampling cost. It also identifies distribution estimation and testing under memory constraints as an area for further research.
summary.tldr: An interval-based streaming algorithm estimates distribution entropy within additive epsilon using only a constant number of memory words.

title: Estimating Entropy of Distributions in Constant Space

abstract: The generalization and learning speed of a multi-class neural network can often be significantly improved by using soft targets that are a weighted average of the hard targets and the uniform distribution over labels. Smoothing the labels in this way prevents the network from becoming over-confident and label smoothing has been used in many state-of-the-art models, including image classification, language translation and speech recognition. Despite its widespread use, label smoothing is still poorly understood. Here we show empirically that in addition to improving generalization, label smoothing improves model calibration which can significantly improve beam search. However, we also observe that if a teacher network is trained with label smoothing, knowledge distillation into a student network is much less effective. To explain these observations, we visualize how label smoothing changes the representations learned by the penultimate layer of the network. We show that label smoothing encourages the representations of training examples from the same class to group in tight clusters. This results in loss of information in the logits about resemblances between instances of different classes, which is necessary for distillation, but does not hurt generalization or calibration of the model's predictions.

paragraphs: Label smoothing replaces a fully concentrated training target with a mixture of that target and a uniform distribution over classes. It discourages overconfident predictions and can improve learning speed and generalization. This paper investigates its effects more closely, asking how benefits to prediction relate to changes in the information learned by a network.

The authors empirically find improved calibration, meaning better agreement between prediction confidence and correctness, which can significantly improve beam search. They also observe a drawback for knowledge distillation: when the teacher is trained with label smoothing, transferring its knowledge to a student becomes much less effective.

Visualizations of the penultimate layer provide an explanation. Label smoothing encourages examples from the same class to form tight clusters, removing information from the logits about similarities between examples belonging to different classes. That information is needed for distillation, even though its loss does not hurt the model's generalization or calibration in the reported findings. The study explains why an effective predictive model can be a less effective teacher.
summary.tldr: Label smoothing improves generalization and calibration but can weaken distillation by removing cross-class similarity information from a teacher's logits.

title: When does label smoothing help?

abstract: This article suggests that deterministic Gradient Descent, which does not use any stochastic gradient approximation, can still exhibit stochastic behaviors. In particular, it shows that if the objective function exhibit multiscale behaviors, then in a large learning rate regime which only resolves the macroscopic but not the microscopic details of the objective, the deterministic GD dynamics can become chaotic and convergent not to a local minimizer but to a statistical distribution. In this sense, deterministic GD resembles stochastic GD even though no stochasticity is injected. A sufficient condition is also established for approximating this long-time statistical limit by a rescaled Gibbs distribution, which for example allows escapes from local minima to be quantified. Both theoretical and numerical demonstrations are provided, and the theoretical part relies on the construction of a stochastic map that uses bounded noise (as opposed to Gaussian noise).

paragraphs: Gradient descent can be entirely deterministic: each update uses the actual gradient without injected noise or stochastic approximation. This paper shows that such an algorithm can nevertheless exhibit behavior resembling a stochastic process. The setting is an objective with structure at multiple scales and a learning rate large enough to miss its fine details.

When updates resolve the objective's broad structure but not its microscopic variation, the resulting dynamics can become chaotic. Instead of settling at a local minimizer, they can approach a statistical distribution in their long-term behavior. The apparent randomness therefore comes from the interaction between deterministic updates and the objective's multiple scales.

The authors establish a sufficient condition under which a rescaled Gibbs distribution approximates this long-term statistical limit. That approximation can, for example, quantify escapes from local minima. They provide theoretical and numerical demonstrations, with the theory using a stochastic map driven by bounded rather than Gaussian noise. The result identifies a conditional mechanism for stochastic-like behavior, rather than asserting that all large-step gradient descent behaves this way.
summary.tldr: On multiscale objectives, deterministic gradient descent with a sufficiently coarse learning rate can exhibit chaotic dynamics and a statistical long-term limit.

title: Stochasticity of Deterministic Gradient Descent: Large Learning Rate for Multiscale Objective Function

abstract: A natural approach to generative modeling of videos is to represent them as a composition of moving objects. Recent works model a set of 2D sprites over a slowly-varying background, but without considering the underlying 3D scene that gives rise to them. We instead propose to model a video as the view seen while moving through a scene with multiple 3D objects and a 3D background. Our model is trained from monocular videos without any supervision, yet learns to generate coherent 3D scenes containing several moving objects. We conduct detailed experiments on two datasets, going beyond the visual complexity supported by state-of-the-art generative approaches. We evaluate our method on depth-prediction and 3D object detection---tasks which cannot be addressed by those earlier works---and show it out-performs them even on 2D instance segmentation and tracking.

Earlier object-centric generative approaches represented videos using two-dimensional sprites over a slowly changing background. The proposed representation instead includes the underlying spatial scene that gives rise to the visible images.

The model learns from monocular videos without supervision and can generate coherent 3D scenes with several moving objects. Its representation connects the visible frames to objects and background in three dimensions. That structure matters because it supports questions about depth and 3D object locations, extending the kinds of scene information available from the model beyond its generated images.

Experiments on two datasets reach greater visual complexity than the earlier leading generative approaches discussed by the authors. Evaluation includes depth prediction and 3D object detection, tasks those approaches could not address. The method also outperforms them on 2D instance segmentation and tracking, showing reported benefits for image-level object understanding as well as the additional capabilities supplied by 3D modeling.
summary.tldr: An unsupervised model learns moving 3D objects and backgrounds from monocular video, enabling 3D analysis and improving reported 2D segmentation and tracking.

title: Unsupervised object-centric video generation and decomposition in 3D

abstract: In this work, we study the causal relations among German regions in terms of the spread of Covid-19 since the beginning of the pandemic, taking into account the restriction policies that were applied by the different federal states. We loose a strictly formulated assumption for a causal feature selection method for time series data, robust to latent confounders, which we subsequently apply on Covid-19 case numbers. We present findings about the spread of the virus in Germany and the causal impact of restriction measures, discussing the role of various policies in containing the spread. Since our results are based on rather limited target time series (only the numbers of reported cases), care should be exercised in interpreting them. However, it is encouraging that already such limited data seems to contain causal signals. This suggests that as more data becomes available, our causal approach may contribute towards meaningful causal analysis of political interventions on the development of Covid-19, and thus also towards the development of rational and data-driven methodologies for choosing interventions.

It uses reported case counts as time series, seeking signals about how regional spread and policy interventions relate to subsequent developments. The objective is to support causal analysis of interventions using the available observational data.

summary.tldr: An adapted causal time-series method finds suggestive signals about Covid-19 spread and restrictions in Germany, with interpretation limited by reliance on reported cases.

title: Causal analysis of Covid-19 Spread in Germany

abstract: We propose AttendLight, an end-to-end Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithm for the problem of traffic signal control. Previous approaches for this problem have the shortcoming that they require training for each new intersection with a different structure or traffic flow distribution. AttendLight solves this issue by training a single, universal model for intersections with any number of roads, lanes, phases (possible signals), and traffic flow. To this end, we propose a deep RL model which incorporates two attention models. The first attention model is introduced to handle different numbers of roads-lanes; and the second attention model is intended for enabling decision-making with any number of phases in an intersection. As a result, our proposed model works for any intersection configuration, as long as a similar configuration is represented in the training set. Experiments were conducted with both synthetic and real-world standard benchmark datasets. Our numerical experiment covers intersections with three or four approaching roads; one-directional/bi-directional roads with one, two, and three lanes; different number of phases; and different traffic flows. We consider two regimes: (i) single-environment training, single-deployment, and (ii) multi-environment training, multi-deployment. AttendLight outperforms both classical and other RL-based approaches on all cases in both regimes.

paragraphs: AttendLight tackles traffic signal control with a single reinforcement learning model that can serve different intersection layouts and traffic patterns. The motivation is that earlier approaches require training again when the intersection structure or traffic distribution changes. Sharing a model across configurations could make learned signal control more broadly usable.

The architecture uses two attention mechanisms to handle variable-sized inputs and decisions. One accommodates different numbers of roads and lanes; the other supports choosing among different numbers of signal phases. This flexibility comes with a stated condition: an intersection configuration must have a similar configuration represented in the training set. The model's universality therefore depends on the coverage of its training environments.

Experiments use synthetic and real-world benchmark datasets with varied road directions, lane counts, phases, and traffic flows. They examine both training and deployment in a single environment and training and deployment across multiple environments. AttendLight outperforms classical and other reinforcement learning approaches in every reported case across both regimes, supporting the value of its shared attention-based design.
summary.tldr: AttendLight uses two attention mechanisms to share a traffic-control policy across intersections whose configurations resemble those seen during training.

title: AttendLight: Universal Attention-Based Reinforcement Learning Model for Traffic Signal Control

abstract: Ensembling is now recognized as an effective approach for increasing the predictive performance and calibration of deep networks. We introduce a new approach, Parameter Ensembling by Perturbation (PEP), that constructs an ensemble of parameter values as random perturbations of the optimal parameter set from training by a Gaussian with a single variance parameter. The variance is chosen to maximize the log-likelihood of the ensemble average (𝕃) on the validation data set. Empirically, and perhaps surprisingly, 𝕃 has a well-defined maximum as the variance grows from zero (which corresponds to the baseline model). Conveniently, calibration level of predictions also tends to grow favorably until the peak of 𝕃 is reached. In most experiments, PEP provides a small improvement in performance, and, in some cases, a substantial improvement in empirical calibration. We show that this "PEP effect'' (the gain in log-likelihood) is related to the mean curvature of the likelihood function and the empirical Fisher information. Experiments on ImageNet pre-trained networks including ResNet, DenseNet, and Inception showed improved calibration and likelihood. We further observed a mild improvement in classification accuracy on these networks. Experiments on classification benchmarks such as MNIST and CIFAR-10 showed improved calibration and likelihood, as well as the relationship between the PEP effect and overfitting; this demonstrates that PEP can be used to probe the level of overfitting that occurred during training. In general, no special training procedure or network architecture is needed, and in the case of pre-trained networks, no additional training is needed.

paragraphs: Parameter Ensembling by Perturbation creates an ensemble by adding Gaussian noise to a trained network's parameters. A single variance controls the perturbation size. The method chooses that variance by maximizing the validation log-likelihood of the ensemble's averaged predictions, starting from zero variance, which recovers the original model.

Empirically, the authors find a well-defined likelihood maximum as the variance increases. Calibration, or the agreement between predictive confidence and outcomes, also tends to improve up to that point. Most experiments show small predictive-performance gains, while some show substantial calibration gains. Tests with pretrained ImageNet networks report better likelihood and calibration together with mild classification-accuracy improvements.

The paper relates the likelihood gain to the mean curvature of the likelihood function and empirical Fisher information. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 also connect the effect to overfitting, supporting its use as a probe of training behavior. PEP requires no special architecture or training procedure, and pretrained networks need no additional training. Its empirical appeal is obtaining useful ensembles from perturbations around an already trained solution.
summary.tldr: PEP ensembles Gaussian perturbations of trained parameters, often improving likelihood and calibration without additional training of pretrained networks.

title: PEP: Parameter Ensembling by Perturbation

abstract: Practical and pervasive needs for robustness and privacy in algorithms have inspired the design of online adversarial and differentially private learning algorithms. The primary quantity that characterizes learnability in these settings is the Littlestone dimension of the class of hypotheses [Ben-David et al., 2009, Alon et al., 2019]. This characterization is often interpreted as an impossibility result because classes such as linear thresholds and neural networks have infinite Littlestone dimension. In this paper, we apply the framework of smoothed analysis [Spielman and Teng, 2004], in which adversarially chosen inputs are perturbed slightly by nature. We show that fundamentally stronger regret and error guarantees are possible with smoothed adversaries than with worst-case adversaries. In particular, we obtain regret and privacy error bounds that depend only on the VC dimension and the bracketing number of a hypothesis class, and on the magnitudes of the perturbations.

In this paper, we apply the framework of smoothed analysis [Spielman and Teng, 2004], in which adversarially chosen inputs are perturbed slightly by nature. paragraphs: Worst-case analysis can make online adversarial learning and differentially private learning appear impossible for important hypothesis classes. The relevant characterization uses Littlestone dimension, which is infinite for classes including linear thresholds and neural networks. This paper asks how the picture changes when adversarial choices undergo small natural perturbations.

The authors use smoothed analysis: an adversary selects inputs, but nature slightly modifies them. This changes the assumptions about how difficult the input sequence can be. Under this model, the paper derives stronger guarantees for online regret and private learning error than those available against fully worst-case adversaries.

The resulting bounds depend on VC dimension, the hypothesis class's bracketing number, and the magnitude of the perturbations. These quantities replace the exclusive focus on the worst-case characterization with a description sensitive to smoothing. The findings show that small perturbations can substantially change theoretical learnability guarantees; their scope remains tied to the smoothed adversary model and the perturbation sizes appearing in the bounds.
summary.tldr: Small natural perturbations to adversarial inputs enable stronger online and private learning guarantees than worst-case analysis permits.

title: Smoothed Analysis of Online and Differentially Private Learning

abstract: Hierarchical multi-label classification (HMC) is a challenging classification task extending standard multi-label classification problems by imposing a hierarchy constraint on the classes. In this paper, we propose C-HMCNN(h), a novel approach for HMC problems, which, given a network h for the underlying multi-label classification problem, exploits the hierarchy information in order to produce predictions coherent with the constraint and improve performance. We conduct an extensive experimental analysis showing the superior performance of C-HMCNN(h) when compared to state-of-the-art models.

paragraphs: In multi-label classification, a single input can receive several labels. Hierarchical multi-label classification adds a further requirement: the predicted labels must respect a hierarchy connecting the classes. This makes prediction a joint problem, because the relationships among labels constrain which outputs are coherent.

The paper introduces C-HMCNN(h), an approach built around a network h for the underlying multi-label problem. It uses the hierarchy information to produce predictions consistent with the required constraint while also seeking better classification performance. The central contribution is therefore a way to bring known class relationships into the predictions of a multi-label network.

The authors report an extensive experimental comparison in which C-HMCNN(h) performs better than state-of-the-art models. That finding supports using the hierarchy as useful predictive information as well as a requirement on valid outputs. The approach addresses two linked needs: predicting the appropriate labels and ensuring those predictions fit the structure of the classification task. Its reported advantage concerns the evaluated hierarchical classification problems.
summary.tldr: C-HMCNN(h) uses class hierarchies to produce coherent multi-label predictions and improves performance in the reported comparisons.

title: Coherent Hierarchical Multi-Label Classification Networks

abstract: Compositional generalization is a basic and essential intellective capability of human beings, which allows us to recombine known parts readily. However, existing neural network based models have been proven to be extremely deficient in such a capability. Inspired by work in cognition which argues compositionality can be captured by variable slots with symbolic functions, we present a refreshing view that connects a memory-augmented neural model with analytical expressions, to achieve compositional generalization. Our model consists of two cooperative neural modules, Composer and Solver, fitting well with the cognitive argument while being able to be trained in an end-to-end manner via a hierarchical reinforcement learning algorithm. Experiments on the well-known benchmark SCAN demonstrate that our model seizes a great ability of compositional generalization, solving all challenges addressed by previous works with 100% accuracies.

paragraphs: Compositional generalization means using familiar parts in combinations that were not previously encountered. The paper addresses the difficulty neural models have with this capability. Its starting point is a cognitive account in which symbolic functions operate on variable slots: reusable structures can accept different contents, allowing known operations and components to participate in new combinations.

The authors connect that idea to a neural model with memory and analytical expressions. Two cooperating modules, called Composer and Solver, form the architecture. Together, they provide a way to organize learning around compositional structure while remaining trainable as one system. A hierarchical reinforcement learning algorithm supplies the end-to-end training procedure.

Experiments use the SCAN benchmark to assess whether the model can generalize compositionally. The authors report 100% accuracy on all the challenges addressed by previous work in that benchmark. This is strong evidence for the proposed architecture within the reported evaluation. The contribution is a concrete connection between symbolic compositional ideas and trainable neural machinery, with benchmark results showing that this connection can support successful recombination.
summary.tldr: A memory-augmented Composer–Solver model learns analytical expressions and achieves 100% accuracy on the reported SCAN compositional generalization challenges.

title: Compositional Generalization by Learning Analytical Expressions

abstract: Undirected graphical models are compact representations of joint probability distributions over random variables. To solve inference tasks of interest, graphical models of arbitrary topology can be trained using empirical risk minimization. However, to solve inference tasks that were not seen during training, these models (EGMs) often need to be re-trained. Instead, we propose an inference-agnostic adversarial training framework which produces an infinitely-large ensemble of graphical models (AGMs). The ensemble is optimized to generate data within the GAN framework, and inference is performed using a finite subset of these models. AGMs perform comparably with EGMs on inference tasks that the latter were specifically optimized for. Most importantly, AGMs show significantly better generalization to unseen inference tasks compared to EGMs, as well as deep neural architectures like GibbsNet and VAEAC which allow arbitrary conditioning. Finally, AGMs allow fast data sampling, competitive with Gibbs sampling from EGMs.

paragraphs: A graphical model represents a joint probability distribution through relationships among variables. Once trained, it can support inference about some variables given information about others. However, the paper explains that graphical models trained through empirical risk minimization often need retraining when asked to solve inference tasks different from those used during training.

The authors propose adversarially learned graphical models, or AGMs, to make training less tied to particular inference tasks. Their framework optimizes an infinitely large ensemble of discrete undirected graphical models to generate data within a GAN framework. Actual inference uses a finite subset of the ensemble, connecting the broad training formulation to a usable inference procedure.

In the reported evaluations, AGMs perform comparably to empirically trained graphical models on tasks those models were specifically optimized to solve. They generalize substantially better to unseen inference tasks than those models and the arbitrary-conditioning architectures GibbsNet and VAEAC. Sampling is also competitive with Gibbs sampling from the empirically trained models. These findings support adversarial ensemble training as a way to obtain more reusable inference capabilities.
summary.tldr: Adversarial training of a graphical-model ensemble improves generalization to inference tasks that were not specified during training.

title: Adversarially-learned Inference via an Ensemble of Discrete Undirected Graphical Models

abstract: Learning monotonic models with respect to a subset of the inputs is a desirable feature to effectively address the fairness, interpretability, and generalization issues in practice. Existing methods for learning monotonic neural networks either require specifically designed model structures to ensure monotonicity, which can be too restrictive/complicated, or enforce monotonicity by adjusting the learning process, which cannot provably guarantee the learned model is monotonic on selected features. In this work, we propose to certify the monotonicity of the general piece-wise linear neural networks by solving a mixed integer linear programming problem. This provides a new general approach for learning monotonic neural networks with arbitrary model structures. Our method allows us to train neural networks with heuristic monotonicity regularizations, and we can gradually increase the regularization magnitude until the learned network is certified monotonic. Compared to prior work, our method does not require human-designed constraints on the weight space and also yields more accurate approximation. Empirical studies on various datasets demonstrate the efficiency of our approach over the state-of-the-art methods, such as Deep Lattice Networks

paragraphs: A monotonic model has a predictable response to selected inputs: changing one in a specified direction cannot make the output move in the opposite direction. Such behavior can help address interpretability, fairness, and generalization concerns. Existing approaches either build monotonicity into restrictive architectures or encourage it during training without providing a proof.

This paper proposes checking monotonicity of general piecewise-linear neural networks by solving a mixed integer linear programming problem. The certification step makes it possible to use flexible model structures and then verify the desired property. Training uses heuristic monotonicity regularization, whose strength can be increased gradually until the resulting network receives a certificate.

The approach separates encouraging monotonic behavior from proving that the trained model has it. It does not require manually designed restrictions on the weight space. The authors report more accurate approximation than prior work and empirical efficiency advantages across several datasets, including comparisons with Deep Lattice Networks. Its guarantee concerns certified monotonicity on selected features; the broader motivation is to make that property available in less restrictive networks.
summary.tldr: Mixed integer optimization certifies monotonicity in piecewise-linear neural networks trained with progressively stronger monotonicity regularization.

title: Certified Monotonic Neural Networks

abstract: Ensemble is a general way of improving the accuracy and stability of learning models, especially for the generalization ability on small datasets. Compared with tree-based methods, relatively less works have been devoted to an in-depth study on effective ensemble design for neural networks. In this paper, we propose a principled ensemble technique by constructing the so-called diversified ensemble layer to combine multiple networks as individual modules. We theoretically show that each individual model in our ensemble layer corresponds to weights in the ensemble layer optimized in different directions. Meanwhile, the devised ensemble layer can be readily integrated into popular neural architectures, including CNNs, RNNs, and GCNs. Extensive experiments are conducted on public tabular datasets, images, and texts. By adopting weight sharing approach, the results show our method can notably improve the accuracy and stability of the original neural networks with ignorable extra time and space overhead.

paragraphs: Combining multiple predictive models can improve accuracy and stability, particularly when training data are limited. This paper focuses on how to design that combination for neural networks. It introduces a diversified ensemble layer that brings multiple networks together as individual modules within a common architecture.

The theoretical analysis shows that each constituent model corresponds to ensemble-layer weights optimized in different directions. This gives the proposed diversity a specific optimization-based interpretation. The layer is designed to fit into several common architecture families, including convolutional, recurrent, and graph convolutional networks, making the ensemble mechanism applicable to different forms of data.

Experiments cover public tabular, image, and text datasets. With weight sharing, the method produces notable improvements in accuracy and stability while adding negligible time and space overhead in the reported results. This combination matters because the practical benefit of an ensemble depends on its cost as well as its predictions. The findings support structured diversity and shared weights as a useful design for efficient neural-network ensembles.
summary.tldr: A diversified ensemble layer combines neural modules optimized in different directions, improving accuracy and stability with negligible reported overhead when weights are shared.

title: The Diversified Ensemble Neural Network

abstract: Meta-learning is a promising strategy for learning to efficiently learn using data gathered from a distribution of tasks. However, the meta-learning literature thus far has focused on the task segmented setting, where at train-time, offline data is assumed to be split according to the underlying task, and at test-time, the algorithms are optimized to learn in a single task. In this work, we enable the application of generic meta-learning algorithms to settings where this task segmentation is unavailable, such as continual online learning with unsegmented time series data. We present meta-learning via online changepoint analysis (MOCA), an approach which augments a meta-learning algorithm with a differentiable Bayesian changepoint detection scheme. The framework allows both training and testing directly on time series data without segmenting it into discrete tasks. We demonstrate the utility of this approach on three nonlinear meta-regression benchmarks as well as two meta-image-classification benchmarks.

paragraphs: Meta-learning aims to learn how to adapt efficiently from experience across tasks. Many approaches assume that training data already comes divided into tasks and that testing involves adapting within one task. A continuous stream does not necessarily provide these boundaries, making that setup awkward for ongoing online learning.

The paper introduces meta-learning via online changepoint analysis, or MOCA. It augments a meta-learning algorithm with a differentiable Bayesian mechanism for detecting changes in the stream. This gives the learning framework a way to reason about changing task structure while processing the observations. Training and testing can both operate directly on time-series data without a supplied segmentation into discrete tasks.

The authors demonstrate the approach on three nonlinear meta-regression benchmarks and two meta-image-classification benchmarks. These evaluations support its usefulness for extending meta-learning to unsegmented data. The central contribution is the combination of adaptation and changepoint reasoning: task organization becomes something the framework handles during learning, reducing its dependence on boundaries prepared in advance.
summary.tldr: MOCA combines meta-learning with differentiable Bayesian changepoint detection to train and adapt on streams without supplied task boundaries.

title: Continuous Meta-Learning without Tasks

abstract: Can we develop visually grounded dialog agents that can efficiently adapt to new tasks without forgetting how to talk to people? Such agents could leverage a larger variety of existing data to generalize to a new task, minimizing expensive data collection and annotation. In this work, we study a setting we call "Dialog without Dialog", which requires agents to develop visually grounded dialog models that can adapt to new tasks without language level supervision. By factorizing intention and language, our model minimizes linguistic drift after fine-tuning for new tasks. We present qualitative results, automated metrics, and human studies that all show our model can adapt to new tasks and maintain language quality. Baselines either fail to perform well at new tasks or experience language drift, becoming unintelligible to humans. Code has been made available at: https://github.com/mcogswell/dialog_without_dialog.

paragraphs: A visual dialogue agent needs to adapt its behavior to a new task while continuing to communicate intelligibly with people. Adaptation can create linguistic drift: the agent’s language changes in ways that undermine human understanding. This paper studies learning visually grounded dialogue from visual question-answering data and adapting to new tasks without language-level supervision.

The model separates intention from language. This factorization gives the system a way to change what it is trying to accomplish while limiting disruption to how it expresses itself. The approach addresses a practical data problem: adapting conversational behavior would be less costly if each new task did not require a fresh collection of language-supervised dialogue examples.

The authors evaluate adaptation through qualitative examples, automated measures, and human studies. All three forms of evidence show that the proposed model can adapt to new tasks while retaining language quality. The compared baselines either perform poorly on the new tasks or drift toward language that people cannot understand. The findings support separating communicative intent from expression as a useful design choice in this setting.
summary.tldr: Separating intention from language helps visual dialogue agents adapt without language-level supervision while preserving human-readable communication.

title: Dialog without Dialog Data: Learning Visual Dialog Agents from VQA Data

abstract: We propose the Canonical 3D Deformer Map, a new representation of the 3D shape of common object categories that can be learned from a collection of 2D images of independent objects. Our method builds in a novel way on concepts from parametric deformation models, non-parametric 3D reconstruction, and canonical embeddings, combining their individual advantages. In particular, it learns to associate each image pixel with a deformation model of the corresponding 3D object point which is canonical, i.e. intrinsic to the identity of the point and shared across objects of the category. The result is a method that, given only sparse 2D supervision at training time, can, at test time, reconstruct the 3D shape and texture of objects from single views, while establishing meaningful dense correspondences between object instances. It also achieves state-of-the-art results in dense 3D reconstruction on public in-the-wild datasets of faces, cars, and birds.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a representation for learning the three-dimensional shapes of an object category from two-dimensional images of different objects. The goal combines reconstruction with correspondence: a model should recover an object’s shape while also recognizing which points have matching identities across different instances of the category.

The Canonical 3D Deformer Map associates each image pixel with a deformation model for its corresponding 3D point. That association is canonical, meaning it is tied to the point’s identity and shared across objects. The representation brings together ideas from parametric deformation models, non-parametric reconstruction, and canonical embeddings, allowing category-wide correspondence and object-specific shape variation to be represented together.

Training requires only sparse two-dimensional supervision. At test time, the method reconstructs shape and texture from a single view and establishes dense correspondences between instances. The authors report state-of-the-art dense reconstruction results on public, in-the-wild datasets of faces, cars, and birds. These results show how shared point identities can support detailed reconstruction even when training supervision is sparse.
summary.tldr: Canonical 3D Deformer Maps learn shared point identities and shape deformations to reconstruct objects from single images with sparse training supervision.

title: Canonical 3D Deformer Maps: Unifying parametric and non-parametric methods for dense weakly-supervised category reconstruction

abstract: In this work we target a learnable output representation that allows continuous, high resolution outputs of arbitrary shape. Recent works represent 3D surfaces implicitly with a Neural Network, thereby breaking previous barriers in resolution, and ability to represent diverse topologies. However, neural implicit representations are limited to closed surfaces, which divide the space into inside and outside. Many real world objects such as walls of a scene scanned by a sensor, clothing, or a car with inner structures are not closed. This constitutes a significant barrier, in terms of data pre-processing (objects need to be artificially closed creating artifacts), and the ability to output open surfaces. In this work, we propose Neural Distance Fields (NDF), a neural network based model which predicts the unsigned distance field for arbitrary 3D shapes given sparse point clouds. NDF represent surfaces at high resolutions as prior implicit models, but do not require closed surface data, and significantly broaden the class of representable shapes in the output. NDF allow to extract the surface as very dense point clouds and as meshes. We also show that NDF allow for surface normal calculation and can be rendered using a slight modification of sphere tracing. We find NDF can be used for multi-target regression (multiple outputs for one input) with techniques that have been exclusively used for rendering in graphics. Experiments on ShapeNet show that NDF, while simple, is the state-of-the art, and allows to reconstruct shapes with inner structures, such as the chairs inside a bus. Notably, we show that NDF are not restricted to 3D shapes, and can approximate more general open surfaces such as curves, manifolds, and functions. Code is available for research at https://virtualhumans.mpi-inf.mpg.de/ndf/.

paragraphs: Many neural implicit surface representations depend on separating inside from outside, which requires closed surfaces. Real scanned scenes and objects can contain open walls, clothing, or internal structures. Artificially closing such surfaces can create artifacts. This paper proposes a representation that avoids requiring that inside–outside distinction.

Neural Distance Fields predict unsigned distance to a surface from sparse point clouds. Because the distance does not encode a side of the surface, the representation accommodates open shapes while retaining continuous, high-resolution outputs. The authors show how to extract dense point clouds and meshes, calculate surface normals, and render the representation with a modified sphere-tracing procedure.

ShapeNet experiments report state-of-the-art performance and demonstrate reconstruction of internal geometry, including chairs inside a bus. The paper also explores multi-target regression using techniques drawn from graphics rendering. Its scope extends beyond three-dimensional objects: the authors show approximation of more general open surfaces, including curves, manifolds, and functions. The contribution broadens the geometry a learned implicit representation can express.
summary.tldr: Neural unsigned distance fields represent high-resolution open surfaces and internal geometry without requiring objects to be artificially closed.

title: Neural Unsigned Distance Fields for Implicit Function Learning

abstract: The problem of finding the unique low dimensional decomposition of a given matrix has been a fundamental and recurrent problem in many areas. In this paper, we study the problem of seeking a unique decomposition of a low-rank matrix $Y\in \mathbb{R}^{p\times n}$ that admits a sparse representation. Specifically, we consider $ Y = AX\in \mathbb{R}^{p\times n}$ where the matrix $A\in \mathbb{R}^{p\times r}$ has full column rank, with $r < \min\{n,p\}$, and the matrix $X\in \mathbb{R}^{r\times n}$ is element-wise sparse. We prove that this sparse decomposition of $Y$ can be uniquely identified by recovering ground-truth $A$ column by column, up to some intrinsic signed permutation. Our approach relies on solving a nonconvex optimization problem constrained over the unit sphere. Our geometric analysis for the nonconvex optimization landscape shows that any {\em strict} local solution is close to the ground truth solution, and can be recovered by a simple data-driven initialization followed with any second-order descent algorithm. At last, we corroborate these theoretical results with numerical experiments

paragraphs: The paper examines when a low-rank matrix can be separated into identifiable underlying factors. It considers a matrix Y expressed as AX, where A has full column rank, the shared rank is smaller than both dimensions of Y, and X is sparse entry by entry. The goal is to recover the underlying sparse decomposition.

The authors prove identification by recovering the columns of A one at a time, up to an intrinsic signed permutation. This qualification allows column order and corresponding signs to remain ambiguous. Their approach solves a nonconvex optimization problem on the unit sphere, so understanding the optimization landscape is central to the recovery argument.

The geometric analysis shows that every strict local solution is close to a ground-truth solution. The authors also establish recovery using a simple data-driven initialization followed by any second-order descent algorithm. Numerical experiments corroborate the theoretical findings. The contribution connects identifiability with an optimization route, while specifically grounding its landscape claim in strict local solutions rather than making an unrestricted statement about every stationary point.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes sparse low-rank factor recovery up to signed permutation using the geometry of a sphere-constrained nonconvex problem.

title: Unique sparse decomposition of low rank matrices

abstract: A common assumption in many domains is that high dimensional data are a smooth nonlinear function of a small number of independent factors. When is it possible to recover the factors from unlabeled data? In the context of deep models this problem is called “disentanglement” and was recently shown to be impossible without additional strong assumptions [17, 19]. In this paper, we show that the assumption of local isometry together with non-Gaussianity of the factors, is sufficient to provably recover disentangled representations from data. We leverage recent advances in deep generative models to construct manifolds of highly realistic images for which the ground truth latent representation is known, and test whether modern and classical methods succeed in recovering the latent factors. For many different manifolds, we find that a spectral method that explicitly optimizes local isometry and non-Gaussianity consistently finds the correct latent factors, while baseline deep autoencoders do not. We propose how to encourage deep autoencoders to find encodings that satisfy local isometry and show that this helps them discover disentangled representations. Overall, our results suggest that in some realistic settings, unsupervised disentanglement is provably possible, without any domain-specific assumptions.

paragraphs: Disentanglement aims to recover the independent factors underlying high-dimensional observations without labeled examples of those factors. Such recovery is impossible in general without additional assumptions. This paper establishes a sufficient combination: local isometry, which preserves local geometry, together with non-Gaussian latent factors. These conditions make provable recovery possible in the studied setting.

The authors use deep generative models to construct manifolds of realistic images with known latent representations. That known structure lets them test whether learning methods recover the underlying factors. Across many of these manifolds, a spectral method explicitly optimizing local isometry and non-Gaussianity consistently recovers the factors, while the baseline deep autoencoders do not.

The paper then proposes encouraging deep autoencoders to satisfy local isometry and shows that this helps them discover disentangled representations. The findings identify structural assumptions that can enable recovery without domain-specific assumptions. They do not establish that those conditions are necessary or that arbitrary unlabeled data are disentangleable; the positive conclusion is that recovery is provably possible in some realistic settings.
summary.tldr: Local isometry and non-Gaussian factors are sufficient for provable unsupervised disentanglement in the studied setting.

title: When Is Unsupervised Disentanglement Possible?

abstract: Effectively predicting molecular interactions has the potential to accelerate molecular dynamics by multiple orders of magnitude and thus revolutionize chemical simulations. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have recently shown great successes for this task, overtaking classical methods based on fixed molecular kernels. However, they still appear very limited from a theoretical perspective, since regular GNNs cannot distinguish certain types of graphs. In this work we close this gap between theory and practice. We show that GNNs with directed edge embeddings and two-hop message passing are indeed universal approximators for predictions that are invariant to translation, and equivariant to permutation and rotation. We then leverage these insights and multiple structural improvements to propose the geometric message passing neural network (GemNet). We demonstrate the benefits of the proposed changes in multiple ablation studies. GemNet outperforms previous models on the COLL, MD17, and OC20 datasets by 34%, 41%, and 20%, respectively, and performs especially well on the most challenging molecules. Our implementation is available online.
originalAbstract: Effectively predicting molecular interactions has the potential to accelerate molecular dynamics by multiple orders of magnitude and thus revolutionize chemical simulations. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have recently shown great successes for this task, overtaking classical methods based on fixed molecular kernels. However, they still appear very limited from a theoretical perspective, since regular GNNs cannot distinguish certain types of graphs. In this work we close this gap between theory and practice. We show that GNNs with directed edge embeddings and two-hop message passing are indeed universal approximators for predictions that are invariant to translation, and equivariant to permutation and rotation. We then leverage these insights and multiple structural improvements to propose the geometric message passing neural network (GemNet). We demonstrate the benefits of the proposed changes in multiple ablation studies. GemNet outperforms previous models on the COLL, MD17, and OC20 datasets by 34%, 41%, and 20%, respectively, and performs especially well on the most challenging molecules. Our implementation is available online.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks have become effective predictors of molecular interactions, yet ordinary graph networks have known limits in distinguishing some structures. This paper addresses the resulting gap between practical success and theoretical expressiveness. It asks which architectural ingredients allow molecular predictions to represent the geometric relationships and symmetries required by the task.

The authors show that directed edge embeddings combined with two-hop message passing give universal approximation for predictions that are translation-invariant and permutation- and rotation-equivariant. In plain terms, the represented predictions can respect moving a molecule, reordering its atoms, and rotating it. These insights, together with further structural improvements, lead to the geometric message passing network GemNet.

Ablation studies examine the benefits of the proposed changes. GemNet reports improvements over previous models of 34%, 41%, and 20% on COLL, MD17, and OC20, respectively, with especially strong performance on challenging molecules. The work connects an expressiveness result to an architecture that also demonstrates substantial empirical gains in molecular prediction.
summary.tldr: GemNet combines a universality result for directional molecular networks with architectural changes that improve molecular prediction.

title: GemNet: Universal Directional Graph Neural Networks for Molecules

abstract: We revisit first-order optimization under local information constraints such as local privacy, gradient quantization, and computational constraints limiting access to a few coordinates of the gradient. In this setting, the optimization algorithm is not allowed to directly access the complete output of the gradient oracle, but only gets limited information about it subject to the local information constraints. We study the role of adaptivity in processing the gradient output to obtain this limited information from it, and obtain tight or nearly tight bounds for both convex and strongly convex optimization when adaptive gradient processing is allowed.

paragraphs: Gradient-based optimization usually relies on information about how an objective changes with its parameters. This paper studies a constrained version of that process: the optimizer cannot directly inspect the complete output of its gradient oracle. Instead, it receives only information that survives a locally imposed restriction on access or processing.

The restrictions include local privacy requirements, gradient quantization, and computational limits that allow access to only a few gradient coordinates. These examples differ in motivation, but all limit what the optimizer can learn from a gradient. The paper asks about adaptivity in processing that output: whether the way restricted information is obtained can change as optimization proceeds.

The authors establish tight or nearly tight bounds for convex and strongly convex optimization when adaptive processing is permitted. Such bounds characterize the achievable limits of optimization under the information restrictions being studied. The contribution makes adaptivity part of the theoretical analysis instead of assuming a fixed processing procedure. The abstract does not assert that adaptive processing always helps; it reports a characterization of performance with adaptivity allowed.
summary.tldr: The paper derives tight or nearly tight optimization bounds when gradients are accessed through adaptive, information-limited processing.

title: Information-constrained optimization: can adaptive processing of gradients help?

abstract: We propose the first general PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds for adversarial robustness, that estimate, at test time, how much a model will be invariant to imperceptible perturbations in the input. Instead of deriving a worst-case analysis of the risk of a hypothesis over all the possible perturbations, we leverage the PAC-Bayesian framework to bound the averaged risk on the perturbations for majority votes (over the whole class of hypotheses). Our theoretically founded analysis has the advantage to provide general bounds (i) that are valid for any kind of attacks (i.e., the adversarial attacks), (ii) that are tight thanks to the PAC-Bayesian framework, (iii) that can be directly minimized during the learning phase to obtain a robust model on different attacks at test time.
