paragraphs: Adversarial robustness concerns whether a model remains reliable when its input is changed in small, hard-to-notice ways. This paper develops PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds for that problem: theoretical tools for relating robustness learned during training to behavior on unseen inputs. Its focus is on predictions formed by majority votes across a class of hypotheses.

The central choice is to bound risk averaged over perturbations rather than the risk of the single worst possible perturbation. This distinction determines what the guarantee means. It describes an aggregate robustness quantity for the voting predictor; it does not establish that every permitted perturbation will leave every prediction unchanged.

The authors present their bounds as general across attack types and tight through the PAC-Bayesian framework. They also make the bounds usable as training objectives, allowing learning to directly target the quantity being controlled. The contribution therefore connects a theoretical account of robustness with a way to train models intended to withstand different attacks at test time.
summary.tldr: The paper develops PAC-Bayesian bounds on perturbation-averaged adversarial risk for majority-vote predictors that can also guide training.

title: A PAC-Bayes Analysis of Adversarial Robustness

abstract: We present a method for differentiable simulation of soft articulated bodies. Our work enables the integration of differentiable physical dynamics into gradient-based pipelines. We develop a top-down matrix assembly algorithm within Projective Dynamics and derive a generalized dry friction model for soft continuum using a new matrix splitting strategy. We derive a differentiable control framework for soft articulated bodies driven by muscles, joint torques, or pneumatic tubes. The experiments demonstrate that our designs make soft body simulation more stable and realistic compared to other frameworks. Our method accelerates the solution of system identification problems by more than an order of magnitude, and enables efficient gradient-based learning of motion control with soft robots.

paragraphs: Soft articulated bodies combine deformation with coordinated motion, making their physical behavior important for both simulation and control. This paper develops a differentiable simulator for such systems. Differentiability allows simulated dynamics to participate in gradient-based optimization, so a learning or estimation procedure can use how outcomes change when its inputs or parameters change.

The method introduces a top-down matrix assembly algorithm within Projective Dynamics. It also develops a generalized dry-friction model for soft continua using a new matrix splitting strategy. These simulation components support a differentiable control framework for bodies actuated through muscles, joint torques, or pneumatic tubes, covering several ways to drive a soft articulated system.

Experiments report more stable and realistic soft-body simulation than other frameworks. The method also accelerates system identification, the estimation of system properties, by more than an order of magnitude. It enables efficient gradient-based learning of soft-robot motion control. The results connect improvements in physical simulation to faster estimation and usable control learning within the same differentiable framework.
summary.tldr: A differentiable soft-body simulator improves physical simulation and supports faster system identification and gradient-based motion control.

title: Differentiable Simulation of Soft Multi-body Systems

abstract: In the fixed budget thresholding bandit problem, an algorithm sequentially allocates a budgeted number of samples to different distributions. It then predicts whether the mean of each distribution is larger or lower than a given threshold. We introduce a large family of algorithms (containing most existing relevant ones), inspired by the Frank-Wolfe algorithm, and provide a thorough yet generic analysis of their performance. This allowed us to construct new explicit algorithms, for a broad class of problems, whose losses are within a small constant factor of the non-adaptive oracle ones. Quite interestingly, we observed that adaptive methodsempirically greatly out-perform non-adaptive oracles, an uncommon behavior in standard online learning settings, such as regret minimization. We explain this surprising phenomenon on an insightful toy problem.

paragraphs: In a fixed-budget thresholding bandit problem, a learner has a limited number of samples to distribute among several unknown distributions. After sampling, it must decide whether each distribution’s mean lies above or below a specified threshold. The allocation matters because the objective is to make as few classification errors as possible with the available observations.

The authors introduce a broad family of allocation algorithms inspired by Frank-Wolfe optimization. The family includes most relevant existing methods and supports a common performance analysis. This analysis leads to explicit new algorithms whose losses are within a small constant factor of those of non-adaptive oracles for a broad class of problems.

The experiments reveal a further effect: adaptive methods can substantially outperform non-adaptive oracles. An oracle benchmark that fixes its allocation does not capture every advantage of responding to observations as they arrive. The paper explains this behavior through a toy problem. Its contribution therefore includes both broadly applicable guarantees and an explanation of why adaptation can be especially valuable for minimizing thresholding errors.
summary.tldr: A unified analysis yields thresholding bandit algorithms with near-oracle guarantees and explains observed advantages of adaptive sampling.

title: Online Sign Identification: Minimization of the Number of Errors in Thresholding Bandits

abstract: The memorization effect of deep neural network (DNN) plays a pivotal role in many state-of-the-art label-noise learning methods. To exploit this property, the early stopping trick, which stops the optimization at the early stage of training, is usually adopted. Current methods generally decide the early stopping point by considering a DNN as a whole. However, a DNN can be considered as a composition of a series of layers, and we find that the latter layers in a DNN are much more sensitive to label noise, while their former counterparts are quite robust. Therefore, selecting a stopping point for the whole network may make different DNN layers antagonistically affect each other, thus degrading the final performance. In this paper, we propose to separate a DNN into different parts and progressively train them to address this problem. Instead of the early stopping which trains a whole DNN all at once, we initially train former DNN layers by optimizing the DNN with a relatively large number of epochs. During training, we progressively train the latter DNN layers by using a smaller number of epochs with the preceding layers fixed to counteract the impact of noisy labels. We term the proposed method as progressive early stopping (PES). Despite its simplicity, compared with the traditional early stopping, PES can help to obtain more promising and stable results. Furthermore, by combining PES with existing approaches on noisy label training, we achieve state-of-the-art performance on image classification benchmarks. The code is made public at https://github.com/tmllab/PES.

paragraphs: Early stopping is often used when training labels contain errors, drawing on how deep networks memorize data during training. Usually, one stopping point is chosen for the whole network. This paper finds that layers respond differently to label noise: later layers are much more sensitive, while earlier layers are comparatively robust.

Progressive early stopping uses that difference to organize training in stages. Earlier layers receive relatively many training epochs. Later layers are then trained progressively for fewer epochs while preceding layers remain fixed. This gives the different parts of the network different amounts of training exposure instead of requiring one stopping decision to serve them all.

The authors report that the method can produce better and more stable results than traditional early stopping. Combined with existing methods for learning from noisy labels, it achieves state-of-the-art performance on image-classification benchmarks. The findings connect a layer-level observation about noise sensitivity to a simple training procedure, showing why treating the network as a single unit can be an unhelpful constraint.
summary.tldr: Progressive early stopping trains noise-sensitive later layers for fewer epochs while giving more robust earlier layers longer training.

title: Understanding and Improving Early Stopping for Learning with Noisy Labels

abstract: Learning representations of stochastic processes is an emerging problem in machine learning with applications from meta-learning to physical object models to time series. Typical methods rely on exact reconstruction of observations, but this approach breaks down as observations become high-dimensional or noise distributions become complex. To address this, we propose a unifying framework for learning contrastive representations of stochastic processes (CReSP) that does away with exact reconstruction. We dissect potential use cases for stochastic process representations, and propose methods that accommodate each. Empirically, we show that our methods are effective for learning representations of periodic functions, 3D objects and dynamical processes. Our methods tolerate noisy high-dimensional observations better than traditional approaches, and the learned representations transfer to a range of downstream tasks.

paragraphs: Learning a representation of a stochastic process means summarizing patterns in observations that can vary randomly. The paper considers this problem across settings such as time series, physical-object models, and meta-learning. A common strategy requires reconstructing observations exactly, but that becomes difficult when observations are high-dimensional or their noise has a complicated distribution.

The proposed framework, CReSP, learns contrastive representations without requiring exact reconstruction. This changes the learning requirement: useful process representations need not reproduce every detail of each observation. The authors examine different uses for process representations and develop methods suited to those uses, organizing them within a common framework.

Experiments demonstrate representation learning for periodic functions, three-dimensional objects, and dynamical processes. The methods cope better with noisy, high-dimensional observations than the traditional approaches considered, and their representations transfer to several downstream tasks. These findings support moving away from exact observation reconstruction when the goal is to capture reusable information about a process. The contribution includes both that general formulation and empirical evidence across different kinds of observations.
summary.tldr: CReSP learns transferable stochastic-process representations through contrastive learning, avoiding exact reconstruction of noisy, high-dimensional observations.

title: On Contrastive Representations of Stochastic Processes

abstract: The sample compressibility of concept classes plays an important role in learning theory, as a sufficient condition for PAC learnability, and more recently as an avenue for robust generalisation in adaptive data analysis. Whether compression schemes of size $O(d)$ must necessarily exist for all classes of VC dimension $d$ is unknown, but conjectured to be true by Warmuth. Recently Chalopin, Chepoi, Moran, and Warmuth (2018) gave a beautiful unlabelled sample compression scheme of size VC dimension for all maximum classes: classes that meet the Sauer-Shelah-Perles Lemma with equality. They also offered a counterexample to compression schemes based on a promising approach known as corner peeling. In this paper we simplify and extend their proof technique to deal with so-called extremal classes of VC dimension $d$ which contain maximum classes of VC dimension $d-1$. A criterion is given which would imply that all extremal classes admit unlabelled compression schemes of size $d$. We also prove that all intersection-closed classes with VC dimension $d$ admit unlabelled compression schemes of size at most $11d$.

paragraphs: Sample compression asks how a learning sample can be represented using a small selection of its examples. Such schemes provide a sufficient condition for PAC learnability and also matter for robust generalization in adaptive data analysis. A central open conjecture asks whether every concept class of VC dimension d admits compression whose size grows only linearly with d.

The paper advances this question for particular families rather than resolving the general conjecture. It simplifies and extends a previous proof technique for maximum classes to certain extremal classes: those of VC dimension d that contain maximum classes of dimension d minus one. It also supplies a criterion that, if satisfied, would imply unlabelled compression schemes of size d for all extremal classes.

A separate result establishes that every intersection-closed class of VC dimension d has an unlabelled compression scheme of size at most 11d. This gives a concrete linear bound for that family. The contributions distinguish a proved guarantee for intersection-closed classes from a conditional route toward a broader result for extremal classes.
summary.tldr: The paper proves an 11d unlabelled compression bound for intersection-closed classes and advances compression results for extremal classes.

title: Unlabelled Sample Compression Schemes for Intersection-Closed Classes and Extremal Classes

abstract: Hundreds of defenses have been proposed to make deep neural networks robust against minimal (adversarial) input perturbations. However, only a handful of these defenses held up their claims because correctly evaluating robustness is extremely challenging: Weak attacks often fail to find adversarial examples even if they unknowingly exist, thereby making a vulnerable network look robust. In this paper, we propose a test to identify weak attacks and, thus, weak defense evaluations. Our test slightly modifies a neural network to guarantee the existence of an adversarial example for every sample. Consequentially, any correct attack must succeed in breaking this modified network. For eleven out of thirteen previously-published defenses, the original evaluation of the defense fails our test, while stronger attacks that break these defenses pass it. We hope that attack unit tests - such as ours - will be a major component in future robustness evaluations and increase confidence in an empirical field that is currently riddled with skepticism.

paragraphs: A failed adversarial attack does not necessarily mean a neural network is robust. The attack may simply be too weak to find a small input change that causes an error. This makes defense evaluation difficult: an ineffective evaluation procedure can make a vulnerable model appear secure. The paper proposes a test aimed directly at detecting such weak attacks.

The test slightly modifies a network so that an adversarial example is guaranteed to exist for every sample. This creates a controlled situation in which the attack should succeed. If it cannot break the modified network, its failure exposes a weakness in the attack procedure, rather than providing evidence that adversarial examples are absent.

For eleven of thirteen previously published defenses, the original evaluation fails this test. Stronger attacks that break those defenses pass it. These results support treating attacks themselves as objects that need validation. The proposed unit test provides a concrete check on evaluation strength and a way to increase confidence in empirical robustness assessments.
summary.tldr: A test plants guaranteed adversarial examples to reveal attacks that are too weak to support reliable robustness evaluations.

title: Increasing Confidence in Adversarial Robustness Evaluations

abstract: We consider imitation learning problems where the learner's ability to mimic the expert increases throughout the course of an episode as more information is revealed. One example of this is when the expert has access to privileged information: while the learner might not be able to accurately reproduce expert behavior early on in an episode, by considering the entire history of states and actions, they might be able to eventually identify the hidden context and act as the expert would. We prove that on-policy imitation learning algorithms (with or without access to a queryable expert) are better equipped to handle these sorts of asymptotically realizable problems than off-policy methods. This is because on-policy algorithms provably learn to recover from their initially suboptimal actions, while off-policy methods treat their suboptimal past actions as though they came from the expert. This often manifests as a latching behavior: a naive repetition of past actions. We conduct experiments in a toy bandit domain that show that there exist sharp phase transitions of whether off-policy approaches are able to match expert performance asymptotically, in contrast to the uniformly good performance of on-policy approaches. We demonstrate that on several continuous control tasks, on-policy approaches are able to use history to identify the context while off-policy approaches actually perform worse when given access to history.

paragraphs: An imitation learner may initially lack information available to its expert. As an episode unfolds, its history of states and actions may reveal the hidden context, eventually allowing it to behave like the expert. This paper studies such asymptotically realizable problems, where the ability to imitate improves as more information becomes available.

The authors prove that on-policy methods are better equipped for this setting, with or without a queryable expert. These methods learn to recover from their own initially suboptimal actions. Off-policy methods instead treat those past actions as though the expert had taken them, which can cause latching: repeatedly choosing earlier actions rather than correcting course as context becomes clearer.

Toy bandit experiments reveal sharp transitions in whether off-policy methods eventually match expert performance, while on-policy methods perform consistently well in that domain. In several continuous-control tasks, on-policy approaches use history to infer context, whereas giving history to off-policy approaches worsens performance. The findings show why access to more history helps only when training handles the learner's own mistakes appropriately.
summary.tldr: When hidden context becomes identifiable over time, on-policy imitation can learn recovery while off-policy methods may latch onto earlier mistakes.

title: Sequence Model Imitation Learning with Unobserved Contexts

abstract: Non-autoregressive Transformer(NAT) significantly accelerates the inference of neural machine translation. However, conventional NAT models suffer from limited expression power and performance degradation compared to autoregressive (AT) models due to the assumption of conditional independence among target tokens. To address these limitations, we propose a novel approach called PCFG-NAT, which leverages a specially designed Probabilistic Context-Free Grammar (PCFG) to enhance the ability of NAT models to capture complex dependencies among output tokens. Experimental results on major machine translation benchmarks demonstrate that PCFG-NAT further narrows the gap in translation quality between NAT and AT models. Moreover, PCFG-NAT facilitates a deeper understanding of the generated sentences, addressing the lack of satisfactory explainability in neural machine translation. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/ictnlp/PCFG-NAT.

paragraphs: Non-autoregressive translation accelerates inference, but conventional models assume that target tokens are conditionally independent. That assumption limits how they represent relationships among the words in a translation and contributes to a quality gap relative to autoregressive models. The paper targets this loss of expressive power in the output model.

PCFG-NAT introduces a specially designed probabilistic context-free grammar to represent more complex dependencies among output tokens. The grammar supplies a structured account of how sentence components relate, allowing the translation model to capture connections that independent token predictions struggle to express. The approach therefore addresses the dependency assumption at the center of the stated problem.

Experiments on major translation benchmarks show that PCFG-NAT further narrows the quality gap between non-autoregressive and autoregressive systems. The authors also describe the grammatical structure as helping explain generated sentences, addressing interpretability alongside translation quality. The reported conclusion is an improvement in that tradeoff, rather than a claim that the remaining quality gap has disappeared.
summary.tldr: PCFG-NAT adds probabilistic grammar structure to non-autoregressive translation to capture token dependencies and narrow the translation-quality gap.

title: Non-autoregressive Machine Translation with Probabilistic Context-free Grammar

abstract: Learning with noisy labels (LNL) poses a significant challenge in training a well-generalized model while avoiding overfitting to corrupted labels.Recent advances have achieved impressive performance by identifying clean labels and correcting corrupted labels for training.However, the current approaches rely heavily on the model’s predictions and evaluate each sample independently without considering either the global or local structure of the sample distribution.These limitations typically result in a suboptimal solution for the identification and correction processes, which eventually leads to models overfitting to incorrect labels.In this paper, we propose a novel optimal transport (OT) formulation, called Curriculum and Structure-aware Optimal Transport (CSOT). CSOT concurrently considers the inter- and intra-distribution structure of the samples to construct a robust denoising and relabeling allocator.During the training process, the allocator incrementally assigns reliable labels to a fraction of the samples with the highest confidence. These labels have both global discriminability and local coherence.Notably, CSOT is a new OT formulation with a nonconvex objective function and curriculum constraints, so it is not directly compatible with classical OT solvers. Here, we develop a lightspeed computational method that involves a scaling iteration within a generalized conditional gradient framework to solve CSOT efficiently.Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of our method over the current state-of-the-arts in LNL.

paragraphs: Training with incorrect labels requires deciding which labels to trust and which to replace. The paper argues that evaluating samples independently, largely through a model’s own predictions, overlooks useful relationships in the data. Those omissions can produce poor corrections and cause the model to keep learning from mistaken labels.

Curriculum and Structure-aware Optimal Transport, or CSOT, treats label allocation as a coordinated problem. Its formulation considers relationships within and between distributions, seeking labels that separate groups globally while remaining coherent locally. During training, the allocator progressively assigns reliable labels to a fraction of samples with the highest confidence, rather than correcting every sample at once.

The resulting optimization problem has a nonconvex objective and curriculum constraints, so standard optimal transport solvers do not apply directly. The authors develop an efficient solution using scaling iterations inside a generalized conditional gradient framework. Their experiments report stronger noisy-label learning performance than the compared state-of-the-art methods, supporting the value of combining structural information with gradual label assignment.
summary.tldr: CSOT uses data relationships and progressive label assignment to improve learning from corrupted labels in the reported experiments.

title: CSOT: Curriculum and Structure-Aware Optimal Transport for Learning with Noisy Labels

abstract: Personalized federated learning (PFL) has been widely investigated to address the challenge of data heterogeneity, especially when a single generic model is inadequate in satisfying the diverse performance requirements of local clients simultaneously. Existing PFL methods are inherently based on the idea that the relations between the generic global and personalized local models are captured by the similarity of model weights. Such a similarity is primarily based on either partitioning the model architecture into generic versus personalized components or modeling client relationships via model weights. To better capture similar (yet distinct) generic versus personalized model representations, we propose $\textit{spectral distillation}$, a novel distillation method based on model spectrum information. Building upon spectral distillation, we also introduce a co-distillation framework that establishes a two-way bridge between generic and personalized model training. Moreover, to utilize the local idle time in conventional PFL, we propose a wait-free local training protocol. Through extensive experiments on multiple datasets over diverse heterogeneous data settings, we demonstrate the outperformance and efficacy of our proposed spectral co-distillation method, as well as our wait-free training protocol.

abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of planning in Minecraft, a popular, democratized yet challenging open-ended environment for developing multi-task embodied agents. We've found two primary challenges of empowering such agents with planning: 1) planning in an open-ended world like Minecraft requires precise and multi-step reasoning due to the long-term nature of the tasks, and 2) as vanilla planners do not consider the achievability of the current agent when ordering parallel sub-goals within a complicated plan, the resulting plan could be inefficient. To this end, we propose ``$\underline{D}$escribe, $\underline{E}$xplain, $\underline{P}$lan and $\underline{S}$elect'' ($\textbf{DEPS}$), an interactive planning approach based on Large Language Models (LLMs). Our approach helps with better error correction from the feedback during the long-haul planning, while also bringing the sense of proximity via goal $\textbf{Selector}$, a learnable module that ranks parallel sub-goals based on the estimated steps of completion and improves the original plan accordingly. Our experiments mark the milestone of the first zero-shot multi-task agent that can robustly accomplish 70+ Minecraft tasks and nearly double the overall performances. Further testing reveals our method's general effectiveness in popularly adopted non-open-ended domains as well (i.e., ALFWorld and tabletop manipulation). The ablation and exploratory studies detail how our design beats the counterparts and provide a promising update on the $\texttt{ObtainDiamond}$ grand challenge with our approach.

This paper introduces DEPS, short for Describe, Explain, Plan and Select, to address both difficulties through an interactive planning approach based on large language models.

DEPS uses feedback during execution to improve error correction over long tasks. It also includes a learned goal Selector that ranks parallel subgoals by their estimated number of steps to completion. This gives the planner a way to adjust the ordering of goals according to their estimated proximity for the agent.

The authors report a zero-shot multitask agent that robustly completes more than 70 Minecraft tasks and nearly doubles overall performance in their experiments. Further evaluations show effectiveness in ALFWorld and tabletop manipulation. Ablation and exploratory studies examine the design and progress on ObtainDiamond. Together, the findings support combining feedback-driven plan revision with a learned estimate of which subgoals are more immediately achievable.
summary.tldr: DEPS combines feedback-based LLM planning with learned subgoal ordering to improve agents’ performance on long, multistep tasks.

title: Describe, Explain, Plan and Select: Interactive Planning with LLMs Enables Open-World Multi-Task Agents

abstract: Recent works have shown that line search methods can speed up Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) and Adam in modern over-parameterized settings. However, existing line searches may take steps that are smaller than necessary since they require a monotone decrease of the (mini-)batch objective function. We explore nonmonotone line search methods to relax this condition and possibly accept larger step sizes. Despite the lack of a monotonic decrease, we prove the same fast rates of convergence as in the monotone case. Our experiments show that nonmonotone methods improve the speed of convergence and generalization properties of SGD/Adam even beyond the previous monotone line searches. We propose a POlyak NOnmonotone Stochastic (PoNoS) method, obtained by combining a nonmonotone line search with a Polyak initial step size. Furthermore, we develop a new resetting technique that in the majority of the iterations reduces the amount of backtracks to zero while still maintaining a large initial step size. To the best of our knowledge, a first runtime comparison shows that the epoch-wise advantage of line-search-based methods gets reflected in the overall computational time.

paragraphs: Line search adjusts an optimizer's step size by checking candidate updates. Requiring every accepted step to decrease the current batch objective can make those steps unnecessarily small. This paper studies relaxing that requirement in over-parameterized models, allowing nonmonotone progress so that larger updates may be accepted.

The authors prove convergence rates matching the fast rates of monotone methods despite removing the requirement of consistent objective decrease. They introduce PoNoS, which combines a nonmonotone line search with a Polyak initial step size. A resetting technique further reduces the need to repeatedly shrink candidate steps, eliminating backtracking in most iterations while preserving a large initial step size.

Experiments report faster convergence and improved generalization for SGD and Adam compared with earlier monotone line searches. A runtime comparison also shows that improvements measured across training epochs carry over to overall computation time. This matters because accepting better steps is useful in practice only when the work required to select them does not erase the training gains.
summary.tldr: Nonmonotone stochastic line search permits larger steps, preserves fast convergence guarantees, and improves training speed in the reported experiments.

title: Don't be so Monotone: Relaxing Stochastic Line Search in Over-Parameterized Models

abstract: This paper proposes a method for hiding the least-important samples during the training of deep neural networks to increase efficiency, i.e., to reduce the cost of training. Using information about the loss and prediction confidence during training, we adaptively find samples to exclude in a given epoch based on their contribution to the overall learning process, without significantly degrading accuracy. We explore the converge properties when accounting for the reduction in the number of SGD updates. Empirical results on various large-scale datasets and models used directly in image classification and segmentation show that while the with-replacement importance sampling algorithm performs poorly on large datasets, our method can reduce total training time by up to 22\% impacting accuracy only by 0.4\% compared to the baseline.

paragraphs: Training a neural network repeatedly processes examples, but those examples need not contribute equally at every stage. KAKURENBO reduces training cost by temporarily hiding samples judged least important to the current learning process. Its selection changes during training, allowing the set of examples used in an epoch to reflect the model's evolving needs.

The method uses sample losses and prediction confidence to decide which examples to exclude. Skipping examples reduces the number of stochastic gradient updates, so the paper also examines convergence properties while accounting for that reduction. The aim is to save actual training work while avoiding a significant deterioration in predictive accuracy.

Experiments use large-scale datasets and models for image classification and segmentation. The authors report training-time reductions of up to 22%, with an accuracy impact of only 0.4% relative to the baseline. They also find that a with-replacement importance sampling algorithm performs poorly on large datasets. These results support adaptive sample omission as a practical way to trade a small reported accuracy change for lower training cost.
summary.tldr: KAKURENBO adaptively skips low-importance training samples, reducing training time by up to 22% with a reported 0.4% accuracy impact.

title: KAKURENBO: Adaptively Hiding Samples in Deep Neural Network Training

abstract: The structure of protein-protein complexes is critical for understanding binding dynamics, biological mechanisms, and intervention strategies. Rigid protein docking, a fundamental problem in this field, aims to predict the 3D structure of complexes from their unbound states without conformational changes. In this scenario, we have access to two types of valuable information: sequence-modal information, such as coevolutionary data obtained from multiple sequence alignments, and structure-modal information, including the 3D conformations of rigid structures. However, existing docking methods typically utilize single-modal information, resulting in suboptimal predictions. In this paper, we propose xTrimoBiDock (or BiDock for short), a novel rigid docking model that effectively integrates sequence- and structure-modal information through bi-level optimization. Specifically, a cross-modal transformer combines multimodal information to predict an inter-protein distance map. To achieve rigid docking, the roto-translation transformation is optimized to align the docked pose with the predicted distance map. In order to tackle this bi-level optimization problem, we unroll the gradient descent of the inner loop and further derive a better initialization for roto-translation transformation based on spectral estimation. Compared to baselines, BiDock achieves a promising result of a maximum 234% relative improvement in challenging antibody-antigen docking problem.

paragraphs: Rigid protein docking predicts a complex from unbound structures without allowing conformational changes. Both sequence-derived coevolutionary information and existing three-dimensional geometry can help, but single-modality methods do not fully combine them. BiDock integrates those information sources within a bilevel optimization framework.

A cross-modal transformer predicts an inter-protein distance map. An inner optimization then selects a rotation and translation that align the rigidly docked pose with that map. The authors differentiate through unrolled gradient descent and use spectral estimation to improve pose initialization.

On challenging antibody-antigen docking, the reported maximum relative improvement over baselines is 234%. The abstract does not specify the corresponding metric or absolute performance, so that number should not be interpreted as a universal accuracy gain. The contribution concerns rigid docking specifically and does not establish equivalent performance when substantial conformational rearrangements are required.
summary.tldr: BiDock combines protein sequence and structure information with differentiable rigid-pose optimization.

title: Injecting Multimodal Information into Rigid Protein Docking via Bi-level Optimization

abstract: We present the first framework to solve linear inverse problems leveraging pre-trained \textit{latent} diffusion models. Previously proposed algorithms (such as DPS and DDRM) only apply to \textit{pixel-space} diffusion models. We theoretically analyze our algorithm showing provable sample recovery in a linear model setting. The algorithmic insight obtained from our analysis extends to more general settings often considered in practice. Experimentally, we outperform previously proposed posterior sampling algorithms in a wide variety of problems including random inpainting, block inpainting, denoising, deblurring, destriping, and super-resolution.

paragraphs: Linear inverse problems involve recovering an underlying signal from measurements that have altered or removed information. This paper presents a framework for solving such problems using pretrained latent diffusion models. Its distinction is operating with models that generate through a latent representation, while earlier posterior-sampling algorithms such as DPS and DDRM apply to pixel-space diffusion models.

The authors theoretically analyze their algorithm and prove sample recovery in a linear model setting. The analysis also provides an algorithmic insight that they extend to more general settings encountered in practice. These are separate levels of support: the recovery guarantee concerns the stated linear setting, while the broader application follows from extending the method’s insight.

Experiments cover random and block inpainting, denoising, deblurring, destriping, and super-resolution. Across the reported range of problems, the method outperforms previously proposed posterior-sampling algorithms. The contribution brings pretrained latent diffusion models into this recovery framework and combines a restricted theoretical guarantee with empirical evidence across several forms of image restoration.
summary.tldr: The paper enables posterior sampling with latent diffusion models, proving recovery in a linear setting and reporting improvements across image-restoration tasks.

title: Solving Linear Inverse Problems Provably via Posterior Sampling with Latent Diffusion Models

abstract: This paper focuses on supervised and unsupervised online label shift,where the class marginals $Q(y)$ variesbut the class-conditionals $Q(x|y)$ remain invariant. In the unsupervised setting, our goal is to adapt a learner, trained on some offline labeled data, to changing label distributions given unlabeled online data. In the supervised setting, we must both learn a classifier and adapt to the dynamically evolving class marginals given only labeled online data. We develop novel algorithms that reduce the adaptation problem to online regression and guarantee optimal dynamic regret without any prior knowledge of the extent of drift in the label distribution. Our solution is based on bootstrapping the estimates of *online regression oracles* that track the drifting proportions. Experiments across numerous simulated and real-world online label shift scenarios demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed approaches, often achieving 1-3% improvement in accuracy while being sample and computationally efficient. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/Anon-djiwh/OnlineLabelShift

That invariant class-conditional distribution is central to the problem: the changing quantity is how common each class is, rather than how examples of a class are distributed.

The authors consider two settings. In the unsupervised setting, a classifier trained on offline labeled data adapts using unlabeled online observations. In the supervised setting, labeled online data must support both classifier learning and adaptation. Their algorithms reduce adaptation to online regression, building on estimates from regression procedures that track changing class proportions.

The methods guarantee optimal dynamic regret without advance knowledge of how much the label distribution will drift. This gives a theoretical characterization of performance while adapting to change. Experiments on simulated and real-world label-shift scenarios show superior performance, often with accuracy improvements of 1–3%, while remaining efficient in data and computation. The results connect a formal adaptation guarantee with practical tracking of changing class frequencies.
summary.tldr: Online regression-based algorithms adapt to changing class frequencies with optimal dynamic regret and no advance knowledge of drift.

title: Online Label Shift: Optimal Dynamic Regret meets Practical Algorithms

abstract: Contrastive learning has recently emerged as a promising approach for learning data representations that discover and disentangle the explanatory factors of the data.Previous analyses of such approaches have largely focused on individual contrastive losses, such as noise-contrastive estimation (NCE) and InfoNCE, and rely on specific assumptions about the data generating process.This paper extends the theoretical guarantees for disentanglement to a broader family of contrastive methods, while also relaxing the assumptions about the data distribution.Specifically, we prove identifiability of the true latents for four contrastive losses studied in this paper, without imposing common independence assumptions.The theoretical findings are validated on several benchmark datasets.Finally, practical limitations of these methods are also investigated.
originalAbstract: Contrastive learning has recently emerged as a promising approach for learning data representations that discover and disentangle the explanatory factors of the data.Previous analyses of such approaches have largely focused on individual contrastive losses, such as noise-contrastive estimation (NCE) and InfoNCE, and rely on specific assumptions about the data generating process.This paper extends the theoretical guarantees for disentanglement to a broader family of contrastive methods, while also relaxing the assumptions about the data distribution.Specifically, we prove identifiability of the true latents for four contrastive losses studied in this paper, without imposing common independence assumptions.The theoretical findings are validated on several benchmark datasets.Finally, practical limitations of these methods are also investigated.

paragraphs: Disentangled representations aim to separate the underlying factors that explain observed data. Contrastive learning has shown promise for discovering those factors, but earlier theoretical analyses often treated individual losses separately and relied on particular assumptions about data generation. This paper seeks a broader account of when these methods can recover the underlying latent structure.

The authors establish identifiability results for four contrastive losses. Identifiability concerns whether the true latent factors can be determined within the theoretical setup, rather than whether a representation merely performs well on a prediction task. Their results remove commonly imposed independence assumptions, extending the guarantees to a broader family of methods and less restrictive data distributions.

Experiments on several benchmark datasets validate the theoretical findings, and the paper also investigates practical limitations. The contribution is a more unified basis for understanding disentanglement across contrastive objectives. Removing independence assumptions broadens that basis, but the abstract does not claim that latent recovery becomes assumption-free or that every practical application will achieve it.
summary.tldr: The paper proves latent identifiability for four contrastive losses without common independence assumptions and examines their practical behavior.

title: Towards a Unified Framework of Contrastive Learning for Disentangled Representations

abstract: Given a set of points, clustering consists of finding a partition of a point set into $k$ clusters such that the center to which a point is assigned is as close as possible. Most commonly, centers are points themselves, which leads to the famous $k$-median and $k$-means objectives. One may also choose centers to be $j$ dimensional subspaces, which gives rise to subspace clustering. In this paper, we consider learning bounds for these problems. That is, given a set of $n$ samples $P$ drawn independently from some unknown, but fixed distribution $\mathcal{D}$, how quickly does a solution computed on $P$ converge to the optimal clustering of $\mathcal{D}$?We give several near optimal results. In particular, 1. For center-based objectives, we show a convergence rate of $\tilde{O}\left(\sqrt{{k}/{n}}\right)$. This matches the known optimal bounds of [Fefferman, Mitter, and Narayanan, Journal of the Mathematical Society 2016] and [Bartlett, Linder, and Lugosi, IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory 1998] for $k$-means and extends it to other important objectives such as $k$-median. 2. For subspace clustering with $j$-dimensional subspaces, we show a convergence rate of $\tilde{O}\left(\sqrt{{(kj^2)}/{n}}\right)$. These are the first provable bounds for most of these problems. For the specific case of projective clustering, which generalizes $k$-means, we show a converge rate of $\Omega\left(\sqrt{{(kj)}/{n}}\right)$ is necessary, thereby proving that the bounds from [Fefferman, Mitter, and Narayanan, Journal of the Mathematical Society 2016] are essentially optimal.

paragraphs: Clustering a finite sample is useful only insofar as the resulting groups represent the underlying population. This paper studies how quickly a clustering solution learned from n independent samples approaches the optimal clustering for a fixed, unknown distribution. It covers both ordinary point centers and centers represented by low-dimensional subspaces.

For point-centered objectives, the authors obtain a convergence rate of approximately sqrt(k/n), up to logarithmic factors, where k is the number of clusters. This matches known optimal results for k-means and extends the rate to objectives such as k-median. For clustering around j-dimensional subspaces, they derive an upper rate of approximately sqrt(kj²/n), again up to logarithmic factors.

The authors also prove a lower bound of order sqrt(kj/n) for projective clustering. This identifies an unavoidable dependence on the number and dimension of the subspaces and supports the essential optimality of earlier bounds. Together, the results quantify how sample requirements grow as the clustering representation becomes more complex.
summary.tldr: New generalization bounds quantify how clustering accuracy depends on sample size, cluster count, and subspace dimension.

title: On Generalization Bounds for Projective Clustering

abstract: We systematically investigate graph transformations that enable standard message passing to simulate state-of-the-art graph neural networks (GNNs) without loss of expressivity. Using these, many state-of-the-art GNNs can be implemented with message passing operations from standard libraries, eliminating many sources of implementation issues and allowing for better code optimization. We distinguish between weak and strong simulation: weak simulation achieves the same expressivity only after several message passing steps while strong simulation achieves this after every message passing step. Our contribution leads to a direct way to translate common operations of non-standard GNNs to graph transformations that allow for strong or weak simulation. Our empirical evaluation shows competitive predictive performance of message passing on transformed graphs for various molecular benchmark datasets, in several cases surpassing the original GNNs.

We distinguish between weak and strong simulation: weak simulation achieves the same expressivity only after several message passing steps while strong simulation achieves this after every message passing step. Our contribution leads to a direct way to translate common operations of non-standard GNNs to graph transformations that allow for strong or weak simulation. paragraphs: Advanced graph neural networks often use operations beyond standard message passing, which can complicate implementation. This paper investigates how transforming the graph itself can let ordinary message passing simulate many such networks without losing expressivity. The central question is whether a different graph representation can preserve what a more specialized network can distinguish.

The authors separate two kinds of simulation. Weak simulation matches expressivity after several message-passing steps, whereas strong simulation does so after every step. They provide a direct way to translate common operations from nonstandard graph networks into graph transformations supporting one of these forms of simulation.

This matters practically because the resulting models can use message-passing operations already available in standard libraries, reducing implementation difficulties and enabling better code optimization. On molecular benchmark datasets, message passing over transformed graphs achieves competitive predictive performance and sometimes exceeds the original networks. Those experiments complement the expressivity analysis by showing that the transformed implementations can also work well in evaluated prediction tasks.
summary.tldr: Graph transformations let standard message passing simulate many advanced graph neural networks while preserving their expressivity.

title: Expressivity-Preserving GNN Simulation

abstract: Controlled variable selection is an important analytical step in various scientific fields, such as brain imaging or genomics. In these high-dimensional data settings, considering too many variables leads to poor models and high costs, hence the need for statistical guarantees on false positives. Knockoffs are a popular statistical tool for conditional variable selection in high dimension. However, they control for the expected proportion of false discoveries (FDR) and not the actual proportion of false discoveries (FDP). We present a new method, KOPI, that controls the proportion of false discoveries for Knockoff-based inference. The proposed method also relies on a new type of aggregation to address the undesirable randomness associated with classical Knockoff inference. We demonstrate FDP control and substantial power gains over existing Knockoff-based methods in various simulation settings and achieve good sensitivity/specificity tradeoffs on brain imaging data.

However, they control for the expected proportion of false discoveries (FDR) and not the actual proportion of false discoveries (FDP). paragraphs: Selecting relevant variables is difficult when a dataset contains many candidates, as in genomics or brain imaging. Including too many variables can increase costs and weaken models, so selection procedures need control over false positives. This paper focuses on a distinction between controlling false discoveries on average and controlling their proportion in the selected set.

Standard knockoff methods control the false discovery rate, which is the expected proportion of false discoveries. The proposed method, KOPI, instead targets the false discovery proportion itself. It also introduces a new aggregation approach to address the unwanted randomness of conventional knockoff inference. These two changes concern both the statistical quantity being controlled and the variability of the selection procedure.

In multiple simulation settings, the authors demonstrate false discovery proportion control and substantial gains in power over existing knockoff-based methods. Higher power means recovering more relevant variables while maintaining the stated control. On brain imaging data, they report good sensitivity and specificity tradeoffs, providing an applied example of balancing useful discoveries against false positives.
summary.tldr: KOPI combines knockoff aggregation with false discovery proportion control and reports improved power in simulations.

title: False Discovery Proportion control for aggregated Knockoffs

abstract: Neural architecture search (NAS) finds high performing networks for a given task. Yet the results of NAS are fairly prosaic; they did not e.g. create a shift from convolutional structures to transformers. This is not least because the search spaces in NAS often aren’t diverse enough to include such transformations *a priori*. Instead, for NAS to provide greater potential for fundamental design shifts, we need a novel expressive search space design which is built from more fundamental operations. To this end, we introduce `einspace`, a search space based on a parameterised probabilistic context-free grammar. Our space is versatile, supporting architectures of various sizes and complexities, while also containing diverse network operations which allow it to model convolutions, attention components and more. It contains many existing competitive architectures, and provides flexibility for discovering new ones. Using this search space, we perform experiments to find novel architectures as well as improvements on existing ones on the diverse Unseen NAS datasets. We show that competitive architectures can be obtained by searching from scratch, and we consistently find large improvements when initialising the search with strong baselines. We believe that this work is an important advancement towards a transformative NAS paradigm where search space expressivity and strategic search initialisation play key roles.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search can only discover networks that its search space permits. The paper argues that many existing spaces are too restricted to enable substantial changes in network design. If the available building blocks already impose a narrow architectural pattern, even effective search may produce variations of that pattern rather than substantially different structures.

Einspace expands the available designs through a parameterized probabilistic context-free grammar. This grammar builds architectures from fundamental operations and can represent networks of different sizes and complexity, including convolution and attention components. The search-space design is therefore a central contribution, alongside the architectures discovered within it.

summary.tldr: Einspace uses a grammar of fundamental operations to broaden neural architecture search and improve architectures, especially from strong starting points.

title: einspace: Searching for Neural Architectures from Fundamental Operations

abstract: Generative modelling paradigms based on denoising diffusion processes have emerged as a leading candidate for conditional sampling in inverse problems. In many real-world applications, we often have access to large, expensively trained unconditional diffusion models, which we aim to exploit for improving conditional sampling.Most recent approaches are motivated heuristically and lack a unifying framework, obscuring connections between them. Further, they often suffer from issues such as being very sensitive to hyperparameters, being expensive to train or needing access to weights hidden behind a closed API. In this work, we unify conditional training and sampling using the mathematically well-understood Doob's h-transform. This new perspective allows us to unify many existing methods under a common umbrella. Under this framework, we propose DEFT (Doob's h-transform Efficient FineTuning), a new approach for conditional generation that simply fine-tunes a very small network to quickly learn the conditional $h$-transform, while keeping the larger unconditional network unchanged. DEFT is much faster than existing baselines while achieving state-of-the-art performance across a variety of linear and non-linear benchmarks. On image reconstruction tasks, we achieve speedups of up to 1.6$\times$, while having the best perceptual quality on natural images and reconstruction performance on medical images. Further, we also provide initial experiments on protein motif scaffolding and outperform reconstruction guidance methods.

paragraphs: DEFT tackles conditional generation using an existing, expensive-to-train unconditional diffusion model. In an inverse problem, generation must account for an observation or constraint. The paper argues that many approaches to this task lack a shared mathematical framework, making their relationships difficult to understand and contributing to practical difficulties involving tuning, training expense, or access to model weights.

The authors use Doob’s h-transform to place conditional training and sampling within one framework. This perspective motivates a concrete method: train a very small network to learn the conditional transformation while leaving the large unconditional network unchanged. Initial protein motif scaffolding experiments outperform reconstruction guidance methods, providing preliminary evidence beyond image reconstruction.
summary.tldr: DEFT learns a small conditioning network through Doob’s h-transform while keeping a large diffusion model fixed, improving speed and reconstruction results.

title: DEFT: Efficient Fine-tuning of Diffusion Models by Learning the Generalised $h$-transform

abstract: In the face of uncertainty, the ability to *seek information* is of fundamental importance. In many practical applications, such as medical diagnosis and troubleshooting, the information needed to solve the task is not initially given, and has to be actively sought by asking follow-up questions (for example, a doctor asking a patient for more details about their symptoms). In this work, we introduce **Uncertainty of Thoughts (UoT)**, an algorithm to augment large language models with the ability to actively seek information by asking effective questions. UoT combines:1. An *uncertainty-aware simulation approach* which enables the model to simulate possible future scenarios and how likely they are to occur,2. *Uncertainty-based rewards* motivated by information gain which incentivizes the model to seek information, and3. A *reward propagation scheme* to select the optimal question to ask in a way that maximizes the expected reward.In experiments on medical diagnosis, troubleshooting and the `20 Questions' game, UoT achieves an average performance improvement of 38.1% in the rate of successful task completion across multiple LLMs compared with direct prompting, and also improves efficiency (i.e., the number of questions needed to complete the task).

paragraphs: Some tasks begin without enough information to solve them. A useful assistant must decide what to ask next, as in diagnosis or troubleshooting. Uncertainty of Thoughts addresses this information-seeking problem by giving language models a planning procedure for choosing effective follow-up questions.

The algorithm combines three mechanisms. It simulates possible future scenarios while accounting for how likely they are. Rewards based on uncertainty and motivated by information gain encourage questions that reveal useful information. A reward-propagation scheme then selects the question with the highest expected reward. Together, these components connect the model's uncertainty to its choice of what to ask.

The authors evaluate the method on medical diagnosis, troubleshooting, and the 20 Questions game across multiple language models. Compared with direct prompting, it delivers a reported average improvement of 38.1% in successful task completion and also improves efficiency measured by the number of questions required. The findings support explicitly planning information gathering when answering well depends on acquiring details that were initially missing.
summary.tldr: Uncertainty of Thoughts plans follow-up questions using simulated outcomes and information-based rewards, improving task success and question efficiency.

title: Uncertainty of Thoughts: Uncertainty-Aware Planning Enhances Information Seeking in LLMs

abstract: A key goal in mechanistic interpretability is circuit analysis: finding sparse subgraphs of models corresponding to specific behaviors or capabilities. However, MLP sublayers make fine-grained circuit analysis on transformer-based language models difficult. In particular, interpretable features—such as those found by sparse autoencoders (SAEs)—are typically linear combinations of extremely many neurons, each with its own nonlinearity to account for. Circuit analysis in this setting thus either yields intractably large circuits or fails to disentangle local and global behavior. To address this we explore **transcoders**, which seek to faithfully approximate a densely activating MLP layer with a wider, sparsely-activating MLP layer. We introduce a novel method for using transcoders to perform weights-based circuit analysis through MLP sublayers. The resulting circuits neatly factorize into input-dependent and input-invariant terms. We then successfully train transcoders on language models with 120M, 410M, and 1.4B parameters, and find them to perform at least on par with SAEs in terms of sparsity, faithfulness, and human-interpretability. Finally, we apply transcoders to reverse-engineer unknown circuits in the model, and we obtain novel insights regarding the "greater-than circuit" in GPT2-small. Our results suggest that transcoders can prove effective in decomposing model computations involving MLPs into interpretable circuits. Code is available at https://github.com/jacobdunefsky/transcoder_circuits/

paragraphs: Circuit analysis seeks small collections of model components that explain particular behaviors. Transformer MLP layers make this difficult because an interpretable feature can combine many neurons, each with its own nonlinearity. Following all those contributions can create unwieldy circuits or blur the distinction between local behavior and broader model structure.

The paper explores transcoders, which approximate a densely active MLP with a wider MLP that activates sparsely. The authors introduce a method for tracing circuits through these approximations using their weights. The resulting circuits separate into terms that depend on the input and terms that remain fixed across inputs, making the computation easier to examine.

Transcoders trained on models with 120M, 410M, and 1.4B parameters perform at least as well as sparse autoencoders on the evaluated sparsity, faithfulness, and human-interpretability criteria. The authors also use them to investigate previously unknown circuits and gain new insights into GPT2-small's greater-than circuit. These findings suggest that transcoders can make computations involving MLPs more accessible to circuit-level interpretation.
summary.tldr: Transcoders approximate dense MLPs with sparse alternatives that support interpretable, weights-based analysis of language-model circuits.

title: Transcoders find interpretable LLM feature circuits

abstract: We study a novel problem to automatically generate video background that tailors to foreground subject motion. It is an important problem for the movie industry and visual effects community, which traditionally requires tedious manual efforts to solve. To this end, we propose ActAnywhere, a video diffusion model that takes as input a sequence of foreground subject segmentation and an image of a novel background and generates a video of the subject interacting in this background. We train our model on a large-scale dataset of 2.4M videos of human-scene interactions. Through extensive evaluation, we show that our model produces videos with realistic foreground-background interaction while strictly following the guidance of the condition image. Our model generalizes to diverse scenarios including non-human subjects, gaming and animation clips, as well as videos with multiple moving subjects. Both quantitative and qualitative comparisons demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms existing methods, which fail to accomplish the studied task. Please visit our project webpage at https://actanywhere.github.io.

paragraphs: ActAnywhere addresses the problem of generating a video background that fits a moving foreground subject. For film and visual effects work, this involves more than choosing scenery: the subject and surroundings need to appear to interact plausibly. The paper aims to automate a process that otherwise requires substantial manual effort.

The method uses a video diffusion model with two inputs: a sequence of foreground subject segmentations and an image specifying the desired background. Together, these describe the subject’s motion and the scene into which it should be placed. The model learns from 2.4 million videos of human interactions with scenes, giving it training examples of how foreground movement relates to surrounding environments.

The evaluations report realistic interactions while closely following the supplied background image. They also demonstrate generalization to non-human subjects, gaming and animation footage, and multiple moving subjects. Quantitative and qualitative comparisons show substantial improvements over existing methods for this task. These findings support using subject motion as a central condition for generating coherent replacement backgrounds.
summary.tldr: ActAnywhere generates video backgrounds guided by a reference image and foreground motion to produce realistic subject–scene interactions.

title: ActAnywhere: Subject-Aware Video Background Generation

abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) are widely used in a variety of applications, while they usually have a fixed architecture that may not match the varying computational resources of different deployment environments. Thus, it is necessary to adapt ViT architectures to devices with diverse computational overheads to achieve an accuracy-efficient trade-off. This concept is consistent with the motivation behind Learngene. To achieve this, inspired by polynomial decomposition in calculus, where a function can be approximated by linearly combining several basic components, we propose to linearly decompose the ViT model into a set of components called learngenes during element-wise training. These learngenes can then be recomposed into differently scaled, pre-initialized models to satisfy different computational resource constraints. Such a decomposition-recomposition strategy provides an economical and flexible approach to generating different scales of ViT models for different deployment scenarios. Compared to model compression or training from scratch, which require to repeatedly train on large datasets for diverse-scale models, such strategy reduces computational costs since it only requires to train on large datasets once. Extensive experiments are used to validate the effectiveness of our method: ViTs can be decomposed and the decomposed learngenes can be recomposed into diverse-scale ViTs, which can achieve comparable or better performance compared to traditional model compression and pre-training methods. The code for our experiments is available in the supplemental material.

paragraphs: This paper addresses the cost of producing vision transformers for devices with different computational resources. A fixed architecture may fit one deployment environment but be too expensive or insufficiently accurate for another. Repeatedly training or compressing separate models can require substantial work on large datasets.

The proposed strategy decomposes a vision transformer into components called learngenes during element-wise training. Inspired by approximating functions through linear combinations of simpler components, it then recomposes these learned pieces into models of different scales. The resulting models are pre-initialized for their intended resource constraints, making the learned components reusable across deployment sizes.

The computational advantage comes from requiring large-dataset training only once for this decomposition-recomposition process. Experiments show that the components can form differently sized vision transformers with performance comparable to or better than traditional compression and pretraining approaches. The findings support reusing a shared set of learned building blocks to obtain a range of accuracy-efficiency trade-offs, rather than paying the full large-dataset training cost separately for every model scale.
summary.tldr: Reusable learngene components let vision transformers be recomposed at different scales after a single large-dataset training process.

title: Linearly Decomposing and Recomposing Vision Transformers for Diverse-Scale Models

abstract: We present a new method for making diffusion models faster to sample. The method distills many-step diffusion models into few-step models by matching conditional expectations of the clean data given noisy data along the sampling trajectory. Our approach extends recently proposed one-step methods to the multi-step case, and provides a new perspective by interpreting these approaches in terms of moment matching. By using up to 8 sampling steps, we obtain distilled models that outperform not only their one-step versions but also their original many-step teacher models, obtaining new state-of-the-art results on the Imagenet dataset. We also show promising results on a large text-to-image model where we achieve fast generation of high resolution images directly in image space, without needing autoencoders or upsamplers.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can require many sampling steps to generate an image. This paper develops a distillation method that transfers a many-step model into a model using only a few steps. Its focus is on preserving useful information about the clean data throughout the shortened sampling trajectory.

The training procedure matches conditional expectations of clean data given noisy data at points along that trajectory. In plain terms, it aligns the expected clean output associated with a noisy input. The authors interpret this as moment matching and extend recently proposed single-step approaches to a multistep setting, allowing the distilled model several opportunities to refine its output.

Using up to eight sampling steps, the resulting models outperform both their single-step versions and their many-step teachers in the reported ImageNet results, achieving a new state of the art. A large text-to-image experiment also shows promising fast, high-resolution generation directly in image space. That demonstration uses neither autoencoders nor upsamplers, illustrating another setting where the shortened process can be useful.
summary.tldr: Moment-matching distillation produces few-step diffusion models that outperform their teachers in the reported ImageNet experiments.

title: Multistep Distillation of Diffusion Models via Moment Matching

abstract: Human annotators typically provide annotated data for training machine learning models, such as neural networks. Yet, human annotations are subject to noise, impairing generalization performances. Methodological research on approaches counteracting noisy annotations requires corresponding datasets for a meaningful empirical evaluation. Consequently, we introduce a novel benchmark dataset, dopanim, consisting of about 15,750 animal images of 15 classes with ground truth labels. For approximately 10,500 of these images, 20 humans provided over 52,000 annotations with an accuracy of circa 67%. Its key attributes include (1) the challenging task of classifying doppelganger animals, (2) human-estimated likelihoods as annotations, and (3) annotator metadata. We benchmark well-known multi-annotator learning approaches using seven variants of this dataset and outline further evaluation use cases such as learning beyond hard class labels and active learning. Our dataset and a comprehensive codebase are publicly available to emulate the data collection process and to reproduce all empirical results.

paragraphs: Training labels supplied by people can contain mistakes, especially when the categories are visually difficult to distinguish. The dopanim dataset turns this difficulty into a benchmark by collecting images of animals that resemble one another. It contains about 15,750 images across 15 classes, together with ground-truth labels for evaluating learning methods.

For approximately 10,500 images, 20 people supplied more than 52,000 annotations, with an overall accuracy of about 67%. The annotations include human-estimated likelihoods, allowing the data to express uncertainty beyond a single class choice. Information about annotators is also included, providing additional material for methods that learn from multiple people's judgments.

The authors benchmark established multi-annotator learning methods on seven dataset variants. They also describe uses such as learning from richer labels and active learning. The dataset's value comes from combining a difficult recognition task with actual human annotation behavior. Its public codebase supports reproducing the reported results and emulating the collection process, making the evaluation easier to inspect and repeat.
summary.tldr: dopanim benchmarks learning from noisy human judgments using visually similar animals, likelihood annotations, and annotator metadata.

title: dopanim: A Dataset of Doppelganger Animals with Noisy Annotations from Multiple Humans

abstract: Detecting and measuring confounding effects from data is a key challenge in causal inference. Existing methods frequently assume causal sufficiency, disregarding the presence of unobserved confounding variables. Causal sufficiency is both unrealistic and empirically untestable. Additionally, existing methods make strong parametric assumptions about the underlying causal generative process to guarantee the identifiability of confounding variables. Relaxing the causal sufficiency and parametric assumptions and leveraging recent advancements in causal discovery and confounding analysis with non-i.i.d. data, we propose a comprehensive approach for detecting and measuring confounding. We consider various definitions of confounding and introduce tailored methodologies to achieve three objectives: (i) detecting and measuring confounding among a set of variables, (ii) separating observed and unobserved confounding effects, and (iii) understanding the relative strengths of confounding bias between different sets of variables. We present useful properties of a confounding measure and present measures that satisfy those properties. Our empirical results support the usefulness of the proposed measures.

paragraphs: Confounding complicates causal inference because relationships between variables may reflect influences beyond the causal relationship being studied. Many existing methods assume that all relevant confounding variables are observed. Others impose strong mathematical assumptions on how the data were generated to make hidden confounding identifiable.

This paper develops an approach that relaxes causal sufficiency and parametric assumptions by using causal mechanism shifts and data that are not independently and identically distributed. It considers multiple definitions of confounding rather than treating every question as the same measurement problem. Its methods address detecting confounding among variables, distinguishing observed from unobserved contributions, and comparing the strength of confounding across different variable sets.

The authors also describe desirable properties for a confounding measure and construct measures that satisfy them. Their empirical results support the usefulness of these measures. The contribution therefore goes beyond flagging whether confounding might exist: it provides a structured way to investigate its sources and relative magnitude under the proposed approach.
summary.tldr: The paper uses causal mechanism shifts to develop measures for detecting, separating, and comparing observed and hidden confounding effects.

title: Detecting and Measuring Confounding Using Causal Mechanism Shifts

abstract: Recently, implicit neural representations (INR) have made significant strides in various vision-related domains, providing a novel solution for Multispectral and Hyperspectral Image Fusion (MHIF) tasks. However, INR is prone to losing high-frequency information and is confined to the lack of global perceptual capabilities. To address these issues, this paper introduces a Fourier-enhanced Implicit Neural Fusion Network (FeINFN) specifically designed for MHIF task, targeting the following phenomena: The Fourier amplitudes of the HR-HSI latent code and LR-HSI are remarkably similar; however, their phases exhibit different patterns. In FeINFN, we innovatively propose a spatial and frequency implicit fusion function (Spa-Fre IFF), helping INR capture high-frequency information and expanding the receptive field. Besides, a new decoder employing a complex Gabor wavelet activation function, called Spatial-Frequency Interactive Decoder (SFID), is invented to enhance the interaction of INR features. Especially, we further theoretically prove that the Gabor wavelet activation possesses a time-frequency tightness property that favors learning the optimal bandwidths in the decoder. Experiments on two benchmark MHIF datasets verify the state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance of the proposed method, both visually and quantitatively. Also, ablation studies demonstrate the mentioned contributions. The code can be available at https://github.com/294coder/Efficient-MIF.
