abstract: Event cameras offer unique advantages in scenarios involving high speed, low light, and high dynamic range, yet their asynchronous and sparse nature poses significant challenges to efficient spatiotemporal representation learning. Specifically, despite notable progress in the field, effectively modeling the full spatiotemporal context, selectively attending to salient dynamic regions, and robustly adapting to the variable density and dynamic nature of event data remain key challenges. Motivated by these challenges, this paper proposes EventMG, a lightweight, efficient, multilevel Mamba-Graph architecture designed for learning high-quality spatiotemporal event representations. EventMG employs a multilevel approach, jointly modeling information at the micro (single event) and macro (event cluster) levels to comprehensively capture the multi-scale characteristics of event data. At the micro-level, it focuses on spatiotemporal details, employing State Space Model (SSM) based Mamba, to precisely capture long-range dependencies among numerous event nodes. Concurrently, at the macro-level, Component Graphs are introduced to efficiently encode the local semantics and global topology of dense event regions. Furthermore, to better accommodate the dynamic and sparse characteristics of data, we propose the Spatiotemporal-aware Event Scanning Technology (SEST), integrating the Adaptive Perturbation Network (APN) and Multidirectional Scanning Module (MSM), which substantially enhances the model's ability to perceive and focus on key spatiotemporal patterns. By employing this novel collaborative paradigm, EventMG demonstrates the ability to effectively capture multi-level spatiotemporal characteristics of event data while maintaining a low parameter count and linear computational complexity, suggesting a promising direction for event representation learning.

These two levels give the model complementary views of detailed activity and larger structures.

abstract: Zero-shot object navigation (ZSON) allows robots to find target objects in unfamiliar environments using natural language instructions, without relying on pre-built maps or task-specific training. Recent general-purpose models, such as large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs), equip agents with semantic reasoning abilities to estimate target object locations in a zero-shot manner. However, these models often greedily select the next goal without maintaining a global understanding of the environment and are fundamentally limited in the spatial reasoning necessary for effective navigation. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel 3D voxel-based belief map that estimates the target’s prior presence distribution within a voxelized 3D space. This approach enables agents to integrate semantic priors from LLMs and visual embeddings with hierarchical spatial structure, alongside real-time observations, to build a comprehensive 3D global posterior belief of the target’s location. Building on this 3D voxel map, we introduce BeliefMapNav, an efficient navigation system with two key advantages: i) grounding LLM semantic reasoning within the 3D hierarchical semantics voxel space for precise target position estimation, and ii) integrating sequential path planning to enable efficient global navigation decisions. Experiments on HM3D and HSSD benchmarks show that BeliefMapNav achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) Success Rate (SR) and Success weighted by Path Length (SPL), with a notable 9.7 SPL improvement over the previous best SR method, validating its effectiveness and efficiency.

title: BeliefMapNav: 3D Voxel-Based Belief Map for Zero-Shot Object Navigation

abstract: We establish a comprehensive finite-sample and asymptotic theory for stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with constant learning rates. First, we propose a novel linear approximation technique to provide a quenched central limit theorem (CLT) for SGD iterates with refined tail properties, showing that regardless of the chosen initialization, the fluctuations of the algorithm around its target point converge to a multivariate normal distribution. Our conditions are substantially milder than those required in the classical CLTs for SGD, yet offering a stronger convergence result. Furthermore, we derive the first Berry-Esseen bound -- the Gaussian approximation error -- for the constant learning-rate SGD, which is sharp compared to the decaying learning-rate schemes in the literature. Beyond the moment convergence, we also provide the Nagaev-type inequality for the SGD tail probabilities by adopting the autoregressive approximation techniques, which entails non-asymptotic large-deviation guarantees. These results are verified via numerical simulations, paving the way for theoretically grounded uncertainty quantification, especially with non-asymptotic validity.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent uses noisy updates, so understanding its behavior requires more than locating a target point. This paper studies the fluctuations around that target when the learning rate remains constant. It develops both asymptotic results and finite-sample guarantees, linking long-run distributional behavior to bounds that apply before an infinite-data limit.

A new linear approximation technique establishes a quenched central limit theorem with refined tail properties. Under the paper's conditions, the fluctuations converge to a multivariate normal distribution regardless of initialization. The authors describe their conditions as substantially milder than those of classical SGD central limit theorems while obtaining a stronger convergence result.

summary.tldr: The paper establishes Gaussian approximation and tail bounds for constant-learning-rate SGD, supporting uncertainty quantification at finite sample sizes.

title: Gaussian Approximation and Concentration of Constant Learning-Rate Stochastic Gradient Descent

abstract: Multimodal Emotion Recognition in Conversations (MERC) enhances emotional understanding through the fusion of multimodal signals. However, unpredictable modality absence in real-world scenarios significantly degrades the performance of existing methods. Conventional missing-modality recovery approaches, which depend on training with complete multimodal data, often suffer from semantic distortion under extreme data distributions, such as fixed-modality absence. To address this, we propose the Federated Dialogue-guided and Semantic-Consistent Diffusion (FedDISC) framework, pioneering the integration of federated learning into missing-modality recovery. By federated aggregation of modality-specific diffusion models trained on clients and broadcasting them to clients missing corresponding modalities, FedDISC overcomes single-client reliance on modality completeness. Additionally, the DISC-Diffusion module ensures consistency in context, speaker identity, and semantics between recovered and available modalities, using a Dialogue Graph Network to capture conversational dependencies and a Semantic Conditioning Network to enforce semantic alignment. We further introduce a novel Alternating Frozen Aggregation strategy, which cyclically freezes recovery and classifier modules to facilitate collaborative optimization. Extensive experiments on the IEMOCAP, CMUMOSI, and CMUMOSEI datasets demonstrate that FedDISC achieves superior emotion classification performance across diverse missing modality patterns, outperforming existing approaches.

paragraphs: Recognizing emotions in conversations benefits from combining multiple kinds of signals, but some signals may be missing. Existing recovery methods often assume complete multimodal training data. That dependence becomes especially problematic when a client consistently lacks a particular modality, because recovered information can lose the meaning of the available conversation.

FedDISC shares recovery capability through federated learning. Clients train diffusion models for individual modalities; these models are aggregated and distributed to clients missing the corresponding signals. This reduces reliance on any single client's having complete data. Within the recovery process, a dialogue graph captures conversational dependencies, while semantic conditioning aligns recovered information with available signals, including context and speaker identity.

Experiments on IEMOCAP, CMUMOSI, and CMUMOSEI report better emotion classification than existing approaches across different missing-modality patterns. The findings support combining shared recovery models with conversation-aware constraints: access to a reconstruction model matters, but preserving the conversation's meaning also matters for the final classification.
summary.tldr: FedDISC shares modality-recovery diffusion models across clients while preserving conversational meaning to improve emotion recognition with missing signals.

title: Federated Dialogue-Semantic Diffusion for Emotion Recognition under Incomplete Modalities

abstract: We consider the privacy amplification properties of a sampling scheme in which a user's data is used in $k$ steps chosen randomly and uniformly from a sequence (or set) of $t$ steps. This sampling scheme has been recently applied in the context of differentially private optimization [Chua et al., 2024a, Choquette-Choo et al., 2024] and is also motivated by communication-efficient high-dimensional private aggregation [Asi et al., 2025]. Existing analyses of this scheme either rely on privacy amplification by shuffling which leads to overly conservative bounds or require Monte Carlo simulations that are computationally prohibitive in most practical scenarios. We give the first theoretical guarantees and numerical estimation algorithms for this sampling scheme. In particular, we demonstrate that the privacy guarantees of random $k$-out-of-$t$ allocation can be upper bounded by the privacy guarantees of the well-studied independent (or Poisson) subsampling in which each step uses the user's data with probability $(1+o(1))k/t$. Further, we provide two additional analysis techniques that lead to numerical improvements in several parameter regimes. Altogether, our bounds give efficiently-computable and nearly tight numerical results for random allocation applied to Gaussian noise addition.

Such allocation appears in private optimization and aggregation. Existing analyses either produce overly conservative guarantees through shuffling arguments or require Monte Carlo computations that are prohibitive in many practical settings.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees and numerical estimation algorithms specifically for random allocation. Their main comparison bounds its privacy guarantees using independent subsampling, where each step includes the person's data with probability approximately k/t, with the stated asymptotic correction. This links a scheme with a fixed number of participations to a better-understood scheme with independent participation decisions.

Two additional analysis techniques improve the numerical bounds in several parameter regimes. For random allocation with Gaussian noise addition, the combined methods yield efficiently computable, nearly tight results. The practical contribution is more usable privacy accounting for this sampling design, while the theoretical contribution explains how its guarantees relate to those of independent subsampling.
summary.tldr: The paper develops efficient, nearly tight privacy bounds for random allocation with Gaussian noise by relating it to independent subsampling.

title: Privacy amplification by random allocation

abstract: Recent advances in Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in solving complex tasks such as mathematics and coding. However, these models frequently exhibit a phenomenon known as *overthinking* during inference, characterized by excessive validation loops and redundant deliberation, leading to substantial computational overheads. In this paper, we aim to mitigate overthinking by investigating the underlying mechanisms from the perspective of mechanistic interpretability. We first showcase that the tendency of overthinking can be effectively captured by a single direction in the model's activation space and the issue can be eased by intervening the activations along this direction. However, this efficacy soon reaches a plateau and even deteriorates as the intervention strength increases. We therefore systematically explore the activation space and find that the overthinking phenomenon is actually tied to a low-dimensional manifold, which indicates that the limited effect stems from the noises introduced by the high-dimensional steering direction. Based on this insight, we propose **Manifold Steering**, a novel approach that elegantly projects the steering direction onto the low-dimensional activation manifold given the theoretical approximation of the interference noise. Extensive experiments on DeepSeek-R1 distilled models validate that our method reduces output tokens by up to 71\% while maintaining and even improving the accuracy on several mathematical benchmarks. Our method also exhibits robust cross-domain transferability, delivering consistent token reduction performance in code generation and knowledge-based QA tasks. Code is available at: https://github.com/Aries-iai/Manifold_Steering.

The authors first identify a single direction that captures the tendency and show that intervening along it can reduce excessive deliberation.

Stronger intervention eventually stops helping and can worsen results. Further analysis links overthinking to a low-dimensional manifold within the larger activation space. The authors attribute the limited effectiveness of the original direction to noise introduced outside that structure. These findings support a more precise form of activation intervention: respecting the structure associated with a behavior can make steering more effective than increasing the strength of a broad directional change.
summary.tldr: Manifold Steering targets the low-dimensional activation structure associated with overthinking, reducing generated tokens while preserving or improving tested mathematical accuracy.

title: Mitigating Overthinking in Large Reasoning Models via Manifold Steering

abstract: Spectral features are widely incorporated within Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to improve their expressive power, or their ability to distinguish among non-isomorphic graphs. One popular example is the usage of graph Laplacian eigenvectors for positional encoding in MPNNs and Graph Transformers. The expressive power of such Spectrally-enhanced GNNs (SGNNs) is usually evaluated via the $k$-WL graph isomorphism test hierarchy and homomorphism counting. Yet, these frameworks align poorly with the graph spectra, yielding limited insight into SGNNs' expressive power. In this paper, we leverage a well-studied paradigm of classifying graphs by their largest eigenvalue multiplicity to introduce an expressivity hierarchy for SGNNs. We then prove that many SGNNs are incomplete even on graphs with distinct eigenvalues. To mitigate this deficiency, we adapt rotation equivariant neural networks to the graph spectra setting, yielding equiEPNN, a novel SGNN that provably improves upon contemporary SGNNs' expressivity on simple spectrum graphs. We then demonstrate that equiEPNN achieves perfect eigenvector canonicalization on ZINC, and performs favorably on image classification on MNIST-Superpixel and graph property regression on ZINC, compared to leading spectral methods.

paragraphs: Spectral graph neural networks use information such as Laplacian eigenvectors to distinguish graph structures more effectively. This paper asks how far that added information actually takes them. It argues that common evaluation frameworks for expressive power align poorly with spectral structure, making some important distinctions difficult to see.

The authors introduce an expressivity hierarchy based on the largest multiplicity of a graph's eigenvalues. Within this framework, they prove that many spectral networks remain incomplete even when all eigenvalues are distinct: such networks still cannot distinguish every pair of non-isomorphic graphs in that class. Distinct eigenvalues therefore do not remove the demonstrated expressivity deficiency.

The work combines a sharper account of existing limitations with an architecture that improves the relevant theoretical distinction and performs well empirically.
summary.tldr: The paper proves expressivity gaps in many spectral graph networks and introduces equiEPNN with stronger guarantees on graphs with distinct eigenvalues.

title: Spectral Graph Neural Networks are Incomplete on Graphs with a Simple Spectrum

abstract: We consider the problem of estimating a causal effect in a multi-domain setting. The causal effect of interest is confounded by an unobserved confounder and can change between the different domains. We assume that we have access to a proxy of the hidden confounder and that all variables are discrete or categorical. We propose methodology to estimate the causal effect in the target domain, where we assume to observe only the proxy variable. Under these conditions, we prove identifiability (even when treatment and response variables are continuous). We introduce two estimation techniques, prove consistency, and derive confidence intervals. The theoretical results are supported by simulation studies and a real-world example studying the causal effect of website rankings on consumer choices.

paragraphs: A causal effect learned in one domain may change in another, especially when an unobserved factor influences the relationship between treatment and outcome. This paper studies transferring causal information when that hidden confounder cannot be measured directly. Instead, the available data include a proxy that provides indirect information about it.

The target domain presents a particularly sparse observation setting: only the proxy variable is observed there. The authors formulate the problem with discrete or categorical variables and prove that the target causal effect is identifiable under their conditions. They also state that identifiability extends to continuous treatment and response variables. Identifiability means the effect can be determined from the available information under the assumed setting.

Beyond identification, the paper introduces two estimation techniques, proves their consistency, and derives confidence intervals. Simulation studies and an application examining the effect of website rankings on consumer choices support the theory. The contribution connects a sparse-data transfer setting with statistical estimation and uncertainty assessment, showing how proxy information can support causal analysis across domains under the stated conditions.
summary.tldr: Under stated proxy and variable assumptions, the paper identifies and estimates target-domain causal effects when only the proxy is observed there.

title: Transferring Causal Effects using Proxies

abstract: Semi-Infinite Programming (SIP) has emerged as a powerful framework for modeling problems with infinite constraints, however, its theoretical development in the context of nonconvex and large-scale optimization remains limited. In this paper, we investigate a class of nonconvex min-max optimization problems with nonconvex infinite constraints, motivated by applications such as adversarial robustness and safety-constrained learning. We propose a novel inexact dynamic barrier primal-dual algorithm and establish its convergence properties. Specifically, under the assumption that the squared infeasibility residual function satisfies the Lojasiewicz inequality with exponent $\theta \in (0,1)$, we prove that the proposed method achieves $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3})$, $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-6\theta})$, and $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3\theta/(1-\theta)})$ iteration complexities to achieve an $\epsilon$-approximate stationarity, infeasibility, and complementarity slackness, respectively. Numerical experiments on robust multitask learning with task priority further illustrate the practical effectiveness of the algorithm.

paragraphs: Some learning problems involve a finite collection of decision variables but infinitely many constraints. Semi-infinite programming provides a way to express such requirements. This paper studies a nonconvex min-max setting with nonconvex infinite constraints, motivated by adversarial robustness and learning subject to safety constraints.

The authors propose an inexact dynamic barrier primal-dual algorithm and prove convergence properties under a specific assumption: the squared infeasibility residual satisfies the Lojasiewicz inequality with exponent θ between zero and one. The guarantees address approximate stationarity, constraint infeasibility, and complementarity slackness, which respectively concern optimization progress, constraint violation, and the relationship between constraints and their multipliers.

For accuracy tolerance ε, the stated iteration bounds are O(ε^-3), O(ε^(-6θ)), and O(ε^(-3θ/(1−θ))) for those three criteria. These are conditional guarantees for approximate conditions, rather than a claim of finding a global optimum. Numerical experiments on robust multitask learning with task priorities also illustrate practical effectiveness, connecting the analysis to a learning problem with competing objectives and constraints.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes a primal-dual algorithm for nonconvex min-max problems with infinitely many constraints and proves conditional iteration bounds.

title: Semi-infinite Nonconvex Constrained Min-Max Optimization

abstract: Outcome‑reward reinforcement learning (RL) is a common—and increasingly significant—way to refine the step‑by‑step reasoning of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). In the multiple‑choice setting—a dominant format for multimodal reasoning benchmarks—the paradigm faces a significant yet often overlooked obstacle: unfaithful trajectories that guess the correct option after a faulty chain of thought receive the same reward as genuine reasoning, which is a flaw that cannot be ignored. We propose Self‑Consistency Sampling (SCS) to correct this issue. For each question, SCS (i) introduces small visual perturbations and (ii) performs repeated truncation‑and‑resampling of a reference trajectory; agreement among the resulting trajectories yields a differentiable consistency score that down‑weights unreliable traces during policy updates. Plugging SCS into RLOO, GRPO, REINFORCE++ series improves accuracy by up to 7.7 percentage points on six multimodal benchmarks with negligible extra computation, offering a simple, general remedy for outcome‑reward RL in MLLMs.

paragraphs: Rewarding only the final answer creates a problem for multimodal reasoning in multiple-choice tasks. A model can follow faulty reasoning and still guess the correct option, receiving the same reward as a sound solution. This paper introduces Self-Consistency Sampling to reduce the influence of those unreliable reasoning traces during reinforcement learning.

For each question, the method slightly perturbs the visual input and repeatedly truncates and resamples a reference reasoning trajectory. Agreement across the resulting trajectories produces a differentiable consistency score. That score downweights unreliable traces when updating the policy, adding a measure of stability to the information supplied by final-answer correctness.

The authors integrate the method into RLOO, GRPO, and the REINFORCE++ series. Across six multimodal benchmarks, they report accuracy improvements of up to 7.7 percentage points with negligible additional computation. The result supports consistency sampling as a practical addition to several outcome-reward training methods. Its role is to make lucky correct answers less influential by checking agreement across related trajectories, while retaining outcome rewards as part of training.
summary.tldr: Self-Consistency Sampling downweights unreliable reasoning traces and improves multimodal outcome-reward training by up to 7.7 percentage points.

title: Enhancing the Outcome Reward-based RL Training of MLLMs with Self-Consistency Sampling

abstract: While large language models (LLMs) can solve PhD-level reasoning problems over long context inputs, they still struggle with a seemingly simpler task: *following explicit length instructions*—e.g., *write a 10,000-word novel*. Additionally, models often generate far too short outputs, terminate prematurely, or even refuse the request. Existing benchmarks focus primarily on evaluating generations quality, but often overlook whether the generations meet length constraints. To this end, we introduce **Length Instruction Following Evaluation Benchmark** (LIFEBench) to comprehensively evaluate LLMs' ability to follow length instructions across diverse tasks and a wide range of specified lengths. LIFEBench consists of 10,800 instances across 4 task categories in both English and Chinese, covering length constraints ranging from 16 to 8192 words. We evaluate 26 widely-used LLMs and find that most models reasonably follow short-length instructions but deteriorate sharply beyond a certain threshold. Surprisingly, almost all models fail to reach the vendor-claimed maximum output lengths in practice, as further confirmed by our evaluations extending up to 32K words. Even long-context LLMs, despite their extended input-output windows, counterintuitively fail to improve length-instructions following. Notably, Reasoning LLMs outperform even specialized long-text generation models, achieving state-of-the-art length following. Overall, LIFEBench uncovers fundamental limitations in current LLMs' length instructions following ability, offering critical insights for future progress.

The motivation is that models may produce much shorter answers, stop early, or refuse requests even when they can handle demanding reasoning tasks.

title: LIFEBENCH: Evaluating Length Instruction Following in Large Language Models

abstract: Despite the growing success of transform-based tensor models such as the t-product, their underlying geometric principles remain poorly understood. Classical differential geometry, built on real-valued function spaces, is not well suited to capture the algebraic and spectral structure induced by transform-based tensor operations. In this work, we take an initial step toward a geometric framework for tensors equipped with tube-wise multiplication via orthogonal transforms. We introduce the notion of smooth t-manifolds, defined as topological spaces locally modeled on structured tensor modules over a commutative t-scalar ring. This formulation enables transform-consistent definitions of geometric objects, including metrics, gradients, Laplacians, and geodesics, thereby bridging discrete and continuous tensor settings within a unified algebraic-geometric perspective. On this basis, we develop a statistical procedure for testing whether tensor data lie near a low-dimensional t-manifold, and provide nonasymptotic guarantees for manifold fitting under noise. We further establish approximation bounds for tensor neural networks that learn smooth functions over t-manifolds, with generalization rates determined by intrinsic geometric complexity. This framework offers a theoretical foundation for geometry-aware learning in structured tensor spaces and supports the development of models that align with transform-based tensor representations.

paragraphs: Transform-based tensor models use algebraic structure that ordinary real-valued differential geometry does not naturally capture. This paper develops an initial geometric framework for tensors whose tube-wise multiplication is defined through orthogonal transforms. The goal is to describe their geometry in a way that respects the operations used by the models themselves.

The central construction is a smooth t-manifold, a space locally represented by structured tensor modules over a commutative t-scalar ring. Within that framework, the authors define metrics, gradients, Laplacians, and geodesics consistently with the transform-based algebra. This provides a common language for relating discrete tensor representations to continuous geometric objects and operations.

The paper then develops a statistical test for whether tensor data lie near a low-dimensional t-manifold and gives finite-sample guarantees for fitting such manifolds under noise. It also establishes approximation bounds for tensor neural networks learning smooth functions on these spaces. Their generalization rates depend on intrinsic geometric complexity, connecting the structure of the data to theoretical learning performance.
summary.tldr: The paper builds a transform-compatible geometry for tensor learning, with guarantees for noisy manifold fitting and neural-network approximation.

title: Towards a Geometric Understanding of Tensor Learning via the t-Product

abstract: We study Online Convex Optimization with adversarial constraints (COCO). At each round a learner selects an action from a convex decision set and then an adversary reveals a convex cost and a convex constraint function. The goal of the learner is to select a sequence of actions to minimize both regret and the cumulative constraint violation (CCV) over a horizon of length $T$. The best-known policy for this problem achieves $O(\sqrt{T})$ regret and $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ CCV. In this paper, we improve this by trading off regret to achieve substantially smaller CCV. This trade-off is especially important in safety-critical applications, where satisfying the safety constraints is non-negotiable. Specifically, for any bounded convex cost and constraint functions, we propose an online policy that achieves $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{dT}+ T^\beta)$ regret and $\tilde{O}(dT^{1-\beta})$ CCV, where $d$ is the dimension of the decision set and $\beta \in [0,1]$ is a tunable parameter. We begin with a special case, called the $\textsf{Constrained Expert}$ problem, where the decision set is a probability simplex and the cost and constraint functions are linear. Leveraging a new adaptive small-loss regret bound, we propose a computationally efficient policy for the $\textsf{Constrained Expert}$ problem, that attains $O(\sqrt{T\ln N}+T^{\beta})$ regret and $\tilde{O}(T^{1-\beta} \ln N)$ CCV for $N$ number of experts. The original problem is then reduced to the $\textsf{Constrained Expert}$ problem via a covering argument. Finally, with an additional $M$-smoothness assumption, we propose a computationally efficient first-order policy attaining $O(\sqrt{MT}+T^{\beta})$ regret and $\tilde{O}(MT^{1-\beta})$ CCV.

paragraphs: This paper studies decisions made before their costs and constraints are revealed. At each round, a learner chooses an action, then an adversary supplies both functions. The learner must control regret and accumulated constraint violations. The paper develops a tunable trade-off that accepts higher regret to reduce violations, motivated by applications where constraint satisfaction has particular importance.

For bounded convex functions, its policy achieves regret of order √(dT) + T^β and cumulative violation of order dT^(1−β), ignoring logarithmic factors. Here d is the decision dimension, T is the number of rounds, and β ranges from zero to one. Increasing β improves the violation bound while increasing the regret contribution.

The construction starts with an efficient algorithm for mixtures of experts and extends it to general convex decision sets through a covering argument. With an additional smoothness assumption, the authors also obtain an efficient first-order policy. These are cumulative guarantees: the stated results reduce accumulated violations without promising that every individual action satisfies its constraint.
summary.tldr: A tunable online optimization policy trades higher regret for smaller cumulative constraint violations, with efficient algorithms for expert and smooth settings.

title: Beyond $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ Constraint Violation for Online Convex Optimization with Adversarial Constraints

abstract: Effective data selection is critical for efficient training of modern Large Language Models (LLMs). This paper introduces Influence Distillation, a novel, mathematically-justified framework for data selection that employs second-order information to optimally weight training samples. By distilling each sample's influence on a target distribution, our method assigns model-specific weights that are used to select training data for LLM fine-tuning, guiding it toward strong performance on the target domain. We derive these optimal weights for both Gradient Descent and Adam optimizers. To ensure scalability and reduce computational cost, we propose a $\textit{landmark-based approximation}$: influence is precisely computed for a small subset of "landmark" samples and then efficiently propagated to all other samples to determine their weights. We validate Influence Distillation by applying it to instruction tuning on the Tulu V2 dataset, targeting a range of tasks including GSM8k, SQuAD, and MMLU, across several models from the Llama and Qwen families. Experiments show that Influence Distillation matches or outperforms state-of-the-art performance while achieving up to $3.5\times$ faster selection.

paragraphs: Choosing useful training examples can make language-model fine-tuning more efficient. Influence Distillation approaches this choice by estimating how each sample affects performance on a target distribution. Its weights are specific to the model and intended target domain, so data selection reflects the learning problem the fine-tuning process is meant to solve.

The framework uses second-order information to derive optimal sample weights for both Gradient Descent and Adam. To make the calculation scalable, it computes influence precisely for a small set of landmark samples. It then propagates that information to the remaining examples, approximating their weights without repeating the full influence calculation for every sample.

The authors evaluate the approach through instruction tuning on Tulu V2, using models from the Llama and Qwen families and targets including GSM8k, SQuAD, and MMLU. The method matches or exceeds state-of-the-art performance while making selection up to 3.5 times faster. The result supports using a small amount of precise influence computation to guide selection across a much larger dataset.
summary.tldr: Influence Distillation uses landmark-based influence estimates to select fine-tuning data, matching or improving performance with up to 3.5 times faster selection.

title: Efficient Data Selection at Scale via Influence Distillation

abstract: We consider the problem of active seriation, where the goal is to recover an unknown ordering of $n$ items based on noisy observations of pairwise similarities. The similarities are assumed to correlate with the underlying ordering: pairs of items that are close in the ordering tend to have higher similarity scores, and vice versa. In the active setting, the learner sequentially selects which item pairs to query and receives noisy similarity measurements. We propose a novel active seriation algorithm that provably recovers the correct ordering with high probability. Furthermore, we provide optimal performance guarantees in terms of both the probability of error and the number of observations required for successful recovery.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to recover a hidden ordering of items from noisy measurements of their pairwise similarity. Its central assumption is that similarity reflects position: items near one another in the underlying order tend to be more similar than items farther apart. The task is therefore to reconstruct a sequence from indirect, imperfect evidence about which items belong near each other.

The setting is active, meaning the learner chooses which pair to measure next. It does not simply receive a fixed collection of observations. This makes measurement selection part of the problem: the algorithm must gather enough useful information to identify the ordering while controlling the number of queries it uses.

The proposed algorithm comes with a high-probability guarantee of recovering the correct order. The authors also establish optimal guarantees for both error probability and observation requirements. These are statistical claims under the stated ordering-and-similarity setting; recovery is highly probable rather than certain. The contribution connects reliable reconstruction with efficient, sequential evidence collection.
summary.tldr: An active algorithm recovers hidden item orderings from noisy similarity queries with optimal statistical guarantees.

title: Active Seriation: Efficient Ordering Recovery with Statistical Guarantees

abstract: Discrete diffusion models have recently gained significant attention due to their ability to process complex discrete structures for language modeling. However, fine-tuning these models with policy gradient methods, as is commonly done in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), remains a challenging task. We propose an efficient, broadly applicable, and theoretically justified policy gradient algorithm, called Score Entropy Policy Optimization (SEPO), for fine-tuning discrete diffusion models over non-differentiable rewards. Our numerical experiments across several discrete generative tasks demonstrate the scalability and efficiency of our method.

We propose an efficient, broadly applicable, and theoretically justified policy gradient algorithm, called Score Entropy Policy Optimization (SEPO), for fine-tuning discrete diffusion models over non-differentiable rewards. Our numerical experiments across several discrete generative tasks demonstrate the scalability and efficiency of our method.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to fine-tune discrete diffusion models using reward signals. These models have attracted interest for generating complex discrete structures, including language, but applying policy-gradient methods to them remains challenging. The objective is to make reward-based adaptation practical for this model family, extending a style of optimization commonly used in reinforcement learning from human feedback.

The proposed algorithm is Score Entropy Policy Optimization, or SEPO. It is designed to optimize non-differentiable rewards: feedback can evaluate a generated result without providing a derivative that can be passed directly through the reward calculation. The authors present SEPO as an efficient, broadly applicable policy-gradient algorithm with theoretical justification for fine-tuning discrete diffusion models.

Numerical experiments across several discrete generation tasks demonstrate the method’s scalability and efficiency. The contribution therefore combines an optimization algorithm, a theoretical basis, and empirical evidence across multiple tasks. Its significance is in making discrete diffusion models more amenable to reward-driven fine-tuning, so their adaptation can be guided by evaluations of generated outputs.
summary.tldr: SEPO provides a theoretically justified policy-gradient method for fine-tuning discrete diffusion models with non-differentiable rewards.

title: Fine-Tuning Discrete Diffusion Models with Policy Gradient Methods

abstract: Graph Transformers (GTs) have shown strong empirical performance, yet current architectures vary widely in their use of attention mechanisms, positional embeddings (PEs), and expressivity. Existing expressivity results are often tied to specific design choices and lack comprehensive empirical validation on large-scale data. This leaves a gap between theory and practice, preventing generalizable insights that exceed particular application domains. Here, we propose the Generalized-Distance Transformer (GDT), a GT architecture using standard attention that incorporates many advancements for GTs from recent years, and develop a fine-grained understanding of the GDT's representation power in terms of attention and PEs. Through extensive experiments, we identify design choices that consistently perform well across various applications, tasks, and model scales, demonstrating strong performance in a few-shot transfer setting without fine-tuning. Our evaluation covers over eight million graphs with roughly 270M tokens across diverse domains, including image-based object detection, molecular property prediction, code summarization, and out-of-distribution algorithmic reasoning. We distill our theoretical and practical findings into several generalizable insights about effective GT design, training, and inference.

paragraphs: Graph Transformers vary substantially in their attention mechanisms and in how they encode structural position. That variety makes it difficult to know whether a successful design reflects a broadly useful principle or a particular application. This paper combines theoretical analysis with a large empirical study to connect architectural choices to both representational capability and practical performance.

The authors introduce the Generalized-Distance Transformer, which uses standard attention and incorporates several recent advances in graph Transformer design. They analyze its representation power in terms of attention and positional embeddings. This provides a shared architecture through which the consequences of those choices can be examined in finer detail.

The evaluation spans more than eight million graphs and roughly 270 million tokens, covering object detection, molecular properties, code summarization, and algorithmic reasoning outside the training distribution. The authors identify choices that perform consistently across tasks, domains, and model scales, and report strong few-shot transfer without fine-tuning. The contribution is a set of design, training, and inference insights supported by both theory and unusually broad empirical coverage.
summary.tldr: The Generalized-Distance Transformer connects expressivity analysis with broad experiments to identify graph Transformer design choices that transfer across applications.

title: Generalizable Insights for Graph Transformers in Theory and Practice

abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models have gained widespread application across various domains, demonstrating remarkable creative potential. However, the strong generalization capabilities of diffusion models can inadvertently lead to the generation of not-safe-for-work (NSFW) content, posing significant risks to their safe deployment. While several concept erasure methods have been proposed to mitigate the issue associated with NSFW content, a comprehensive evaluation of their effectiveness across various scenarios remains absent. To bridge this gap, we introduce a full-pipeline toolkit specifically designed for concept erasure and conduct the first systematic study of NSFW concept erasure methods. By examining the interplay between the underlying mechanisms and empirical observations, we provide in-depth insights and practical guidance for the effective application of concept erasure methods in various real-world scenarios, with the aim of advancing the understanding of content safety in diffusion models and establishing a solid foundation for future research and development in this critical area.

paragraphs: Text-to-image diffusion models can generate unwanted NSFW imagery as well as useful creative content. Concept erasure methods seek to reduce this behavior, but the paper identifies a gap in how their effectiveness has been assessed across different scenarios. Its central contribution is a systematic evaluation effort supported by a toolkit covering the concept-erasure pipeline.

The study connects the mechanisms behind erasure methods with their observed behavior. This makes the assessment concerned with both how a method operates and how it performs in practice. The authors describe the work as the first systematic study of NSFW concept erasure, with coverage intended to inform use across varied real-world situations.

The stated outcome is a set of insights and practical guidance for applying existing erasure methods. The significance lies in giving content-safety research a more comprehensive basis for comparing and understanding these interventions. The abstract presents this as groundwork for better application and further research, rather than as a claim that concept erasure guarantees the absence of unwanted output.
summary.tldr: This paper introduces a toolkit and systematic assessment of NSFW concept erasure in text-to-image diffusion models.

title: Comprehensive Assessment and Analysis for NSFW Content Erasure in Text-to-Image Diffusion models

abstract: Sparse plus Low-Rank $(\mathbf{S} + \mathbf{L}\mathbf{R})$ decomposition of Large Language Models (LLMs) has emerged as a promising direction in $\textit{model compression}$, aiming to decompose pre-trained model weights into a sum of sparse and low-rank matrices $\mathbf{W} \approx \mathbf{S} + \mathbf{LR}$. Despite recent progress, existing methods often suffer from substantial performance degradation compared to dense models. In this work, we introduce $\texttt{3BASiL-TM}$, an efficient one-shot post-training method for $(\mathbf{S} + \mathbf{L}\mathbf{R})$ decomposition of LLMs that addresses this gap. Our approach first introduces a novel 3-Block Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) method, termed $\texttt{3BASiL}$, to minimize the layer-wise reconstruction error with convergence guarantees. We then design a transformer-matching ($\texttt{TM}$) refinement step that jointly optimizes the sparse and low-rank components across transformer layers. This step minimizes a novel memory-efficient loss that aligns outputs at the transformer level. Notably, the $\texttt{TM}$ procedure is universal as it can enhance any $(\mathbf{S} + \mathbf{L}\mathbf{R})$ decomposition, including pure sparsity. Our numerical experiments show that $\texttt{3BASiL-TM}$ reduces the WikiText2 perplexity gap to dense LLaMA-8B model by over 30% under a (2:4 Sparse + 64 LR) configuration, compared to prior methods. Moreover, our method achieves over 2.5x faster compression runtime on an A100 GPU compared to SOTA $(\mathbf{S} + \mathbf{L}\mathbf{R})$ method. Our code is available at https://github.com/mazumder-lab/3BASiL.

paragraphs: 3BASiL-TM compresses a pretrained language model by approximating its weight matrices with two complementary parts: a sparse matrix and a product of low-rank matrices. This representation offers a way to reduce model size, but existing decompositions can substantially damage prediction quality. The paper addresses both the initial approximation and its subsequent refinement.

The transformer-matching stage then jointly adjusts the sparse and low-rank components across transformer layers. Its memory-efficient objective matches transformer outputs, extending the optimization beyond separate layer reconstructions. This refinement can also be applied to other decompositions, including purely sparse ones.

For LLaMA-8B with the reported 2:4 sparsity and rank-64 configuration, the method reduces the WikiText2 perplexity gap from the dense model by over 30% relative to prior methods. Compression itself runs over 2.5 times faster than the compared state-of-the-art method on an A100 GPU. These results concern compression runtime and retained prediction quality.
summary.tldr: 3BASiL-TM combines layer reconstruction and transformer-level refinement to compress language models more quickly while better preserving prediction quality.

title: 3BASiL: An Algorithmic Framework for Sparse plus Low-Rank Compression of LLMs

abstract: We study the problem of smooth imitation learning for online sequence prediction, where the goal is to train a policy that can smoothly imitate demonstrated behavior in a dynamic and continuous environment in response to online, sequential context input. Since the mapping from context to behavior is often complex, we take a learning reduction approach to reduce smooth imitation learning to a regression problem using complex function classes that are regularized to ensure smoothness. We present a learning meta-algorithm that achieves fast and stable convergence to a good policy. Our approach enjoys several attractive properties, including being fully deterministic, employing an adaptive learning rate that can provably yield larger policy improvements compared to previous approaches, and the ability to ensure stable convergence. Our empirical results demonstrate significant performance gains over previous approaches.

paragraphs: This paper studies policies that imitate demonstrated behavior while responding to context arriving sequentially in a dynamic, continuous environment. The goal includes smooth behavior, so learning must account for how responses evolve over time. A complex relationship between context and behavior makes this more demanding than simply matching isolated demonstrated outputs.

The authors reduce the imitation-learning problem to regression. This allows complex function classes to represent the context-to-behavior mapping, while regularization enforces smoothness. They then introduce a learning meta-algorithm designed to reach a good policy quickly and stably. The reduction connects the behavioral objective to a regression problem that explicitly includes the desired smoothness property.

The approach is fully deterministic and uses an adaptive learning rate. The authors prove that this rate can yield larger policy improvements than previous approaches, and the method can ensure stable convergence. Empirical results show significant performance gains over earlier methods. Together, the contributions address expressive behavior modeling, controlled changes in behavior, and stability of the learning process.
summary.tldr: Smooth imitation learning is reduced to regularized regression, with a deterministic adaptive procedure supporting stable policy improvement.

title: Smooth Imitation Learning for Online Sequence Prediction

abstract: Generic generation and manipulation of text is challenging and has limited success compared to recent deep generative modeling in visual domain. This paper aims at generating plausible text sentences, whose attributes are controlled by learning disentangled latent representations with designated semantics. We propose a new neural generative model which combines variational auto-encoders (VAEs) and holistic attribute discriminators for effective imposition of semantic structures. The model can alternatively be seen as enhancing VAEs with the wake-sleep algorithm for leveraging fake samples as extra training data. With differentiable approximation to discrete text samples, explicit constraints on independent attribute controls, and efficient collaborative learning of generator and discriminators, our model learns interpretable representations from even only word annotations, and produces short sentences with desired attributes of sentiment and tenses. Quantitative experiments using trained classifiers as evaluators validate the accuracy of sentence and attribute generation.

paragraphs: The paper aims to generate plausible sentences while controlling attributes such as sentiment and tense. It seeks latent representations whose parts have designated meanings, so that generation can respond to interpretable controls. The proposed neural model combines a variational autoencoder with attribute discriminators that assess generated text as a whole.

Several components support this learning process: a differentiable approximation to discrete text samples, explicit constraints on independent attribute controls, and collaborative training of the generator and discriminators. The contribution is a framework that builds semantic controls into generative learning, with evidence focused on short sentences and the specified attributes rather than unrestricted control over every aspect of text.
summary.tldr: A variational text generator with attribute discriminators learns interpretable controls for producing short sentences with desired sentiment and tense.

title: Toward Controlled Generation of Text

abstract: We consider the popular problem of sparse empirical risk minimization with linear predictors and a large number of both features and observations. With a convex-concave saddle point objective reformulation, we propose a Doubly Greedy Primal-Dual Coordinate Descent algorithm that is able to exploit sparsity in both primal and dual variables. It enjoys a low cost per iteration and our theoretical analysis shows that it converges linearly with a good iteration complexity, provided that the set of primal variables is sparse. We then extend this algorithm further to leverage active sets. The resulting new algorithm is even faster, and experiments on large-scale Multi-class data sets show that our algorithm achieves up to 30 times speedup on several state-of-the-art optimization methods.

paragraphs: Training sparse linear predictors can be costly when a dataset contains both many observations and many features. This paper tackles sparse empirical risk minimization by reformulating the objective as a convex-concave saddle-point problem. That representation exposes both primal and dual variables, giving the optimizer two places where sparsity can reduce work.

The proposed Doubly Greedy Primal-Dual Coordinate Descent algorithm exploits sparsity in both sets of variables and has a low cost per iteration. The theoretical analysis establishes linear convergence with favorable iteration complexity provided the primal variable set is sparse. This condition matters: the convergence statement is explicitly tied to the sparse setting analyzed by the authors.

An extension uses active sets to make the algorithm faster still. Experiments on large-scale multiclass datasets report speedups of up to thirtyfold over several state-of-the-art optimization methods. Together, the results connect inexpensive individual updates, a conditional convergence guarantee, and substantial observed acceleration on the tested problems.
summary.tldr: A primal-dual coordinate method exploits sparsity on both sides of the optimization problem, with conditional linear convergence and reported speedups up to thirtyfold.

title: Doubly Greedy Primal-Dual Coordinate Descent for Sparse Empirical Risk Minimization

abstract: Relational data are usually highly incomplete in practice, which inspires us to leverage side information to improve the performance of community detection and link prediction. This paper presents a Bayesian probabilistic approach that incorporates various kinds of node attributes encoded in binary form in relational models with Poisson likelihood. Our method works flexibly with both directed and undirected relational networks. The inference can be done by efficient Gibbs sampling which leverages sparsity of both networks and node attributes. Extensive experiments show that our models achieve the state-of-the-art link prediction results, especially with highly incomplete relational data.

paragraphs: Relational datasets often reveal only part of a network's connections. That incompleteness makes community detection and link prediction difficult when the model relies on relationships alone. This paper introduces a Bayesian approach that incorporates attributes of the nodes as additional information for learning about the network.

The method accepts different kinds of node attributes encoded in binary form and incorporates them into relational models with a Poisson likelihood. It works with both directed and undirected networks. Inference uses Gibbs sampling, with efficiency coming from exploiting sparsity in both the observed network and the attribute representation.

Extensive experiments yield link-prediction results reported as state of the art, especially when the relational data is highly incomplete. The stated evidence is strongest for predicting links in those settings. The broader contribution is a flexible probabilistic framework that uses two available sources of information together: observed relationships and descriptions of the entities involved. Its inference procedure also uses their sparse structure to keep computation efficient.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian relational model incorporates binary node attributes and achieves strong link prediction, particularly for highly incomplete networks.

title: Leveraging Node Attributes for Incomplete Relational Data

abstract: Many continuous control tasks have bounded action spaces. When policy gradient methods are applied to such tasks, out-of-bound actions need to be clipped before execution, while policies are usually optimized as if the actions are not clipped. We propose a policy gradient estimator that exploits the knowledge of actions being clipped to reduce the variance in estimation. We prove that our estimator, named clipped action policy gradient (CAPG), is unbiased and achieves lower variance than the conventional estimator that ignores action bounds. Experimental results demonstrate that CAPG generally outperforms the conventional estimator, indicating that it is a better policy gradient estimator for continuous control tasks. The source code is available at https://github.com/pfnet-research/capg.

We prove that our estimator, named clipped action policy gradient (CAPG), is unbiased and achieves lower variance than the conventional estimator that ignores action bounds. paragraphs: Many continuous control problems allow actions only within specified bounds. A policy may nevertheless generate an action outside those bounds, requiring it to be clipped before execution. The paper identifies a mismatch in the usual learning procedure: policy optimization commonly treats the sampled action as though this clipping had not occurred.

Clipped Action Policy Gradient, or CAPG, incorporates knowledge of clipping into the gradient estimator. The purpose is to reduce variability in the estimated learning signal by accounting for how actions are actually executed. The authors prove that the estimator is unbiased and has lower variance than the conventional estimator that ignores the action bounds.

Experiments show that CAPG generally performs better than the conventional estimator. The theoretical result establishes properties of gradient estimation, while the empirical result supports its usefulness for learning control policies. The broader contribution is a way to use an existing feature of bounded-action environments to improve estimation, with experimental superiority described as general rather than universal.
summary.tldr: CAPG accounts for action clipping to produce unbiased policy gradients with lower variance than an estimator that ignores action bounds.

title: Clipped Action Policy Gradient

abstract: Planning problems are among the most important and well-studied problems in artificial intelligence. They are most typically solved by tree search algorithms that simulate ahead into the future, evaluate future states, and back-up those evaluations to the root of a search tree. Among these algorithms, Monte-Carlo tree search (MCTS) is one of the most general, powerful and widely used. A typical implementation of MCTS uses cleverly designed rules, optimised to the particular characteristics of the domain. These rules control where the simulation traverses, what to evaluate in the states that are reached, and how to back-up those evaluations. In this paper we instead learn where, what and how to search. Our architecture, which we call an MCTSnet, incorporates simulation-based search inside a neural network, by expanding, evaluating and backing-up a vector embedding. The parameters of the network are trained end-to-end using gradient-based optimisation. When applied to small searches in the well-known planning problem Sokoban, the learned search algorithm significantly outperformed MCTS baselines.

paragraphs: Tree-search planners simulate possible futures, evaluate the states they reach, and return information toward the current decision. Monte-Carlo tree search commonly relies on carefully designed rules for these operations. This paper asks whether a neural network can learn where to search, what to evaluate, and how to combine the resulting information.

The proposed MCTSnet embeds simulation-based search within a neural architecture. It expands, evaluates, and backs up vector representations through the search process. All network parameters are trained together using gradient-based optimization. This makes the search procedure itself learnable, including how information from simulated futures contributes to the eventual decision.

The authors evaluate the approach on Sokoban using small searches. In that setting, the learned search algorithm significantly outperforms the MCTS baselines tested. The result demonstrates that learning the internal operations of search can improve planning within a limited-search regime. Its stated empirical scope is small Sokoban searches, where the learned representation and search rules are assessed together as one planning system.
summary.tldr: MCTSnets learn the operations of simulation-based tree search and significantly outperform tested MCTS baselines on small Sokoban searches.

title: Learning to search with MCTSnets

abstract: Can we efficiently extract useful information from a large user-generated dataset while protecting the privacy of the users and/or ensuring fairness in representation? We cast this problem as an instance of a deletion-robust submodular maximization where part of the data may be deleted or masked due to privacy concerns or fairness criteria. We propose the first memory-efficient centralized, streaming, and distributed methods with constant-factor approximation guarantees against any number of adversarial deletions. We extensively evaluate the performance of our algorithms on real-world applications, including (i) Uber-pick up locations with location privacy constraints; (ii) feature selection with fairness constraints for income prediction and crime rate prediction; and (iii) robust to deletion summarization of census data, consisting of 2,458,285 feature vectors. Our experiments show that our solution is robust against even $80%$ of data deletion.

We cast this problem as an instance of a deletion-robust submodular maximization where part of the data may be deleted or masked due to privacy concerns or fairness criteria. We propose the first memory-efficient centralized, streaming, and distributed methods with constant-factor approximation guarantees against any number of adversarial deletions. We extensively evaluate the performance of our algorithms on real-world applications, including (i) Uber-pick up locations with location privacy constraints; (ii) feature selection with fairness constraints for income prediction and crime rate prediction; and (iii) robust to deletion summarization of census data, consisting of 2,458,285 feature vectors. paragraphs: A useful data summary may need to survive the removal or masking of records because of privacy concerns or fairness criteria. This paper formulates that challenge as deletion-robust submodular maximization. The aim is to retain useful information even when an adversary chooses which data to delete.

The authors propose memory-efficient methods for centralized, streaming, and distributed computation. They report constant-factor approximation guarantees against any number of adversarial deletions. These guarantees formalize the quality of the resulting solution, while the different processing settings address how the approach can operate on large datasets.

The experiments examine Uber pickup locations under location-privacy constraints, feature selection with fairness constraints for income and crime-rate prediction, and deletion-robust census summarization. The census dataset contains 2,458,285 feature vectors. The authors report robustness even when 80% of the data is deleted. That empirical result complements the approximation theory by showing substantial deletion tolerance in the evaluated applications, where privacy or representation requirements can remove much of the available information.
summary.tldr: Memory-efficient summarization algorithms offer approximation guarantees under adversarial deletions and show empirical robustness to 80% data removal.

title: Scalable Deletion-Robust Submodular Maximization: Data Summarization with Privacy and Fairness Constraints

abstract: We present a generalization of the adversarial linear bandits framework, where the underlying losses are kernel functions (with an associated reproducing kernel Hilbert space) rather than linear functions. We study a version of the exponential weights algorithm and bound its regret in this setting. Under conditions on the eigen-decay of the kernel we provide a sharp characterization of the regret for this algorithm. When we have polynomial eigen-decay ($\mu_j \le \mathcal{O}(j^{-\beta})$), we find that the regret is bounded by $\mathcal{R}_n \le \mathcal{O}(n^{\beta/2(\beta-1)})$. While under the assumption of exponential eigen-decay ($\mu_j \le \mathcal{O}(e^{-\beta j })$) we get an even tighter bound on the regret $\mathcal{R}_n \le \tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{1/2})$. When the eigen-decay is polynomial we also show a non-matching minimax lower bound on the regret of $\mathcal{R}_n \ge \Omega(n^{(\beta+1)/2\beta})$ and a lower bound of $\mathcal{R}_n \ge \Omega(n^{1/2})$ when the decay in the eigen-values is exponentially fast. We also study the full information setting when the underlying losses are kernel functions and present an adapted exponential weights algorithm and a conditional gradient descent algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper extends adversarial linear bandits to settings where losses are kernel functions associated with a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. This broadens the loss structure beyond linear functions. The authors analyze a version of exponential weights, measuring performance through regret: the accumulated cost of learning relative to a hindsight benchmark.

The guarantees depend on how quickly the kernel's eigenvalues decrease. With polynomial decay controlled by beta, the upper bound grows as n raised to beta divided by twice beta minus two. With exponential decay, the upper bound is approximately square-root growth in the number of rounds, apart from logarithmic factors. Faster spectral decay thus supports a tighter guarantee in the analyzed setting.

Lower bounds clarify how close these guarantees are to the best possible. The exponential-decay lower bound also has square-root growth, while the polynomial-decay lower bound does not match the upper bound. The paper additionally studies full-information feedback and provides both an adapted exponential-weights method and a conditional-gradient method for kernel losses.
summary.tldr: Online learning with kernel losses admits regret guarantees controlled by spectral decay, with nearly matching bounds for exponential decay.

title: Online learning with kernel losses

abstract: The last few years have seen a staggering number of empirical studies of the robustness of neural networks in a model of adversarial perturbations of their inputs. Most rely on an adversary which carries out local modifications within prescribed balls. None however has so far questioned the broader picture: how to frame a resource-bounded adversary so that it can be severely detrimental to learning, a non-trivial problem which entails at a minimum the choice of loss and classifiers. We suggest a formal answer for losses that satisfy the minimal statistical requirement of being proper . We pin down a simple sufficient property for any given class of adversaries to be detrimental to learning, involving a central measure of “harmfulness” which generalizes the well-known class of integral probability metrics. A key feature of our result is that it holds for all proper losses, and for a popular subset of these, the optimisation of this central measure appears to be independent of the loss . When classifiers are Lipschitz – a now popular approach in adversarial training –, this optimisation resorts to optimal transport to make a low-budget compression of class marginals. Toy experiments reveal a finding recently separately observed: training against a sufficiently budgeted adversary of this kind improves generalization.

paragraphs: This paper asks how to formalize an adversary with limited resources that can seriously obstruct learning. It examines the interaction among adversarial capabilities, classifier choices, and losses satisfying the statistical requirement of being proper. The authors identify a sufficient property of an adversary class for it to be harmful to learning.

That property involves a measure of harmfulness generalizing integral probability metrics. The result applies to all proper losses. For a popular subset, optimizing the measure appears to be independent of the loss, a qualified observation rather than an unconditional conclusion. When classifiers are Lipschitz, the optimization takes an optimal-transport form that compresses class-conditional distributions within a limited budget.

Toy experiments also show that training against an adversary of this kind can improve generalization when its budget is sufficiently large. This empirical observation sits alongside the theoretical account of adversarial harmfulness: an adversary capable of making learning difficult can also be useful during training. The improvement is reported for the toy experiments and the specified budget condition.
summary.tldr: A sufficient condition characterizes harmful resource-limited adversaries, connecting Lipschitz classifiers to optimal transport and revealing generalization benefits in toy experiments.

title: Monge blunts Bayes: Hardness Results for Adversarial Training

abstract: The study of adversarial robustness has so far largely focused on perturbations bound in $\ell_p$-norms. However, state-of-the-art models turn out to be also vulnerable to other, more natural classes of perturbations such as translations and rotations. In this work, we thoroughly investigate the vulnerability of neural network–based classifiers to rotations and translations. While data augmentation offers relatively small robustness, we use ideas from robust optimization and test-time input aggregation to significantly improve robustness. Finally we find that, in contrast to the $\ell_p$-norm case, first-order methods cannot reliably find worst-case perturbations. This highlights spatial robustness as a fundamentally different setting requiring additional study.

However, state-of-the-art models turn out to be also vulnerable to other, more natural classes of perturbations such as translations and rotations. In this work, we thoroughly investigate the vulnerability of neural network–based classifiers to rotations and translations. While data augmentation offers relatively small robustness, we use ideas from robust optimization and test-time input aggregation to significantly improve robustness. Finally we find that, in contrast to the $\ell_p$-norm case, first-order methods cannot reliably find worst-case perturbations. This highlights spatial robustness as a fundamentally different setting requiring additional study.

paragraphs: An image classifier can fail when an image is shifted or rotated, even though these transformations are natural changes in how an object is presented. This paper studies that vulnerability directly. It expands the investigation of adversarial robustness beyond perturbations constrained by numerical measures of pixel changes to spatial transformations of the input.

The authors examine both the vulnerability and ways to reduce it. In their investigation, data augmentation provides relatively modest robustness. Approaches drawing on robust optimization and combining information from inputs at prediction time produce substantially larger improvements. These findings identify training and prediction procedures that can help classifiers cope with rotations and translations.

The work also finds that first-order methods cannot reliably locate the most damaging spatial perturbations. This matters for evaluation: an unsuccessful search may fail to expose an existing weakness. The authors therefore identify spatial robustness as a setting with distinct challenges, where methods used for norm-bounded perturbations do not automatically provide reliable worst-case assessments.
summary.tldr: Rotations and translations expose classifier weaknesses that require distinct robustness improvements and more reliable attack searches.

title: Exploring the Landscape of Spatial Robustness

abstract: A significant challenge for the practical application of reinforcement learning to real world problems is the need to specify an oracle reward function that correctly defines a task. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) seeks to avoid this challenge by instead inferring a reward function from expert demonstrations. While appealing, it can be impractically expensive to collect datasets of demonstrations that cover the variation common in the real world (e.g. opening any type of door). Thus in practice, IRL must commonly be performed with only a limited set of demonstrations where it can be exceedingly difficult to unambiguously recover a reward function. In this work, we exploit the insight that demonstrations from other tasks can be used to constrain the set of possible reward functions by learning a "prior" that is specifically optimized for the ability to infer expressive reward functions from limited numbers of demonstrations. We demonstrate that our method can efficiently recover rewards from images for novel tasks and provide intuition as to how our approach is analogous to learning a prior.
