We demonstrate that our method can efficiently recover rewards from images for novel tasks and provide intuition as to how our approach is analogous to learning a prior.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning requires a reward function that specifies the intended task. Inverse reinforcement learning attempts to infer that function from expert demonstrations, but a small demonstration set may be compatible with several different rewards. Collecting enough demonstrations to cover the variety of real-world tasks can also be impractically expensive.

This paper uses demonstrations from other tasks to constrain the reward functions considered for a new task. It learns a prior specifically optimized to support the inference of expressive rewards from limited demonstrations. The transferred knowledge therefore concerns how to infer intent, helping narrow the ambiguity that remains when examples of the current task are scarce.

The authors demonstrate efficient recovery of rewards from images for novel tasks and explain how their approach is analogous to learning a prior. This result connects experience across tasks to the practical problem of reward specification. Its significance is that earlier demonstrations can contribute useful structure to a new inference problem, reducing reliance on an extensive set of demonstrations for every individual task.
summary.tldr: The method learns from demonstrations across tasks to help infer expressive reward functions for new tasks from limited examples.

title: Learning a Prior over Intent via Meta-Inverse Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Generalized zero-shot learning is a significant topic but faced with bias problem, which leads to unseen classes being easily misclassified into seen classes. Hence we propose a embedding model called co-representation network to learn a more uniform visual embedding space that effectively alleviates the bias problem and helps with classification. We mathematically analyze our model and find it learns a projection with high local linearity, which is proved to cause less bias problem. The network consists of a cooperation module for representation and a relation module for classification, it is simple in structure and can be easily trained in an end-to-end manner. Experiments show that our method outperforms existing generalized zero-shot learning methods on several benchmark datasets.
originalAbstract: Generalized zero-shot learning is a significant topic but faced with bias problem, which leads to unseen classes being easily misclassified into seen classes. Hence we propose a embedding model called co-representation network to learn a more uniform visual embedding space that effectively alleviates the bias problem and helps with classification. We mathematically analyze our model and find it learns a projection with high local linearity, which is proved to cause less bias problem. The network consists of a cooperation module for representation and a relation module for classification, it is simple in structure and can be easily trained in an end-to-end manner. Experiments show that our method outperforms existing generalized zero-shot learning methods on several benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Generalized zero-shot learning requires recognizing classes that were seen during training alongside classes that were not. A central difficulty is bias toward the seen classes: examples from unseen classes can be assigned to familiar categories too readily. The paper addresses this problem by changing the visual representation on which classification operates.

The proposed co-representation network learns a more uniform embedding space. It combines a cooperation module that builds representations with a relation module that performs classification, and the whole network can be trained end to end. The authors also analyze the learned projection mathematically. They find that it has high local linearity and prove a connection between this property and reduced bias.

The representation design therefore has both an architectural motivation and a mathematical explanation for why it can help unseen classes. Experiments report better performance than existing generalized zero-shot methods on several benchmark datasets. The findings support the idea that improving the geometry of the embedding space can reduce the tendency to classify unfamiliar categories as familiar ones, rather than addressing classification only at the final decision stage.
summary.tldr: A co-representation network learns a more uniform visual embedding to reduce bias toward seen classes in generalized zero-shot learning.

title: Co-Representation Network for Generalized Zero-Shot Learning

abstract: Many real-world applications have to tackle the Positive-Unlabeled (PU) learning problem, i.e., learning binary classifiers from a large amount of unlabeled data and a few labeled positive examples. While current state-of-the-art methods employ importance reweighting to design various biased or unbiased risk estimators, they completely ignored the learning capability of the model itself, which could provide reliable supervision. This motivates us to propose a novel Self-PU learning framework, which seamlessly integrates PU learning and self-training. Self-PU highlights three “self”-oriented building blocks: a self-paced training algorithm that adaptively discovers and augments confident positive/negative examples as the training proceeds; a self-reweighted, instance-aware loss; and a self-distillation scheme that introduces teacher-students learning as an effective regularization for PU learning. We demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of Self-PU on common PU learning benchmarks (MNIST and CIFAR10), which compare favorably against the latest competitors. Moreover, we study a real-world application of PU learning, i.e., classifying brain images of Alzheimer’s Disease. Self-PU obtains significantly improved results on the renowned Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database over existing methods.

This motivates us to propose a novel Self-PU learning framework, which seamlessly integrates PU learning and self-training. paragraphs: Positive-unlabeled learning trains a binary classifier from a few known positive examples and many examples whose labels are unknown. An instance-aware loss adjusts the weighting of examples. A self-distillation scheme uses teacher-student learning as regularization. Together, these components address how to expand supervision, how to weight it, and how to regularize the resulting learning process.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance on positive-unlabeled benchmarks based on MNIST and CIFAR10. They also evaluate the framework on brain-image classification for Alzheimer’s disease, reporting significant gains over existing methods on the ADNI database. These results support using the model’s own confidence and teacher-student training to improve learning when explicit negative labels are unavailable.
summary.tldr: Self-PU improves positive-unlabeled classification through confident-example selection, instance-aware reweighting, and teacher-student regularization.

title: Self-PU: Self Boosted and Calibrated Positive-Unlabeled Training

abstract: An acknowledged weakness of neural networks is their vulnerability to adversarial perturbations to the inputs. To improve the robustness of these models, one of the most popular defense mechanisms is to alternatively maximize the loss over the constrained perturbations (or called adversaries) on the inputs using projected gradient ascent and minimize over weights. In this paper, we analyze the dynamics of the maximization step towards understanding the experimentally observed effectiveness of this defense mechanism. Specifically, we investigate the non-concave landscape of the adversaries for a two-layer neural network with a quadratic loss. Our main result proves that projected gradient ascent finds a local maximum of this non-concave problem in a polynomial number of iterations with high probability. To our knowledge, this is the first work that provides a convergence analysis of the first-order adversaries. Moreover, our analysis demonstrates that, in the initial phase of adversarial training, the scale of the inputs matters in the sense that a smaller input scale leads to faster convergence of adversarial training and a “more regular” landscape. Finally, we show that these theoretical findings are in excellent agreement with a series of experiments.

paragraphs: Adversarial training often alternates between finding input perturbations that increase loss and updating network weights to reduce it. The perturbation search commonly uses projected gradient ascent. This paper analyzes that maximization step to help explain why the procedure can work despite the non-concave landscape faced by the adversary.

The analysis considers a two-layer neural network with quadratic loss. In this setting, the authors prove that projected gradient ascent reaches a local maximum in a polynomial number of iterations with high probability. The distinction between a local and global maximum is central: the guarantee concerns convergence to a local solution of the perturbation problem.

Experiments closely agree with the theoretical findings. Together, these results provide a convergence account for first-order adversaries and identify input scale as a meaningful factor in their early training dynamics.
summary.tldr: For a two-layer network with quadratic loss, projected gradient ascent finds a local adversarial maximum efficiently with high probability.

title: Towards Understanding the Dynamics of the First-Order Adversaries

abstract: Designing video prediction models that account for the inherent uncertainty of the future is challenging. Most works in the literature are based on stochastic image-autoregressive recurrent networks, which raises several performance and applicability issues. An alternative is to use fully latent temporal models which untie frame synthesis and temporal dynamics. However, no such model for stochastic video prediction has been proposed in the literature yet, due to design and training difficulties. In this paper, we overcome these difficulties by introducing a novel stochastic temporal model whose dynamics are governed in a latent space by a residual update rule. This first-order scheme is motivated by discretization schemes of differential equations. It naturally models video dynamics as it allows our simpler, more interpretable, latent model to outperform prior state-of-the-art methods on challenging datasets.

paragraphs: Video prediction must account for uncertainty because a sequence of observed frames can have multiple possible futures. Many existing approaches use stochastic recurrent models that predict through the image sequence itself. This paper develops an alternative in which temporal evolution takes place fully in a latent space, separating the dynamics from the process that synthesizes frames.

The proposed stochastic temporal model updates its latent state through a residual rule. Each step modifies the current latent representation, using a first-order scheme motivated by methods for discretizing differential equations. This provides a structured way to describe change over time while retaining stochasticity for uncertain futures. The authors present the model as overcoming design and training difficulties that had hindered this fully latent approach.

On challenging datasets, the model outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods while being simpler and more interpretable according to the authors. The finding supports residual latent dynamics as an effective way to model video evolution. Its significance lies in treating temporal change and image synthesis as separable components within a stochastic prediction model.
summary.tldr: A stochastic residual model predicts video dynamics entirely in latent space and outperforms prior methods on challenging datasets.

title: Stochastic Latent Residual Video Prediction

abstract: Communication cost is often a bottleneck in federated learning and other client-based distributed learning scenarios. To overcome this, several gradient compression and model compression algorithms have been proposed. In this work, we propose an alternative approach whereby an ensemble of pre-trained base predictors is trained via federated learning. This method allows for training a model which may otherwise surpass the communication bandwidth and storage capacity of the clients to be learned with on-device data through federated learning. Motivated by language modeling, we prove the optimality of ensemble methods for density estimation for standard empirical risk minimization and agnostic risk minimization. We provide communication-efficient ensemble algorithms for federated learning, where per-round communication cost is independent of the size of the ensemble. Furthermore, unlike works on gradient compression, our proposed approach reduces the communication cost of both server-to-client and client-to-server communication.

paragraphs: Communication can restrict federated learning when clients have limited bandwidth and storage. FedBoost approaches this problem by federatively training an ensemble of predictors that have already been pretrained. This creates a way to learn from data held on devices even when the resulting model could exceed what individual clients can comfortably communicate or store.

The paper develops ensemble algorithms whose communication cost per round does not depend on the ensemble's size. The savings apply in both directions: messages from the server to clients and messages from clients back to the server. This directly addresses the exchange required to coordinate learning across devices, rather than focusing exclusively on compressing gradient messages.

Motivated by language modeling, the authors also prove optimality results for ensemble methods in density estimation under standard empirical risk minimization and agnostic risk minimization. Those results provide theoretical support in the specified learning settings. Together, the analysis and algorithms connect ensemble learning with a concrete way to control federated communication costs.
summary.tldr: FedBoost trains ensembles through federated learning with per-round communication independent of ensemble size and savings in both communication directions.

title: FedBoost: A Communication-Efficient Algorithm for Federated Learning

abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of constrained min-max optimization in a black-box setting, where the desired optimizer cannot access the gradients of the objective function but may query its values. We present a principled optimization framework, integrating a zeroth-order (ZO) gradient estimator with an alternating projected stochastic gradient descent-ascent method, where the former only requires a small number of function queries and the later needs just one-step descent/ascent update. We show that the proposed framework, referred to as ZO-Min-Max, has a sublinear convergence rate under mild conditions and scales gracefully with problem size. We also explore a promising connection between black-box min-max optimization and black-box evasion and poisoning attacks in adversarial machine learning (ML). Our empirical evaluations on these use cases demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach and its scalability to dimensions that prohibit using recent black-box solvers.

paragraphs: Min-max optimization couples variables that seek opposite outcomes from an objective. This paper considers constrained problems where the optimizer can query objective values but cannot access gradients. That black-box setting makes ordinary gradient-based descent and ascent unavailable directly, while still allowing information to be gathered through evaluations.

The proposed ZO-Min-Max framework estimates gradients from a small number of function queries. It combines this zeroth-order estimator with alternating projected stochastic descent and ascent, using one-step updates. Projection handles the constraints. Under conditions described as mild, the authors establish a sublinear convergence rate and report favorable scaling with problem size.

The paper also connects this framework to black-box evasion and poisoning attacks in adversarial machine learning. Empirical evaluations on these applications demonstrate effectiveness at dimensions that make recent black-box solvers impractical. The results give both conditional convergence support and application evidence for solving competing-objective problems when function values, rather than derivatives, are the accessible source of information.
summary.tldr: ZO-Min-Max solves constrained black-box min-max problems using function-query gradient estimates and alternating descent-ascent updates.

title: Min-Max Optimization without Gradients: Convergence and Applications to Black-Box Evasion and Poisoning Attacks

abstract: One of the most effective algorithms for differentially private learning and optimization is \emph{objective perturbation}. This technique augments a given optimization problem (e.g. deriving from an ERM problem) with a random linear term, and then exactly solves it. However, to date, analyses of this approach crucially rely on the convexity and smoothness of the objective function. We give two algorithms that extend this approach substantially. The first algorithm requires nothing except boundedness of the loss function, and operates over a discrete domain. Its privacy and accuracy guarantees hold even without assuming convexity. We are able to extend traditional analyses of objective perturbation by introducing a novel “normalization“ step into the algorithm, which provides enough stability to be differentially private even without second-order conditions. The second algorithm operates over a continuous domain and requires only that the loss function be bounded and Lipschitz in its continuous parameter. Its privacy analysis does not even require convexity. Its accuracy analysis does require convexity, but does not require second order conditions like smoothness. We complement our theoretical results with an empirical evaluation of the non-convex case, in which we use an integer program solver as our optimization oracle. We find that for the problem of learning linear classifiers, directly optimizing for 0/1 loss using our approach can out-perform the more standard approach of privately optimizing a convex-surrogate loss function on the Adult dataset.

paragraphs: Objective perturbation achieves private optimization by adding a random linear term to an objective and then solving the modified problem exactly. Earlier analyses relied on convexity and smoothness. This paper extends the approach with two algorithms whose guarantees require weaker assumptions, separating the conditions needed for privacy from those needed for accuracy.

The discrete-domain algorithm requires a bounded loss and provides privacy and accuracy guarantees without convexity. A new normalization step supplies the stability needed for privacy. This empirical finding supports the practical potential of the nonconvex approach while remaining distinct from the continuous algorithm’s convexity-dependent accuracy guarantee.
summary.tldr: Two objective-perturbation algorithms weaken assumptions for private optimization, with nonconvex accuracy guarantees for the discrete-domain method.

title: Oracle Efficient Private Non-Convex Optimization

abstract: We propose a novel algorithm for quantizing continuous latent representations in trained models. Our approach applies to deep probabilistic models, such as variational autoencoders (VAEs), and enables both data and model compression. Unlike current end-to-end neural compression methods that cater the model to a fixed quantization scheme, our algorithm separates model design and training from quantization. Consequently, our algorithm enables “plug-and-play” compression with variable rate-distortion trade-off, using a single trained model. Our algorithm can be seen as a novel extension of arithmetic coding to the continuous domain, and uses adaptive quantization accuracy based on estimates of posterior uncertainty. Our experimental results demonstrate the importance of taking into account posterior uncertainties, and show that image compression with the proposed algorithm outperforms JPEG over a wide range of bit rates using only a single standard VAE. Further experiments on Bayesian neural word embeddings demonstrate the versatility of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Quantization turns continuous latent representations into forms that can be stored compactly. This paper introduces a quantization algorithm for trained probabilistic models, including variational autoencoders. It separates quantization from model design and training, allowing a single trained model to support different trade-offs between compressed size and reconstruction distortion.

The algorithm adapts quantization accuracy using estimates of posterior uncertainty. The authors interpret it as an extension of arithmetic coding to the continuous domain. Its practical appeal is plug-and-play compression: the quantization stage can be adjusted after training instead of requiring the model to be trained around one fixed quantization scheme. The proposed approach supports both data and model compression.

Experiments demonstrate the importance of accounting for posterior uncertainty when choosing quantization precision. With a single standard variational autoencoder, the image-compression results outperform JPEG across a wide range of bit rates. Additional experiments on Bayesian neural word embeddings demonstrate applicability beyond image compression, supporting the method’s intended role as a reusable quantization procedure for probabilistic representations.
summary.tldr: Uncertainty-aware quantization enables adjustable compression of already-trained probabilistic models without tying training to a fixed quantization scheme.

title: Variational Bayesian Quantization

abstract: Symbolic equations are at the core of scientific discovery. The task of discovering the underlying equation from a set of input-output pairs is called symbolic regression. Traditionally, symbolic regression methods use hand-designed strategies that do not improve with experience. In this paper, we introduce the first symbolic regression method that leverages large scale pre-training. We procedurally generate an unbounded set of equations, and simultaneously pre-train a Transformer to predict the symbolic equation from a corresponding set of input-output-pairs. At test time, we query the model on a new set of points and use its output to guide the search for the equation. We show empirically that this approach can re-discover a set of well-known physical equations, and that it improves over time with more data and compute.

paragraphs: Symbolic regression seeks an equation that explains observed input-output pairs. Traditional search strategies are often hand-designed and do not improve from previous problems. This paper asks whether large-scale pretraining can teach a model reusable knowledge about the relationship between numerical observations and symbolic expressions.

The authors procedurally generate an unbounded supply of equations and corresponding observations. A Transformer is pretrained to predict an equation from its input-output pairs. At test time, the model receives points from a new problem, and its predictions guide the search for an explanatory equation rather than relying solely on a fixed search heuristic.

Experiments show that the method can rediscover a collection of well-known physical equations and improves with additional data and computation. The contribution is a learned prior for equation discovery that benefits from experience across generated problems. The abstract does not establish recovery guarantees for arbitrary equations or claim that numerical fit alone proves a discovered expression is a physical law.
summary.tldr: A Transformer pretrained on generated equations guides symbolic-regression search and improves with more pretraining data and compute.

title: Neural Symbolic Regression that scales

abstract: Democratization of machine learning requires architectures that automatically adapt to new problems. Neural Differential Equations (NDEs) have emerged as a popular modeling framework by removing the need for ML practitioners to choose the number of layers in a recurrent model. While we can control the computational cost by choosing the number of layers in standard architectures, in NDEs the number of neural network evaluations for a forward pass can depend on the number of steps of the adaptive ODE solver. But, can we force the NDE to learn the version with the least steps while not increasing the training cost? Current strategies to overcome slow prediction require high order automatic differentiation, leading to significantly higher training time. We describe a novel regularization method that uses the internal cost heuristics of adaptive differential equation solvers combined with discrete adjoint sensitivities to guide the training process towards learning NDEs that are easier to solve. This approach opens up the blackbox numerical analysis behind the differential equation solver’s algorithm and directly uses its local error estimates and stiffness heuristics as cheap and accurate cost estimates. We incorporate our method without any change in the underlying NDE framework and show that our method extends beyond Ordinary Differential Equations to accommodate Neural Stochastic Differential Equations. We demonstrate how our approach can halve the prediction time and, unlike other methods which can increase the training time by an order of magnitude, we demonstrate similar reduction in training times. Together this showcases how the knowledge embedded within state-of-the-art equation solvers can be used to enhance machine learning.

paragraphs: Neural differential equations let an adaptive numerical solver determine how many computation steps are needed. This flexibility can make prediction expensive when the learned dynamics require many network evaluations. Existing approaches to accelerating prediction can themselves impose substantial training costs through high-order automatic differentiation.

The paper proposes using information already produced inside adaptive solvers to guide training toward dynamics that are easier to solve. Its regularizer draws on local error estimates and stiffness heuristics as inexpensive estimates of computational difficulty. The broader contribution is to connect what the numerical solver finds difficult with what the neural model is encouraged to learn.
summary.tldr: Regularizing neural differential equations with solver-internal cost estimates can reduce both prediction and training time.

title: Opening the Blackbox: Accelerating Neural Differential Equations by Regularizing Internal Solver Heuristics

abstract: In this paper, we propose a unified pre-training approach called UniSpeech to learn speech representations with both labeled and unlabeled data, in which supervised phonetic CTC learning and phonetically-aware contrastive self-supervised learning are conducted in a multi-task learning manner. The resultant representations can capture information more correlated with phonetic structures and improve the generalization across languages and domains. We evaluate the effectiveness of UniSpeech for cross-lingual representation learning on public CommonVoice corpus. The results show that UniSpeech outperforms self-supervised pretraining and supervised transfer learning for speech recognition by a maximum of 13.4% and 26.9% relative phone error rate reductions respectively (averaged over all testing languages). The transferability of UniSpeech is also verified on a domain-shift speech recognition task, i.e., a relative word error rate reduction of 6% against the previous approach.

paragraphs: UniSpeech combines labeled and unlabeled speech during pre-training to learn representations that transfer across languages and domains. Its multi-task setup joins supervised phonetic CTC learning with contrastive self-supervised learning that is aware of phonetic information. The aim is to make the learned representation more closely reflect the structure of speech sounds.

The authors evaluate cross-language transfer on the public CommonVoice corpus. They report maximum relative phone-error-rate reductions of 13.4% against self-supervised pre-training and 26.9% against supervised transfer learning, with the comparisons averaged across testing languages. These results support combining the two learning signals as a way to improve speech recognition beyond either comparison approach.

A separate speech-recognition task tests transfer under domain shift and shows a 6% relative reduction in word error rate against the previous approach. Together, the evaluations connect the phonetic emphasis of pre-training with improved transfer in two settings. The reported gains concern recognition errors, providing evidence that the unified representation helps downstream speech tasks as well as capturing phonetic structure.
summary.tldr: UniSpeech combines supervised phonetic and self-supervised learning to improve speech representation transfer across languages and domains.

title: UniSpeech: Unified Speech Representation Learning with Labeled and Unlabeled Data

abstract: We study representation learning for Offline Reinforcement Learning (RL), focusing on the important task of Offline Policy Evaluation (OPE). Recent work shows that, in contrast to supervised learning, realizability of the Q-function is not enough for learning it. Two sufficient conditions for sample-efficient OPE are Bellman completeness and coverage. Prior work often assumes that representations satisfying these conditions are given, with results being mostly theoretical in nature. In this work, we propose BCRL, which directly learns from data an approximately linear Bellman complete representation with good coverage. With this learned representation, we perform OPE using Least Square Policy Evaluation (LSPE) with linear functions in our learned representation. We present an end-to-end theoretical analysis, showing that our two-stage algorithm enjoys polynomial sample complexity provided some representation in the rich class considered is linear Bellman complete. Empirically, we extensively evaluate our algorithm on challenging, image-based continuous control tasks from the Deepmind Control Suite. We show our representation enables better OPE compared to previous representation learning methods developed for off-policy RL (e.g., CURL, SPR). BCRL achieve competitive OPE error with the state-of-the-art method Fitted Q-Evaluation (FQE), and beats FQE when evaluating beyond the initial state distribution. Our ablations show that both linear Bellman complete and coverage components of our method are crucial.

paragraphs: Offline policy evaluation estimates how a policy would perform using previously collected data. Having a representation that can express the correct Q-function is insufficient by itself. The paper focuses on two sufficient ingredients: Bellman completeness, which concerns compatibility with value-update operations, and coverage, which concerns whether the data adequately support evaluation.

BCRL learns a representation designed to be approximately linear Bellman complete while providing good coverage. A second stage applies least-squares policy evaluation with linear functions of that representation. The authors analyze both stages together and establish polynomial sample complexity, conditional on the considered representation class containing a linear Bellman-complete representation.

Ablations identify both completeness and coverage as crucial components. The contribution is therefore a method for learning properties that previous analyses often assumed were already supplied, together with theoretical and empirical evidence for their usefulness.
summary.tldr: BCRL learns representations with Bellman-completeness and coverage properties to support accurate offline policy evaluation.

title: Learning Bellman Complete Representations for Offline Policy Evaluation

abstract: Embedding-based entity alignment (EEA) has recently received great attention. Despite significant performance improvement, few efforts have been paid to facilitate understanding of EEA methods. Most existing studies rest on the assumption that a small number of pre-aligned entities can serve as anchors connecting the embedding spaces of two KGs. Nevertheless, no one has investigated the rationality of such an assumption. To fill the research gap, we define a typical paradigm abstracted from existing EEA methods and analyze how the embedding discrepancy between two potentially aligned entities is implicitly bounded by a predefined margin in the score function. Further, we find that such a bound cannot guarantee to be tight enough for alignment learning. We mitigate this problem by proposing a new approach, named NeoEA, to explicitly learn KG-invariant and principled entity embeddings. In this sense, an EEA model not only pursues the closeness of aligned entities based on geometric distance, but also aligns the neural ontologies of two KGs by eliminating the discrepancy in embedding distribution and underlying ontology knowledge. Our experiments demonstrate consistent and significant performance improvement against the best-performing EEA methods.

paragraphs: Entity alignment seeks corresponding entities across knowledge graphs. Many embedding-based methods assume that a small set of known matches can anchor the two graphs' representation spaces. This paper examines that assumption by extracting a common paradigm from existing methods and analyzing what their scoring functions actually constrain.

The analysis shows that a predefined scoring margin implicitly bounds the embedding discrepancy between potentially matching entities. However, this bound is not guaranteed to be tight enough for alignment learning. This identifies a gap between imposing a mathematical constraint on the representations and ensuring that the constraint is sufficiently informative for finding matches.

The proposed NeoEA method explicitly learns embeddings intended to be invariant across knowledge graphs. Alongside bringing aligned entities geometrically closer, it aligns embedding distributions and underlying ontology knowledge, described as aligning the graphs' neural ontologies. Experiments show consistent, significant improvements over the best-performing comparison methods. The work combines a diagnosis of an existing assumption with a method that addresses alignment at the distribution and ontology levels as well as through entity distances.
summary.tldr: NeoEA improves entity alignment by addressing weaknesses in anchor-based embedding constraints and aligning distributions and ontology knowledge.

title: Understanding and Improving Knowledge Graph Embedding for Entity Alignment

abstract: To improve model generalization, model designers often restrict the features that their models use, either implicitly or explicitly. In this work, we explore the design space of leveraging such feature priors by viewing them as distinct perspectives on the data. Specifically, we find that models trained with diverse sets of explicit feature priors have less overlapping failure modes, and can thus be combined more effectively. Moreover, we demonstrate that jointly training such models on additional (unlabeled) data allows them to correct each other’s mistakes, which, in turn, leads to better generalization and resilience to spurious correlations.

paragraphs: Model designers often influence generalization by restricting the features a model can use. Such restrictions encode feature priors: assumptions about which information should guide predictions. This paper examines how to combine models built with different explicit priors, treating each set of restrictions as a distinct perspective on the same data.

The authors find that models trained with diverse feature priors tend to make less overlapping mistakes. This matters because combining models is more useful when one model succeeds on cases where another fails. The relevant diversity therefore concerns their patterns of failure, giving a concrete reason to consider different feature restrictions when constructing a group of models.

The paper further shows that joint training on additional unlabeled data lets these models correct one another's mistakes. In the reported findings, this improves generalization and resilience to spurious correlations, or associations that can mislead prediction. The approach makes feature priors useful at two connected stages: they create complementary models, and those models then exchange useful learning signals through joint training.
summary.tldr: Models with diverse feature priors make complementary mistakes and can improve generalization by learning together on unlabeled data.

title: Combining Diverse Feature Priors

abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) that mimic information transmission in the brain can energy-efficiently process spatio-temporal information through discrete and sparse spikes, thereby receiving considerable attention. To improve accuracy and energy efficiency of SNNs, most previous studies have focused solely on training methods, and the effect of architecture has rarely been studied. We investigate the design choices used in the previous studies in terms of the accuracy and number of spikes and figure out that they are not best-suited for SNNs. To further improve the accuracy and reduce the spikes generated by SNNs, we propose a spike-aware neural architecture search framework called AutoSNN. We define a search space consisting of architectures without undesirable design choices. To enable the spike-aware architecture search, we introduce a fitness that considers both the accuracy and number of spikes. AutoSNN successfully searches for SNN architectures that outperform hand-crafted SNNs in accuracy and energy efficiency. We thoroughly demonstrate the effectiveness of AutoSNN on various datasets including neuromorphic datasets.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks process information through discrete, sparse signals, offering a way to handle information across space and time efficiently. Much previous work has concentrated on how to train these networks. This paper instead investigates how architectural choices affect both predictive accuracy and the number of spikes a network generates.

The authors examine design choices used in earlier studies and find that they are not especially well suited to spiking networks. They then introduce AutoSNN, a neural architecture search framework that excludes undesirable choices from its search space. Its search criterion considers both accuracy and spike count, so candidate architectures are evaluated on their predictive performance together with their signaling activity.

Across several datasets, including neuromorphic datasets, the resulting architectures outperform hand-designed spiking networks in accuracy and energy efficiency. The stated findings support treating architecture as an important part of efficient spiking computation. AutoSNN makes that design problem explicit by incorporating spike activity into the process that selects the network itself.
summary.tldr: AutoSNN searches for spiking-network architectures using both accuracy and spike count, improving on hand-designed networks in the reported experiments.

title: AutoSNN: Towards Energy-Efficient Spiking Neural Networks

abstract: Tensorial Convolutional Neural Networks (TCNNs) have attracted much research attention for their power in reducing model parameters or enhancing the generalization ability. However, exploration of TCNNs is hindered even from weight initialization methods. To be specific, general initialization methods, such as Xavier or Kaiming initialization, usually fail to generate appropriate weights for TCNNs. Meanwhile, although there are ad-hoc approaches for specific architectures (e.g., Tensor Ring Nets), they are not applicable to TCNNs with other tensor decomposition methods (e.g., CP or Tucker decomposition). To address this problem, we propose a universal weight initialization paradigm, which generalizes Xavier and Kaiming methods and can be widely applicable to arbitrary TCNNs. Specifically, we first present the Reproducing Transformation to convert the backward process in TCNNs to an equivalent convolution process. Then, based on the convolution operators in the forward and backward processes, we build a unified paradigm to control the variance of features and gradients in TCNNs. Thus, we can derive fan-in and fan-out initialization for various TCNNs. We demonstrate that our paradigm can stabilize the training of TCNNs, leading to faster convergence and better results.

paragraphs: Tensorial convolutional neural networks use tensor decompositions to reduce parameter counts or improve generalization. However, their structure creates problems even before training begins: standard Xavier and Kaiming initialization often produce unsuitable starting weights. Initialization rules tailored to one decomposition also do not readily transfer to another, making architecture exploration harder.

The paper proposes a common initialization framework that generalizes Xavier and Kaiming methods across tensorial architectures. Its first step is a Reproducing Transformation, which expresses the backward computation as an equivalent convolution process. This places forward signal propagation and backward gradient propagation within a shared mathematical treatment.

Using the convolution operators in both directions, the framework controls the variance of features and gradients and derives fan-in and fan-out initialization rules for different tensorial networks. The authors demonstrate more stable training, faster convergence, and improved results. The contribution is therefore both a practical way to choose starting weights and a unified basis for handling architectures that previously needed separate initialization approaches.
summary.tldr: A unified initialization framework controls signal and gradient variance across tensorial convolutional networks, improving their reported training behavior.

title: A Unified Weight Initialization Paradigm for Tensorial Convolutional Neural Networks

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent must contend with noisy gradients and problem-specific quantities that affect useful step sizes. For smooth, strongly convex objectives, this paper shows that exponentially decreasing step sizes can adapt to unknown gradient-noise variance when smoothness is known. The resulting rate combines an exponentially decaying term with a noise term proportional to variance divided by the iteration count.

Adapting to unknown smoothness creates a separate challenge. The authors show that stochastic line search achieves the desired rate only to a neighborhood of the solution. An offline smoothness estimate instead permits convergence to the minimizer, with a slowdown proportional to the estimation error. These results separate noise adaptation from adaptation to the objective’s geometry.

Adding Nesterov acceleration improves the exponential term’s condition-number dependence from the condition number to its square root, while retaining noise adaptation. Offline estimates of smoothness and strong convexity still allow convergence, but more slowly. Experiments also support exponential step sizes combined with a new stochastic-line-search variant.
summary.tldr: Exponential step sizes give SGD and accelerated SGD noise-adaptive rates, while adapting to unknown problem constants introduces distinct convergence trade-offs.

title: Towards Noise-adaptive, Problem-adaptive (Accelerated) Stochastic Gradient Descent

abstract: The vast majority of existing algorithms for unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) focus on adapting from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain directly in a one-off way. Gradual domain adaptation (GDA), on the other hand, assumes a path of $(T-1)$ unlabeled intermediate domains bridging the source and target, and aims to provide better generalization in the target domain by leveraging the intermediate ones. Under certain assumptions, Kumar et al. (2020) proposed a simple algorithm, Gradual Self-Training, along with a generalization bound in the order of $e^{O(T)} \left(\varepsilon_0+O\left(\sqrt{log(T)/n}\right)\right)$ for the target domain error, where $\varepsilon_0$ is the source domain error and $n$ is the data size of each domain. Due to the exponential factor, this upper bound becomes vacuous when $T$ is only moderately large. In this work, we analyze gradual self-training under more general and relaxed assumptions, and prove a significantly improved generalization bound as $\widetilde{O}\left(\varepsilon_0 + T\Delta + T/\sqrt{n} + 1/\sqrt{nT}\right)$, where $\Delta$ is the average distributional distance between consecutive domains. Compared with the existing bound with an exponential dependency on $T$ as a multiplicative factor, our bound only depends on $T$ linearly and additively. Perhaps more interestingly, our result implies the existence of an optimal choice of $T$ that minimizes the generalization error, and it also naturally suggests an optimal way to construct the path of intermediate domains so as to minimize the accumulative path length $T\Delta$ between the source and target. To corroborate the implications of our theory, we examine gradual self-training on multiple semi-synthetic and real datasets, which confirms our findings. We believe our insights provide a path forward toward the design of future GDA algorithms.

paragraphs: Gradual domain adaptation moves from a labeled source to an unlabeled target through intermediate unlabeled domains. These intermediate stages can help bridge distribution changes. However, an earlier guarantee for gradual self-training grew exponentially with the number of stages, making the bound uninformative even when that number was only moderately large.

Under more general and relaxed assumptions, this paper establishes a substantially improved target-error bound. Its terms depend on source error, accumulated distributional change TΔ, and sample-related quantities T/√n and 1/√(nT), with logarithmic factors suppressed. The dependence on T is linear and additive in the growing terms, replacing the earlier exponential multiplier.

The result implies an optimal choice of the number of stages and suggests constructing intermediate domains to minimize total path length TΔ. Thus, both how many domains are used and how they connect matter to the analysis. Experiments on semi-synthetic and real datasets corroborate these implications, supporting the theory as guidance for designing adaptation paths.
summary.tldr: A tighter analysis of gradual self-training reveals how the number and distributional path of intermediate domains affect generalization.

title: Understanding Gradual Domain Adaptation: Improved Analysis, Optimal Path and Beyond

abstract: We present SkexGen, a novel autoregressive generative model for computer-aided design (CAD) construction sequences containing sketch-and-extrude modeling operations. Our model utilizes distinct Transformer architectures to encode topological, geometric, and extrusion variations of construction sequences into disentangled codebooks. Autoregressive Transformer decoders generate CAD construction sequences sharing certain properties specified by the codebook vectors. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our disentangled codebook representation generates diverse and high-quality CAD models, enhances user control, and enables efficient exploration of the design space. The code is available at https://samxuxiang.github.io/skexgen.

Our model utilizes distinct Transformer architectures to encode topological, geometric, and extrusion variations of construction sequences into disentangled codebooks. Autoregressive Transformer decoders generate CAD construction sequences sharing certain properties specified by the codebook vectors. The code is available at https://samxuxiang.github.io/skexgen.

paragraphs: SkexGen generates CAD models through construction sequences containing sketch-and-extrude operations. The generated object is therefore described through a sequence of modeling actions. The paper’s focus is on representing different kinds of variation within these sequences so that generation can produce diverse designs while giving users control over selected properties.

The model uses separate Transformer architectures to encode topological, geometric, and extrusion variations into disentangled codebooks. These codebooks provide distinct representations of the different aspects of a construction sequence. Autoregressive Transformer decoders then generate sequences whose shared properties are specified by the chosen codebook vectors. Generation proceeds sequentially, with the codebook representation guiding which properties the resulting designs share.

Extensive experiments report diverse, high-quality CAD models, improved user control, and efficient exploration of the design space. These findings support the value of separating construction properties in the learned representation. The contribution links controllable sequence generation to the structure of CAD modeling operations, allowing codebook choices to guide families of designs with specified common characteristics.
summary.tldr: SkexGen generates controllable CAD construction sequences using separate codebooks for topology, geometry, and extrusion properties.

title: SkexGen: Autoregressive Generation of CAD Construction Sequences with Disentangled Codebooks

abstract: Injecting discrete logical constraints into neural network learning is one of the main challenges in neuro-symbolic AI. We find that a straight-through-estimator, a method introduced to train binary neural networks, could effectively be applied to incorporate logical constraints into neural network learning. More specifically, we design a systematic way to represent discrete logical constraints as a loss function; minimizing this loss using gradient descent via a straight-through-estimator updates the neural network’s weights in the direction that the binarized outputs satisfy the logical constraints. The experimental results show that by leveraging GPUs and batch training, this method scales significantly better than existing neuro-symbolic methods that require heavy symbolic computation for computing gradients. Also, we demonstrate that our method applies to different types of neural networks, such as MLP, CNN, and GNN, making them learn with no or fewer labeled data by learning directly from known constraints.

paragraphs: Logical rules can provide learning signals, but their discrete nature makes them difficult to integrate with neural-network training. This paper adapts straight-through estimators, previously introduced for binary neural networks, to incorporate such constraints. The aim is to let known rules influence network weights through gradient-based optimization.

The authors systematically express discrete logical constraints as a loss function. A straight-through estimator enables gradient descent to use this loss, directing weight updates toward binary outputs that satisfy the constraints. This provides a route from discrete requirements to neural training without relying on the heavy symbolic gradient computations used by the compared neuro-symbolic approaches.

Experiments show substantially better scaling through GPU computation and batch training. The method is also demonstrated with multilayer perceptrons, convolutional networks, and graph neural networks. In those applications, learning directly from constraints allows training with fewer labels or no labels. The findings support a broadly applicable training mechanism, while the stated optimization effect is movement toward constraint satisfaction rather than a claim that every trained output must satisfy every rule.
summary.tldr: Straight-through estimators turn logical constraints into usable neural-network training signals, improving scalability and reducing reliance on labeled data in experiments.

title: Injecting Logical Constraints into Neural Networks via Straight-Through Estimators

abstract: In this work, we investigate the online learning problem of revenue maximization in ad auctions, where the seller needs to learn the click-through rates (CTRs) of each ad candidate and charge the price of the winner through a pay-per-click manner. We focus on two models of the advertisers’ strategic behaviors. First, we assume that the advertiser is completely myopic; i.e. in each round, they aim to maximize their utility only for the current round. In this setting, we develop an online mechanism based on upper-confidence bounds that achieves a tight $O(\sqrt{T})$ regret in the worst-case and negative regret when the values are static across all the auctions and there is a gap between the highest expected value (i.e. value multiplied by their CTR) and second highest expected value ad. Next, we assume that the advertiser is non-myopic and cares about their long term utility. This setting is much more complex since an advertiser is incentivized to influence the mechanism by bidding strategically in earlier rounds. In this setting, we provide an algorithm to achieve negative regret for the static valuation setting (with a positive gap), which is in sharp contrast with the prior work that shows $O(T^{2/3})$ regret when the valuation is generated by adversary.

paragraphs: An advertising auction seller must learn how likely each ad is to receive a click while choosing winners and charging per click. This creates an online revenue-learning problem complicated by advertiser incentives. The paper analyzes two cases: advertisers concerned only with the current auction and advertisers who consider their long-term utility.

For myopic advertisers, the authors develop a mechanism based on upper-confidence bounds. It achieves a tight worst-case regret bound of O(sqrt(T)) over T rounds. When valuations remain fixed and the largest value-times-click-rate exceeds the second largest by a positive gap, the mechanism instead achieves negative regret, meaning revenue exceeds its regret benchmark.

Long-term advertisers create an additional challenge because early bids can strategically influence the mechanism. The paper also provides an algorithm with negative regret in that setting under fixed valuations and a positive gap. Its comparison with earlier O(T^(2/3)) regret results involves a different valuation setting: the earlier valuations can be chosen adversarially. The favorable guarantees therefore depend on the stated stability and gap conditions.
summary.tldr: The paper improves revenue-learning guarantees in ad auctions, including negative regret under fixed valuations and a positive expected-value gap.

title: Improved Online Learning Algorithms for CTR Prediction in Ad Auctions

abstract: In this paper, we analyze the convergence of gradient flow on a multi-layer linear model with a loss function of the form $f(W_1W_2\cdots W_L)$. We show that when $f$ satisfies the gradient dominance property, proper weight initialization leads to exponential convergence of the gradient flow to a global minimum of the loss. Moreover, the convergence rate depends on two trajectory-specific quantities that are controlled by the weight initialization: the imbalance matrices , which measure the difference between the weights of adjacent layers, and the least singular value of the weight product $W=W_1W_2\cdots W_L$. Our analysis exploits the fact that the gradient of the overparameterized loss can be written as the composition of the non-overparametrized gradient with a time-varying (weight-dependent) linear operator whose smallest eigenvalue controls the convergence rate. The key challenge we address is to derive a uniform lower bound for this time-varying eigenvalue that lead to improved rates for several multi-layer network models studied in the literature.

paragraphs: The paper examines gradient flow, a continuous-time model of optimization, for a linear network with multiple layers. Although each layer is linear, the loss depends on a product of weight matrices. The authors ask when optimizing this layered parameterization converges to a global minimum and how quickly that happens.

They show exponential convergence when the underlying loss satisfies gradient dominance and the weights are initialized appropriately. The rate depends on two quantities along the optimization trajectory: imbalance matrices describing differences between adjacent layers and the smallest singular value of the overall weight product. Initialization controls these quantities and therefore plays a direct role in the convergence analysis.

The proof expresses the layered loss gradient through a changing, weight-dependent linear operator applied to the underlying loss gradient. Bounding the operator's smallest eigenvalue uniformly is the main technical challenge. Solving it produces improved rates for several previously studied multilayer models, with the conclusion explicitly tied to the stated loss property and initialization.
summary.tldr: For gradient-dominated losses, suitable initialization yields exponential gradient-flow convergence in multilayer linear models.

title: On the Convergence of Gradient Flow on Multi-layer Linear Models

abstract: We study the problem of online generalized linear regression in the stochastic setting, where the label is generated from a generalized linear model with possibly unbounded additive noise. We provide a sharp analysis of the classical follow-the-regularized-leader (FTRL) algorithm to cope with the label noise. More specifically, for $\sigma$-sub-Gaussian label noise, our analysis provides a regret upper bound of $O(\sigma^2 d \log T) + o(\log T)$, where $d$ is the dimension of the input vector, $T$ is the total number of rounds. We also prove an $\Omega(\sigma^2d\log(T/d))$ lower bound for stochastic online linear regression, which indicates that our upper bound is nearly optimal. In addition, we extend our analysis to a more refined Bernstein noise condition. As an application, we study generalized linear bandits with heterogeneous noise and propose an algorithm based on FTRL to achieve the first variance-aware regret bound.

We provide a sharp analysis of the classical follow-the-regularized-leader (FTRL) algorithm to cope with the label noise. More specifically, for $\sigma$-sub-Gaussian label noise, our analysis provides a regret upper bound of $O(\sigma^2 d \log T) + o(\log T)$, where $d$ is the dimension of the input vector, $T$ is the total number of rounds. We also prove an $\Omega(\sigma^2d\log(T/d))$ lower bound for stochastic online linear regression, which indicates that our upper bound is nearly optimal. In addition, we extend our analysis to a more refined Bernstein noise condition. As an application, we study generalized linear bandits with heterogeneous noise and propose an algorithm based on FTRL to achieve the first variance-aware regret bound.

paragraphs: Online generalized linear regression makes predictions over successive rounds while learning from noisy labels. This paper considers labels generated by a generalized linear model with additive stochastic noise that may be unbounded. It develops a sharper analysis of follow-the-regularized-leader, or FTRL, to describe how noise affects accumulated regret.

For sigma-sub-Gaussian label noise, the regret upper bound is O(sigma² d log T) plus a term that grows more slowly than log T. Here, d is the input dimension and T is the number of rounds. A lower bound of order sigma² d log(T/d) for stochastic online linear regression shows that the upper bound is nearly optimal.

The analysis also extends to a more refined Bernstein noise condition. As an application, the authors study generalized linear bandits with heterogeneous noise and design an FTRL-based algorithm with a variance-aware regret bound. This connects the regression analysis to sequential action selection, where accounting for differences in noise levels can yield a more informative performance guarantee than treating all observations as equally noisy.
summary.tldr: A sharper FTRL analysis gives nearly optimal noise-dependent regression regret and enables a variance-aware guarantee for generalized linear bandits.

title: Optimal Online Generalized Linear Regression with Stochastic Noise and Its Application to Heteroscedastic Bandits

abstract: Deep learning models are known to overfit and memorize spurious features in the training dataset. While numerous empirical studies have aimed at understanding this phenomenon, a rigorous theoretical framework to quantify it is still missing. In this paper, we consider spurious features that are uncorrelated with the learning task, and we provide a precise characterization of how they are memorized via two separate terms: (i) the stability of the model with respect to individual training samples, and (ii) the feature alignment between the spurious pattern and the full sample. While the first term is well established in learning theory and it is connected to the generalization error in classical work, the second one is, to the best of our knowledge, novel. Our key technical result gives a precise characterization of the feature alignment for the two prototypical settings of random features (RF) and neural tangent kernel (NTK) regression. We prove that the memorization of spurious features weakens as the generalization capability increases and, through the analysis of the feature alignment, we unveil the role of the model and of its activation function. Numerical experiments show the predictive power of our theory on standard datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10).

title: How Spurious Features are Memorized: Precise Analysis for Random and NTK Features

abstract: Imitation learning mimics high-quality policies from expert data for sequential decision-making tasks. However, its efficacy is hindered in scenarios where optimal demonstrations are unavailable, and only imperfect demonstrations are present. To address this issue, introducing additional limited human preferences is a suitable approach as it can be obtained in a human-friendly manner, offering a promising way to learn the policy that exceeds the performance of imperfect demonstrations. In this paper, we propose a novel imitation learning (IL) algorithm, Preference Aided Imitation Learning from imperfect demonstrations (PAIL). Specifically, PAIL learns a preference reward by querying experts for limited preferences from imperfect demonstrations. This serves two purposes during training: 1) Reweighting imperfect demonstrations with the preference reward for higher quality. 2) Selecting explored trajectories with high cumulative preference rewards to augment imperfect demonstrations. The dataset with continuously improving quality empowers the performance of PAIL to transcend the initial demonstrations. Comprehensive empirical results across a synthetic task and two locomotion benchmarks show that PAIL surpasses baselines by 73.2% and breaks through the performance bottleneck of imperfect demonstrations.

paragraphs: Imitation learning is most straightforward when demonstrations show high-quality behavior. When the available examples are imperfect, copying them can restrict the quality of the learned policy. PAIL adds a limited amount of expert preference feedback to help the learner distinguish better behavior and improve beyond the demonstrations it initially receives.

The algorithm learns a preference reward from expert judgments about imperfect demonstrations. It uses this reward in two ways: to reweight the original demonstrations toward higher quality, and to select newly explored trajectories with high cumulative reward. Those selected trajectories are added to the demonstration data, creating a training set whose quality improves over time.

This connects preference learning to both data selection and continued exploration. The learner is guided by the original examples, but its training data can grow to include better behavior discovered during learning. Experiments on a synthetic task and two locomotion benchmarks show performance exceeding the initial demonstrations. The abstract reports a 73.2% improvement over baselines, supporting the usefulness of limited preference feedback in the evaluated imperfect-demonstration settings.
summary.tldr: PAIL uses limited expert preferences to reweight demonstrations and add better explored trajectories, enabling learning beyond imperfect examples.

title: Limited Preference Aided Imitation Learning from Imperfect Demonstrations

abstract: Self-attention and masked self-attention are at the heart of Transformers’ outstanding success. Still, our mathematical understanding of attention, in particular of its Lipschitz properties — which are key when it comes to analyzing robustness and expressive power — is incomplete. We provide a detailed study of the Lipschitz constant of self-attention in several practical scenarios, discussing the impact of the sequence length $n$ and layer normalization on the local Lipschitz constant of both unmasked and masked self-attention. In particular, we show that for inputs of length $n$ in any compact set, the Lipschitz constant of self-attention is bounded by $\sqrt{n}$ up to a constant factor and that this bound is tight for reasonable sequence lengths. When the sequence length $n$ is too large for the previous bound to be tight, which we refer to as the mean-field regime, we provide an upper bound and a matching lower bound which are independent of $n$. Our mean-field framework for masked self-attention is novel and of independent interest. Our experiments on pretrained and randomly initialized BERT and GPT-2 support our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: How much can an attention layer’s output change when its input changes slightly? A Lipschitz constant quantifies this sensitivity, making it relevant to both robustness and expressive power. This paper studies the local Lipschitz properties of self-attention and masked self-attention, examining how sequence length and layer normalization affect them.

For inputs of length n within any compact set, the authors establish an upper bound proportional to the square root of n. They show that this bound is tight for reasonable sequence lengths, so its dependence on length captures attainable sensitivity in that range. The compact-set qualification is part of the result and matters when interpreting its scope.

For sufficiently long sequences, the square-root bound is no longer tight. In this mean-field regime, the paper gives an upper bound and a matching lower bound that do not depend on sequence length. It also develops a new mean-field framework for masked attention. Experiments using pretrained and randomly initialized BERT and GPT-2 support the theoretical account of these different sensitivity regimes.
summary.tldr: Attention’s sensitivity has a tight square-root sequence-length bound in one regime and length-independent bounds in a sufficiently long-sequence regime.

title: How Smooth Is Attention?

abstract: Foundation models are powerful technologies: how they are released publicly directly shapes their societal impact. In this position paper, we focus on *open* foundation models, defined here as those with broadly available model weights (e.g., Llama 3, Stable Diffusion XL). We identify five distinctive properties (e.g., greater customizability, poor monitoring) that mediate their benefits and risks. Open foundation models present significant benefits, with some caveats, that span innovation, competition, the distribution of decision-making power, and transparency. To understand their risks of misuse, we design a risk assessment framework for analyzing their *marginal risk*. Across several misuse vectors (e.g., cyberattacks, bioweapons), we find that current research is insufficient to effectively characterize the marginal risk of open foundation models relative to pre-existing technologies. The framework helps explain why the marginal risk is low in some cases, clarifies disagreements about misuse risks by revealing that past work has focused on different subsets of the framework with different assumptions, and articulates a way forward for more constructive debate. Overall, our work helps support a more grounded assessment of the societal impact of open foundation models by outlining what research is needed to empirically validate their theoretical benefits and risks.

The paper outlines research needed to test proposed benefits and risks empirically and to make public debate more grounded.
summary.tldr: A marginal-risk framework clarifies open foundation models’ societal tradeoffs and identifies evidence needed to assess their added misuse risks.

title: Position: On the Societal Impact of Open Foundation Models

abstract: Speculative decoding is a pivotal technique to accelerate the inference of large language models (LLMs) by employing a smaller draft model to predict the target model’s outputs. However, its efficacy can be limited due to the low predictive accuracy of the draft model, particularly when faced with diverse text inputs and a significant capability gap between the draft and target models. We introduce online speculative decoding to address this challenge. The main idea is to continuously update the (multiple) draft model(s) on observed user query data. Adapting to query distribution mitigates the shifts between the training distribution of the draft model and the query distribution, enabling the draft model to more accurately predict the target model’s outputs. We develop a prototype of online speculative decoding based on knowledge distillation and evaluate it using both synthetic and real query data. The results show a substantial increase in the token acceptance rate by 0.1 to 0.65, bringing 1.42x to 2.17x latency reduction. Our code is available at https://github.com/LiuXiaoxuanPKU/OSD.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding accelerates a large language model by asking a smaller draft model to predict its outputs. Its usefulness depends on how often those predictions are accepted. Diverse user requests and a large capability gap between the models can reduce draft accuracy, limiting the speed advantage of the approach.

Online speculative decoding continuously updates one or more draft models using observed user queries. The idea is to adapt the draft model to the requests it actually encounters. This reduces the mismatch between its original training distribution and the query distribution, helping it predict the target model's outputs more accurately.

The authors implement a prototype using knowledge distillation and evaluate it on synthetic and real query data. They report token acceptance-rate increases of 0.1 to 0.65 and latency reduction factors of 1.42 to 2.17. These findings connect adaptation to serving performance: improving agreement on the active query distribution can make speculative decoding more effective. The contribution is an ongoing adaptation process for draft models during use.
summary.tldr: Continuously adapting draft models to observed queries improves speculative decoding acceptance rates and reduces latency.

title: Online Speculative Decoding

abstract: Following natural language instructions by executing actions in digital environments (e.g. web-browsers and REST APIs) is a challenging task for language model (LM) agents. Unfortunately, LM agents often fail to generalize to new environments without human demonstrations. This work presents BAGEL, a method for bootstrapping LM agents without human supervision. BAGEL converts a seed set of randomly explored trajectories to synthetic demonstrations via round-trips between two noisy LM components: an LM labeler which converts a trajectory into a synthetic instruction, and a zero-shot LM agent which maps the synthetic instruction into a refined trajectory. By performing these round-trips iteratively, BAGEL quickly converts the initial distribution of trajectories towards those that are well-described by natural language. We adapt the base LM agent at test time with in-context learning by retrieving relevant BAGEL demonstrations based on the instruction, and find improvements of over 2-13% absolute on ToolQA and MiniWob++, with up to 13x reduction in execution failures.

paragraphs: Language model agents must turn instructions into sequences of actions when working with browsers or APIs. Generalizing to a new environment often requires human demonstrations. BAGEL addresses this dependence by constructing synthetic demonstrations from the agent’s own exploration, without human supervision.

The process begins with randomly explored trajectories, meaning sequences of actions in an environment. One language model component labels a trajectory with a synthetic instruction. A second component, a zero-shot agent, attempts that instruction and produces a refined trajectory. Repeating this round trip gradually shifts the initial trajectories toward behavior that natural language can describe well, despite both components being noisy.

At test time, BAGEL retrieves demonstrations relevant to the current instruction and supplies them through in-context learning. The reported experiments on ToolQA and MiniWob++ show absolute improvements described as over 2–13%, alongside reductions in execution failures of up to thirteenfold. These findings support using iterative synthetic demonstration generation to help agents adapt to digital environments.
summary.tldr: BAGEL turns random exploration into synthetic demonstrations through repeated language-guided refinement, improving agents without human supervision.

title: BAGEL: Bootstrapping Agents by Guiding Exploration with Language

abstract: Identifying latent variables and the causal structure involving them is essential across various scientific fields. While many existing works fall under the category of constraint-based methods (with e.g. conditional independence or rank deficiency tests), they may face empirical challenges such as testing-order dependency, error propagation, and choosing an appropriate significance level. These issues can potentially be mitigated by properly designed score-based methods, such as Greedy Equivalence Search (GES) (Chickering, 2002) in the specific setting without latent variables. Yet, formulating score-based methods with latent variables is highly challenging. In this work, we develop score-based methods that are capable of identifying causal structures containing causally-related latent variables with identifiability guarantees. Specifically, we show that a properly formulated scoring function can achieve score equivalence and consistency for structure learning of latent variable causal models. We further provide a characterization of the degrees of freedom for the marginal over the observed variables under multiple structural assumptions considered in the literature, and accordingly develop both exact and continuous score-based methods. This offers a unified view of several existing constraint-based methods with different structural assumptions. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

paragraphs: Discovering causal structure becomes harder when some relevant variables are unobserved and may themselves be causally connected. Existing constraint-based approaches use tests such as conditional independence or rank deficiency, but can encounter testing-order effects, propagated errors, and difficult significance choices. The paper develops score-based alternatives for this latent-variable setting.

The authors show that an appropriately formulated scoring function can achieve score equivalence and consistency for learning latent causal structures. They also establish identifiability guarantees for structures containing causally related hidden variables. These results provide a theoretical basis for comparing candidate structures through a score rather than relying solely on sequences of individual constraint tests.

To construct the methods, the paper characterizes degrees of freedom in the distribution over observed variables under several structural assumptions from the literature. This supports both exact and continuous score-based methods and connects existing approaches within a common perspective. Experiments validate their effectiveness. The guarantees remain associated with the structural settings analyzed, making those assumptions central to interpreting what hidden causal structure can be recovered.
summary.tldr: The paper develops score-based methods with theoretical guarantees for discovering causal structures containing causally related latent variables.

title: Score-Based Causal Discovery of Latent Variable Causal Models

abstract: STOchastic Recursive Momentum (STORM)-based algorithms have been widely developed to solve one to $K$-level ($K \geq 3$) stochastic optimization problems. Specifically, they use estimators to mitigate the biased gradient issue and achieve near-optimal convergence results. However, there is relatively little work on understanding their generalization performance, particularly evident during the transition from one to $K$-level optimization contexts. This paper provides a comprehensive generalization analysis of three representative STORM-based algorithms: STORM, COVER, and SVMR, for one, two, and $K$-level stochastic optimizations under both convex and strongly convex settings based on algorithmic stability. Firstly, we define stability for $K$-level optimizations and link it to generalization. Then, we detail the stability results for three prominent STORM-based algorithms. Finally, we derive their excess risk bounds by balancing stability results with optimization errors. Our theoretical results provide strong evidence to complete STORM-based algorithms: (1) Each estimator may decrease their stability due to variance with its estimation target. (2) Every additional level might escalate the generalization error, influenced by the stability and the variance between its cumulative stochastic gradient and the true gradient. (3) Increasing the batch size for the initial computation of estimators presents a favorable trade-off, enhancing the generalization performance.
