paragraphs: STORM-based optimization methods use estimators to handle biased gradients and have strong convergence results. Convergence, however, does not by itself describe how well the learned solution generalizes. This paper studies that second question for STORM, COVER, and SVMR in one-level, two-level, and deeper stochastic optimization problems under convex and strongly convex assumptions.

The analysis uses algorithmic stability to connect the learning procedure to generalization. The authors define stability for optimization with multiple nested levels, derive stability results for the three algorithms, and combine them with optimization error. This produces excess risk bounds that account for both how well optimization proceeds and how the procedure generalizes.

The theory indicates that variance in each estimator may reduce stability, and that additional levels might increase generalization error depending on stability and gradient variance. These are conditional effects rather than inevitable consequences of nesting. The analysis also supports using larger batches when initializing estimators, identifying a favorable trade-off that can improve generalization performance.
summary.tldr: A stability analysis explains how estimator variance and nested optimization levels can affect STORM-based generalization and supports larger initialization batches.

title: Stability and Generalization for Stochastic Recursive Momentum-based Algorithms for (Strongly-)Convex One to $K$-Level Stochastic Optimizations

abstract: Estimating the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) from observational data is relevant for many applications such as personalized medicine. Here, we focus on the widespread setting where the observational data come from multiple environments, such as different hospitals, physicians, or countries. Furthermore, we allow for violations of standard causal assumptions, namely, overlap within the environments and unconfoundedness. To this end, we move away from point identification and focus on partial identification. Specifically, we show that current assumptions from the literature on multiple environments allow us to interpret the environment as an instrumental variable (IV). This allows us to adapt bounds from the IV literature for partial identification of CATE by leveraging treatment assignment mechanisms across environments. Then, we propose different model-agnostic learners (so-called meta-learners) to estimate the bounds that can be used in combination with arbitrary machine learning models. We further demonstrate the effectiveness of our meta-learners across various experiments using both simulated and real-world data. Finally, we discuss the applicability of our meta-learners to partial identification in instrumental variable settings, such as randomized controlled trials with non-compliance.

paragraphs: Estimating treatment effects from observational data often depends on assumptions that may fail in practice. This paper studies data collected across environments such as hospitals, physicians, or countries. It allows violations of both within-environment overlap and unconfoundedness, moving from a single identified conditional average treatment effect to bounds on that effect.

Under existing multiple-environment assumptions from the literature, the authors show that environment can be interpreted as an instrumental variable. This lets them adapt instrumental-variable bounds by using differences in how environments assign treatment. The approach makes those assignment differences useful for constraining possible treatment effects, even when the stated assumptions do not support a unique estimate.

The paper then develops model-agnostic meta-learners for estimating these bounds with arbitrary machine learning models. Experiments on simulated and real-world data demonstrate their effectiveness. The authors also discuss application to other partially identified instrumental-variable problems, including randomized trials with noncompliance. The practical output is an estimated range of effects that reflects the available identification information.
summary.tldr: Model-agnostic learners estimate treatment-effect bounds by using environments as instruments under stated multiple-environment assumptions.

title: Meta-Learners for Partially-Identified Treatment Effects Across Multiple Environments

abstract: Diffusion models benefit from instillation of task-specific information into the score function to steer the sample generation towards desired properties. Such information is coined as guidance. For example, in text-to-image synthesis, text input is encoded as guidance to generate semantically aligned images. Proper guidance inputs are closely tied with the performance of diffusion models. A common observation is that strong guidance promotes a tight alignment to the task-specific information, while reduces the diversity of the generated samples. In this paper, we provide the first theoretical study towards the influence of guidance on diffusion models in the context of Gaussian mixture models. Under mild conditions, we prove that incorporating diffusion guidance not only boosts prediction confidence but also diminishes distribution diversity, leading to a reduction in the differential entropy of the output distribution. Our analysis covers the widely used DDPM and DDIM sampling schemes, and leverages comparison inequalities in differential equations as well as the Fokker-Planck equation that characterizes the evolution of probability density function, which may be of independent theoretical interest.

Stronger guidance is commonly associated with tighter alignment to the requested task and less varied output. This paper investigates that relationship theoretically using Gaussian mixture models, giving a mathematical setting in which the effect can be analyzed.

Under mild conditions, the authors prove that guidance increases prediction confidence while reducing distributional diversity. They express the latter effect through a decrease in differential entropy of the output distribution. This connects two observed consequences of guidance within a common analysis: stronger confidence about the desired outcome and a narrowing of generated variation.

The contribution is a conditional theoretical explanation within the Gaussian-mixture setting, supporting a clearer understanding of the confidence–diversity trade-off. The authors also identify the analytical techniques as potentially useful beyond this particular study.
summary.tldr: For Gaussian mixture models under mild conditions, diffusion guidance increases prediction confidence while reducing output diversity.

title: Theoretical insights for diffusion guidance: A case study for Gaussian mixture models

abstract: Adversarial training (AT) trains models using adversarial examples (AEs), which are natural images modified with specific perturbations to mislead the model. These perturbations are constrained by a predefined perturbation budget $\epsilon$ and are equally applied to each pixel within an image. However, in this paper, we discover that not all pixels contribute equally to the accuracy on AEs (i.e., robustness) and accuracy on natural images (i.e., accuracy). Motivated by this finding, we propose Pixel-reweighted AdveRsarial Training (PART), a new framework that partially reduces $\epsilon$ for less influential pixels, guiding the model to focus more on key regions that affect its outputs. Specifically, we first use class activation mapping (CAM) methods to identify important pixel regions, then we keep the perturbation budget for these regions while lowering it for the remaining regions when generating AEs. In the end, we use these pixel-reweighted AEs to train a model. PART achieves a notable improvement in accuracy without compromising robustness on CIFAR-10, SVHN and TinyImagenet-200, justifying the necessity to allocate distinct weights to different pixel regions in robust classification.

Pixel-reweighted Adversarial Training, or PART, uses class activation mapping to identify image regions important to the model’s output. On CIFAR-10, SVHN, and TinyImagenet-200, PART improves ordinary-image accuracy without compromising the reported robustness. The result supports treating image regions differently when constructing adversarial training data. Its practical significance is an improved accuracy–robustness tradeoff in the evaluated settings: the method changes the training examples so that robustness training places greater emphasis on regions that affect predictions.
summary.tldr: PART reduces adversarial perturbation budgets in less influential image regions, improving clean accuracy without reducing robustness on three evaluated datasets.

title: Improving Accuracy-robustness Trade-off via Pixel Reweighted Adversarial Training

abstract: Developing policies that can adapt to non-stationary environments is essential for real-world reinforcement learning applications. Nevertheless, learning such adaptable policies in offline settings, with only a limited set of pre-collected trajectories, presents significant challenges. A key difficulty arises because the limited offline data makes it hard for the context encoder to differentiate between changes in the environment dynamics and shifts in the behavior policy, often leading to context misassociations. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach called debiased offline representation learning for fast online adaptation (DORA). DORA incorporates an information bottleneck principle that maximizes mutual information between the dynamics encoding and the environmental data, while minimizing mutual information between the dynamics encoding and the actions of the behavior policy. We present a practical implementation of DORA, leveraging tractable bounds of the information bottleneck principle. Our experimental evaluation across six benchmark MuJoCo tasks with variable parameters demonstrates that DORA not only achieves a more precise dynamics encoding but also significantly outperforms existing baselines in terms of performance.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning policy may need to adapt when an environment's dynamics change, even if its initial training uses only previously collected trajectories. Limited offline data creates an ambiguity: observations may differ because the environment changed or because the policy collecting the data chose different actions. A context encoder can confuse these sources of variation.

DORA addresses this ambiguity through an information bottleneck objective. It encourages the dynamics representation to retain information about environmental data while reducing information about the behavior policy's actions. The intended effect is to make the representation more informative about how the environment behaves and less tied to the particular behavior that produced the training trajectories.

The authors turn this principle into a practical method using tractable bounds on the information objective. Across six MuJoCo benchmark tasks with variable parameters, they report more accurate dynamics encodings and significantly better performance than existing baselines. These results support learning representations that separate environmental changes from behavior-policy shifts as a route toward faster online adaptation.
summary.tldr: DORA improves adaptation by training offline dynamics representations to retain environmental information while reducing behavior-policy bias.

title: Debiased Offline Representation Learning for Fast Online Adaptation in Non-stationary Dynamics

abstract: We present an operator-theoretic framework for temporal and spatio-temporal forecasting based on learning a continuous time-shift operator. Our operator learning paradigm offers a continuous relaxation of the discrete lag factor used in traditional autoregressive models, enabling the history of a system up to a given time to be mapped to its future values. We parametrize the time-shift operator using Khatri-Rao neural operators (KRNOs), a novel architecture based on non-stationary integral transforms with nearly linear computational scaling. Our framework naturally handles irregularly sampled observations and enables forecasting at super-resolution in both space and time. Extensive numerical studies across diverse temporal and spatio-temporal benchmarks demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance with leading methods.

This paper instead learns a continuous time-shift operator: a mapping from a system's history up to a given time to its later values. The formulation covers both temporal data and data that varies across space and time.

The authors represent this mapping with Khatri-Rao neural operators, a proposed architecture built from non-stationary integral transforms. The architecture has nearly linear computational scaling. The contribution is therefore both a forecasting formulation and an architecture for implementing it efficiently. The stated results support the framework across the evaluated benchmarks, while its continuous operator structure supplies the mechanism for handling irregular sampling and forecasting at super-resolution.
summary.tldr: Khatri-Rao neural operators learn a continuous time-shift mapping that supports irregular observations and finer-resolution forecasting with competitive benchmark performance.

title: Shifting Time: Time-series Forecasting with Khatri-Rao Neural Operators

abstract: Rehearsal-based methods have shown superior performance in addressing catastrophic forgetting in continual learning (CL) by storing and training on a subset of past data alongside new data in current task. While such a concurrent rehearsal strategy is widely used, it remains unclear if this approach is always optimal. Inspired by human learning, where sequentially revisiting tasks helps mitigate forgetting, we explore whether sequential rehearsal can offer greater benefits for CL compared to standard concurrent rehearsal. To address this question, we conduct a theoretical analysis of rehearsal-based CL in overparameterized linear models, comparing two strategies: 1) Concurrent Rehearsal, where past and new data are trained together, and 2) Sequential Rehearsal, where new data is trained first, followed by revisiting past data sequentially. By explicitly characterizing forgetting and generalization error, we show that sequential rehearsal performs better when tasks are less similar. These insights further motivate a novel Hybrid Rehearsal method, which trains similar tasks concurrently and revisits dissimilar tasks sequentially. We characterize its forgetting and generalization performance, and our experiments with deep neural networks further confirm that the hybrid approach outperforms standard concurrent rehearsal. This work provides the first comprehensive theoretical analysis of rehearsal-based CL.

paragraphs: Continual-learning systems can forget earlier tasks when learning new ones. Rehearsal addresses this by retaining some past data, usually mixing it with current-task data during training. This paper asks whether the order of rehearsal matters and whether revisiting old tasks sequentially can sometimes work better than training everything together.

The authors analyze overparameterized linear models and explicitly characterize forgetting and generalization error. They compare concurrent rehearsal with a sequential strategy that learns new data first and then revisits past tasks. Their analysis shows an advantage for sequential rehearsal when tasks are less similar, making task relationships central to the choice of training schedule.

That result motivates Hybrid Rehearsal, which trains similar tasks together and revisits dissimilar tasks sequentially. The paper characterizes its forgetting and generalization behavior and evaluates the idea with deep neural networks. Those experiments find that the hybrid method outperforms standard concurrent rehearsal. The theoretical results apply to the analyzed linear models, while the neural-network experiments provide additional empirical support for adapting rehearsal order to task similarity.
summary.tldr: Analysis links rehearsal effectiveness to task similarity and motivates a hybrid schedule that outperforms concurrent rehearsal in neural-network experiments.

title: Unlocking the Power of Rehearsal in Continual Learning: A Theoretical Perspective

abstract: In this work, we propose a novel approach that combines the strengths of FEAT and TabNet through knowledge distillation (KD), which we term FEAT-KD. FEAT is an intrinsically interpretable machine learning (ML) algorithm that constructs a weighted linear combination of concisely-represented features discovered via genetic programming optimization, which can often be inefficient. FEAT-KD leverages TabNet’s deep-learning-based optimization and feature selection mechanisms instead. FEAT-KD finds a weighted linear combination of concisely-represented, symbolic features that are derived from piece-wise distillation of a trained TabNet model. We analyze FEAT-KD on regression tasks from two perspectives: (i) compared to TabNet, FEAT-KD significantly reduces model complexity while retaining competitive predictive performance, effectively converting a black-box deep learning model into a more interpretable white-box representation, (ii) compared to FEAT, our method consistently outperforms in prediction accuracy, produces more compact models, and reduces the complexity of learned symbolic expressions. In addition, we demonstrate that FEAT-KD easily supports multi-target regression, in which the shared features contribute to the interpretability of the system. Our results suggest that FEAT-KD is a promising direction for interpretable ML, bridging the gap between deep learning’s predictive power and the intrinsic transparency of symbolic models.

paragraphs: FEAT produces interpretable predictions by combining compact symbolic features with linear weights. Finding those features through genetic programming can be inefficient. This paper introduces FEAT-KD, which instead draws on a trained TabNet model’s optimization and feature selection capabilities to help construct a concise symbolic regression model.

The method distills TabNet piece by piece into symbolic features and combines those features through a weighted linear expression. Knowledge distillation therefore serves as a bridge from a deep learning model to a more transparent representation. The resulting model retains an explicit feature-based structure, making the learned predictive relationship more accessible than the original neural model.

In the reported regression evaluations, FEAT-KD substantially reduces complexity relative to TabNet while maintaining competitive predictive performance. Compared with FEAT, it consistently improves accuracy, model compactness, and symbolic expression simplicity. The method also supports multiple prediction targets, with shared features contributing to interpretability across outputs. These findings suggest a practical route for using deep learning to guide the construction of compact, intrinsically interpretable models.
summary.tldr: FEAT-KD distills TabNet into compact symbolic regression models that retain competitive predictions and improve on FEAT in the reported evaluations.

title: FEAT-KD: Learning Concise Representations for Single and Multi-Target Regression via TabNet Knowledge Distillation

abstract: Recent RL research has utilized reward shaping–particularly complex shaping rewards such as intrinsic motivation (IM)–to encourage agent exploration in sparse-reward environments. While often effective, “reward hacking” can lead to the shaping reward being optimized at the expense of the extrinsic reward, resulting in a suboptimal policy. Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS) techniques such as Generalized Reward Matching (GRM) and Policy-Invariant Explicit Shaping (PIES) have mitigated this. These methods allow for implementing IM without altering optimal policies. In this work we show that they are effectively unsuitable for complex, exploration-heavy environments with long-duration episodes. To remedy this, we introduce Action-Dependent Optimality Preserving Shaping (ADOPS), a method of converting intrinsic rewards to an optimality-preserving form that allows agents to utilize IM more effectively in the extremely sparse environment of Montezuma’s Revenge. We also prove ADOPS accommodates reward shaping functions that cannot be written in a potential-based form: while PBRS-based methods require the cumulative discounted intrinsic return be independent of actions, ADOPS allows for intrinsic cumulative returns to be dependent on agents’ actions while still preserving the optimal policy set. We show how action-dependence enables ADOPS’s to preserve optimality while learning in complex, sparse-reward environments where other methods struggle.

paragraphs: Extra rewards can help a reinforcement learning agent explore when the environment rarely provides feedback. But the agent may learn to pursue those bonuses at the expense of the actual task. This paper studies how to make intrinsic rewards useful for exploration while preserving the set of policies that are optimal for the original objective.

The proposed method, Action-Dependent Optimality Preserving Shaping, converts intrinsic rewards into a form that preserves optimality. Its central distinction concerns accumulated discounted intrinsic reward. The potential-based approaches discussed in the paper require this return to be independent of the agent’s actions. ADOPS permits action dependence and is proved to accommodate shaping functions that cannot be expressed in potential-based form.

The authors show that existing methods struggle in complex environments with long episodes and heavy exploration demands. In Montezuma’s Revenge, ADOPS lets agents use intrinsic motivation more effectively despite extremely sparse task rewards. The contribution connects a broader mathematical form of reward shaping with practical learning in an environment where exploration is particularly difficult.
summary.tldr: ADOPS allows action-dependent exploration rewards while preserving the original optimal policies and improving learning in Montezuma’s Revenge.

title: Action-Dependent Optimality-Preserving Reward Shaping

abstract: In this paper, we propose an improved online confidence bound for multinomial logistic (MNL) models and apply this result to MNL bandits, achieving variance-dependent optimal regret. Recently, Lee & Oh (2024) established an online confidence bound for MNL models and achieved nearly minimax-optimal regret in MNL bandits. However, their results still depend on the norm-boundedness of the unknown parameter $B$ and the maximum size of possible outcomes $K$. To address this, we first derive an online confidence bound of $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{d \log t} + B \sqrt{d} )$, which is a significant improvement over the previous bound of $\mathcal{O} (B \sqrt{d} \log t \log K )$ (Lee & Oh, 2024). This is mainly achieved by establishing tighter self-concordant properties of the MNL loss and applying Ville’s inequality to bound the estimation error. Using this new online confidence bound, we propose a constant-time algorithm, OFU-MNL++, which achieves a variance-dependent regret bound of $\mathcal{O} \Big( d \log T \sqrt{ \sum_{t=1}^T \sigma_t^2 } \Big) $ for sufficiently large $T$, where $\sigma_t^2$ denotes the variance of the rewards at round $t$, $d$ is the dimension of the contexts, and $T$ is the total number of rounds. Furthermore, we introduce a Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)-based algorithm, OFU-M$^2$NL, which achieves an anytime $\operatorname{poly}(B)$-free regret of $\mathcal{O} \Big( d \log (BT) \sqrt{ \sum_{t=1}^T \sigma_t^2 } \Big) $.

paragraphs: Multinomial logistic bandits require learning from uncertain outcomes while choosing actions over time. Confidence bounds describe how much uncertainty remains in the model estimates and help guide those choices. This paper improves an online bound whose earlier form depended more heavily on both the unknown parameter's norm bound and the maximum number of outcomes.

The new confidence bound has order √(d log t) + B√d, where d is context dimension and B bounds the parameter norm. Its displayed form removes the previous explicit dependence on the outcome count and separates the time-growing term from B. The proof uses tighter self-concordant properties of the loss together with Ville's inequality.

The authors turn this bound into OFU-MNL++, a constant-time algorithm with variance-dependent optimal regret for sufficiently large horizons. They also introduce an algorithm based on maximum likelihood estimation with an anytime regret guarantee free of polynomial dependence on B. Both regret bounds track accumulated reward variance, connecting their guarantees to the uncertainty of the observed rewards.
summary.tldr: Tighter online confidence bounds yield multinomial logistic bandit algorithms with improved variance-dependent regret guarantees.

title: Improved Online Confidence Bounds for Multinomial Logistic Bandits

abstract: Continual learning (CL) focuses on the ability of models to learn sequentially from a stream of tasks. A major challenge in CL is catastrophic forgetting (CF). CF is a phenomenon where the model experiences significant performance degradation on previously learned tasks after training on new tasks. Although CF is commonly observed in convolutional neural networks (CNNs), the theoretical understanding about CF within CNNs remains limited. To fill the gap, we present a theoretical analysis of CF in a two-layer CNN. By employing a multi-view data model, we analyze the learning dynamics of different features throughout CL and derive theoretical insights. The findings are supported by empirical results from both simulated and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Continual learning trains a model on a sequence of tasks, making retention of earlier knowledge part of the learning problem. Catastrophic forgetting occurs when training on new tasks substantially degrades performance on previous ones. Although this behavior is commonly observed in convolutional neural networks, the paper notes that its theoretical explanation within these networks remains limited.

The authors study a two-layer convolutional neural network using a multi-view data model. Their analysis follows the learning dynamics of different features as the network moves through sequential tasks. This feature-level perspective examines how learning unfolds within the model, connecting the study of forgetting to changes in its internal feature learning over time.

The paper derives theoretical insights and supports them with experiments on both simulated and real-world datasets. Its contribution is explanatory: it develops a theoretical account within the specified two-layer architecture and data model. The empirical support connects that analysis to observed learning behavior, adding evidence to a subject where the practical phenomenon has been more established than its theoretical understanding.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes feature-learning dynamics in a two-layer CNN to develop a theoretical understanding of catastrophic forgetting.

title: Towards Understanding Catastrophic Forgetting in Two-layer Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: Few-shot image classification remains challenging due to the scarcity of labeled training examples. Augmenting them with synthetic data has emerged as a promising way to alleviate this issue, but models trained on synthetic samples often face performance degradation due to the inherent gap between real and synthetic distributions. To address this limitation, we develop a theoretical framework that quantifies the impact of such distribution discrepancies on supervised learning, specifically in the context of image classification. More importantly, our framework suggests practical ways to generate good synthetic samples and to train a predictor with high generalization ability. Building upon this framework, we propose a novel theoretical-based algorithm that integrates prototype learning to optimize both data partitioning and model training, effectively bridging the gap between real few-shot data and synthetic data. Extensive experiments results show that our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods, outperforming them across multiple datasets.

paragraphs: Few-shot image classification has very little labeled real data available for training. Synthetic images can increase the training supply, but differences between synthetic and real distributions can also hurt performance. This paper develops a theoretical framework for understanding how those discrepancies affect supervised image classification.

The framework is intended to guide both the generation of useful synthetic samples and the training of a predictor that generalizes well. Building on it, the authors introduce an algorithm that incorporates prototype learning and jointly addresses data partitioning and model training. This connects the way real and synthetic data are organized with the way the classifier learns from them.

Experiments across multiple datasets report better performance than the compared state-of-the-art approaches. The findings support treating synthetic-data augmentation as a distribution-alignment problem, rather than assuming additional generated examples will automatically help. The paper’s contribution joins a theoretical account of the real–synthetic gap with a concrete learning procedure designed to reduce its effect in few-shot classification.
summary.tldr: A theory-guided prototype-learning method improves few-shot classification by addressing distribution differences between real and synthetic data.

title: Provably Improving Generalization of Few-shot models with Synthetic Data

abstract: Directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) are a class of graphs commonly used in practice, with examples that include electronic circuits, Bayesian networks, and neural architectures. While many effective encoders exist for DAGs, it remains challenging to decode them in a principled manner, because the nodes of a DAG can have many different topological orders. In this work, we propose a grammar-based approach to constructing a principled, compact and equivalent sequential representation of a DAG. Specifically, we view a graph as derivations over an unambiguous grammar, where the DAG corresponds to a unique sequence of production rules. Equivalently, the procedure to construct such a description can be viewed as a lossless compression of the data. Such a representation has many uses, including building a generative model for graph generation, learning a latent space for property prediction, and leveraging the sequence representational continuity for Bayesian Optimization over structured data.

paragraphs: Directed acyclic graphs represent structures such as electronic circuits, Bayesian networks, and neural architectures. Turning these graphs into sequences is attractive for learning, but a single graph can admit many valid topological node orders. That ambiguity complicates the task of decoding a sequence into a graph in a principled way.

The paper proposes representing a graph as a derivation under an unambiguous grammar. Each DAG corresponds to a unique sequence of production rules, giving a compact sequential description that preserves the graph. The authors also interpret this construction as lossless compression: the sequence provides an equivalent representation rather than discarding structural information to simplify the input.

This representation can support several kinds of learning over structured objects. The paper identifies graph generation, property prediction through a learned latent space, and Bayesian optimization as uses. For optimization, continuity in the sequential representation provides a way to work with structured candidates. The central contribution is a common, unambiguous description that connects DAG structure with sequence-based modeling.
summary.tldr: An unambiguous graph grammar gives each DAG a unique, lossless sequence representation for learning and generation.

title: Directed Graph Grammars for Sequence-based Learning

abstract: The primary goal of brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) is to establish a direct linkage between neural activities and behavioral actions via neural decoders. Due to the nonstationary property of neural signals, BCIs trained on one day usually obtain degraded performance on other days, hindering the user experience. Existing studies attempted to address this problem by aligning neural signals across different days. However, these neural adaptation methods may exhibit instability and poor performance when only a few trials are available for alignment, limiting their practicality in real-world BCI deployment. To achieve efficient and stable neural adaptation with few trials, we propose Flow-Based Distribution Alignment (FDA), a novel framework that utilizes flow matching to learn flexible neural representations with stable latent dynamics, thereby facilitating source-free domain alignment through likelihood maximization. The latent dynamics of FDA framework is theoretically proven to be stable using Lyapunov exponents, allowing for robust adaptation. Further experiments across multiple motor cortex datasets demonstrate the superior performance of FDA, achieving reliable results with fewer than five trials. Our FDA approach offers a novel and efficient solution for few-trial neural data adaptation, offering significant potential for improving the long-term viability of real-world BCI applications.

Existing studies attempted to address this problem by aligning neural signals across different days. However, these neural adaptation methods may exhibit instability and poor performance when only a few trials are available for alignment, limiting their practicality in real-world BCI deployment. To achieve efficient and stable neural adaptation with few trials, we propose Flow-Based Distribution Alignment (FDA), a novel framework that utilizes flow matching to learn flexible neural representations with stable latent dynamics, thereby facilitating source-free domain alignment through likelihood maximization. The latent dynamics of FDA framework is theoretically proven to be stable using Lyapunov exponents, allowing for robust adaptation. Further experiments across multiple motor cortex datasets demonstrate the superior performance of FDA, achieving reliable results with fewer than five trials. Our FDA approach offers a novel and efficient solution for few-trial neural data adaptation, offering significant potential for improving the long-term viability of real-world BCI applications.

Aligning signals between days can help, yet the paper identifies instability and poor performance when only a few trials are available to perform that alignment.

The authors introduce Flow-Based Distribution Alignment, or FDA, to make adaptation effective with very little new data. It uses flow matching to learn flexible neural representations whose latent dynamics are stable. These representations support source-free alignment through likelihood maximization, allowing adaptation without requiring source data during the alignment process.

The paper proves stability of the latent dynamics using Lyapunov exponents and evaluates the framework across multiple motor cortex datasets. Experiments report superior performance and reliable adaptation with fewer than five trials. The theoretical result addresses stability, while the experiments show practical few-trial performance. Together, they suggest a route toward reducing the recalibration burden that limits the long-term usefulness of brain-computer interfaces.
summary.tldr: FDA uses flow matching with provably stable latent dynamics to adapt neural decoders, reporting reliable results with fewer than five trials.

title: Flow Matching for Few-Trial Neural Adaptation with Stable Latent Dynamics

abstract: Jailbreaking techniques trick Large Language Models (LLMs) into producing restricted output, posing a potential threat. One line of defense is to use another LLM as a Judge to evaluate the harmfulness of generated text. However, we reveal that these Judge LLMs are vulnerable to token segmentation bias, an issue that arises when delimiters alter the tokenization process, splitting words into smaller sub-tokens. This alters the embeddings of the entire sequence, reducing detection accuracy and allowing harmful content to be misclassified as safe. In this paper, we introduce Emoji Attack, a novel strategy that amplifies existing jailbreak prompts by exploiting token segmentation bias. Our method leverages in-context learning to systematically insert emojis into text before it is evaluated by a Judge LLM, inducing embedding distortions that significantly lower the likelihood of detecting unsafe content. Unlike traditional delimiters, emojis also introduce semantic ambiguity, making them particularly effective in this attack. Through experiments on state-of-the-art Judge LLMs, we demonstrate that Emoji Attack substantially reduces the unsafe prediction rate, bypassing existing safeguards.

This result concerns the reliability of the evaluator as well as the broader jailbreak pipeline: a judge can miss harmful content because its presentation has changed. The study identifies a concrete sensitivity in model-based safeguards, showing that successful detection in ordinary text does not establish equivalent detection for the tested emoji-modified text.
summary.tldr: Emoji insertion exploits token segmentation bias to reduce judge language models' detection of unsafe content.

title: Emoji Attack: Enhancing Jailbreak Attacks Against Judge LLM Detection

abstract: Feature evolvable learning studies the scenario where old features will vanish and new features will emerge when learning with data streams, and various methods have been developed by utilizing some useful relationships from old features to new features, rather than re-training from scratch. In this work, we focus on two fundamental problems: How to characterize the relationships between two different feature spaces, and how to exploit those relationships for feature evolvable learning. We introduce the Kernel Ortho-Mapping (KOM) discrepancy to characterize relationships between two different feature spaces via kernel functions, and correlate with the optimal classifiers learned from different feature spaces. Based on this discrepancy, we develop the one-pass algorithm for feature evolvable learning, which requires going through all instances only once without storing the entire or partial training data. Our basic idea is to take online kernel learning with the random Fourier features and incorporate some feature and label relationships via the KOM discrepancy for feature evolvable learning. We finally validate the effectiveness of our proposed method both theoretically and empirically.

paragraphs: Feature evolvable learning concerns data streams whose available inputs change: old features disappear and new ones become available. The goal is to use relationships between those feature spaces so that learning can continue without starting over. This paper asks both how to describe those relationships and how to make them useful for prediction.

The authors introduce Kernel Ortho-Mapping discrepancy, a kernel-based measure connecting different feature spaces. They relate this discrepancy to the optimal classifiers associated with those spaces. This gives the proposed measure a predictive role: it helps characterize relationships relevant to transferring learning when the input representation changes.

The resulting algorithm combines online kernel learning, random Fourier features, and feature-label relationships incorporated through the discrepancy. It processes each instance once without retaining all or part of the training data. The authors provide theoretical and empirical validation. The contribution therefore links a formal account of changing feature spaces with a streaming procedure designed to avoid storing and revisiting past examples.
summary.tldr: A kernel-based measure of relationships between changing feature spaces enables one-pass learning without retaining training examples.

title: One-Pass Feature Evolvable Learning with Theoretical Guarantees

abstract: Federated learning (FL), aimed at leveraging vast distributed datasets, confronts a crucial challenge: the heterogeneity of data across different silos. While previous studies have explored discrete representations to enhance model generalization across minor distributional shifts, these approaches often struggle to adapt to new data silos with significantly divergent distributions. In response, we have identified that models derived from FL exhibit markedly increased uncertainty when applied to data silos with unfamiliar distributions. Consequently, we propose an innovative yet straightforward iterative framework, termed Uncertainty-Based Extensible-Codebook Federated Learning (UEFL). This framework dynamically maps latent features to trainable discrete vectors, assesses the uncertainty, and specifically extends the discretization dictionary or codebook for silos exhibiting high uncertainty. Our approach aims to simultaneously enhance accuracy and reduce uncertainty by explicitly addressing the diversity of data distributions, all while maintaining minimal computational overhead in environments characterized by heterogeneous data silos. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that UEFL outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving significant improvements in accuracy (by 3%–22.1%) and uncertainty reduction (by 38.83%–96.24%). The source code is available at https://github.com/destiny301/uefl.

Discrete representations have helped with smaller shifts, but can struggle when a new silo contains unfamiliar data. This paper identifies increased model uncertainty on unfamiliar distributions and uses that observation to decide when the representation should expand.

UEFL maps latent features to trainable discrete vectors stored in a codebook. Its iterative procedure assesses uncertainty and extends that codebook specifically for silos showing high uncertainty. The representation can therefore acquire additional discrete vectors where the existing dictionary appears inadequate for the local distribution.

The framework aims to improve accuracy and reduce uncertainty with minimal computational overhead. Across multiple datasets, the authors report accuracy improvements of 3%–22.1% and uncertainty reductions of 38.83%–96.24% over state-of-the-art methods. These findings support uncertainty as a practical signal for targeted codebook growth in heterogeneous federated settings. The reported ranges describe the evaluated settings, showing how adaptive discrete representations can help accommodate substantial differences among silos.
summary.tldr: UEFL expands discrete representation codebooks for high-uncertainty data silos, improving reported federated-learning accuracy and reducing uncertainty.

title: Uncertainty-Based Extensible Codebook for Discrete Federated Learning in Heterogeneous Data Silos

abstract: This paper addresses online learning with ”corrupted” feedback. Our learner is provided with potentially corrupted gradients $\tilde g_t$ instead of the ”true” gradients $g_t$. We make no assumptions about how the corruptions arise: they could be the result of outliers, mislabeled data, or even malicious interference. We focus on the difficult “unconstrained” setting in which our algorithm must maintain low regret with respect to any comparison point $u \in \mathbb{R}^d$. The unconstrained setting is significantly more challenging as existing algorithms suffer extremely high regret even with very tiny amounts of corruption (which is not true in the case of a bounded domain). Our algorithms guarantee regret $ \|u\|G (\sqrt{T} + k) $ when $G \ge \max_t \|g_t\|$ is known, where $k$ is a measure of the total amount of corruption. When $G$ is unknown we incur an extra additive penalty of $(\|u\|^2+G^2) k$.

paragraphs: Online learning updates decisions as feedback arrives, but that feedback may contain corrupted gradients. This paper allows the corruption to arise without assumptions about its origin, including outliers, mislabeled data, or malicious interference. It studies an unconstrained setting, where the learner must compete with any comparison point in the full space rather than a fixed bounded region.

This requirement makes robustness especially difficult: existing unconstrained algorithms can incur extremely high regret even under tiny amounts of corruption. Regret measures the learner’s accumulated disadvantage relative to a comparison point. The proposed algorithms bound that disadvantage in terms of the comparison point’s size, the number of rounds, gradient magnitude, and total corruption.

When a bound G on all true gradient norms is known, the stated guarantee is ||u||G(√T + k), with comparison point u, T rounds, and corruption measure k. When G is unknown, an additional (||u||² + G²)k penalty appears. The results quantify the cost of corruption and the extra cost of lacking a gradient bound.
summary.tldr: These online algorithms provide explicit regret guarantees under arbitrarily arising gradient corruption, even when comparison points are unbounded.

title: Unconstrained Robust Online Convex Optimization

abstract: In continual RL we want agents capable of never-ending learning, and yet our evaluation methodologies do not reflect this. The standard practice in RL is to assume unfettered access to the deployment environment for the full lifetime of the agent. For example, agent designers select the best performing hyperparameters in Atari by testing each for 200 million frames and then reporting results on 200 million frames. In this position paper, we argue and demonstrate the pitfalls of this inappropriate empirical methodology: lifetime tuning. We provide empirical evidence to support our position by testing DQN and SAC across several of continuing and non-stationary environments with two main findings: (1) lifetime tuning does not allow us to identify algorithms that work well for continual learning---all algorithms equally succeed; (2) recently developed continual RL algorithms outperform standard non-continual algorithms when tuning is limited to a fraction of the agent's lifetime. The goal of this paper is to provide an explanation for why recent progress in continual RL has been mixed and motivate the development of empirical practices that better match the goals of continual RL.

paragraphs: This paper challenges a mismatch between continual reinforcement learning and its evaluation practices. Continual learning aims for agents that keep learning indefinitely, but researchers often choose settings using access to the deployment environment for an entire evaluated lifetime. The authors call this lifetime tuning and argue that it undermines assessment of ongoing learning ability.

They provide empirical evidence using DQN and SAC in continuing and changing environments. Under lifetime tuning, the tested algorithms succeed equally, making it difficult to identify which approaches are better suited to continual learning. When tuning is restricted to only part of an agent’s lifetime, recently developed continual-learning algorithms outperform standard approaches in the reported experiments.

The finding concerns what the evaluation procedure makes visible. Extensive tuning across the full lifetime can conceal differences that emerge when designers have less advance access to the conditions an agent will encounter. The authors use this result to help explain mixed progress in continual reinforcement learning and to motivate empirical practices that better reflect the goal of sustained adaptation.
summary.tldr: The experiments suggest that full-lifetime tuning hides advantages of continual reinforcement-learning methods that appear under limited tuning.

title: Position: Lifetime tuning is incompatible with continual reinforcement learning

abstract: Modern AI hardware, such as Nvidia’s Blackwell architecture, is increasingly embracing low-precision floating-point (FP) formats to handle the pervasive activation outliers in Large Language Models (LLMs). Despite this industry trend, a unified comparison of FP and integer (INT) quantization across varying granularities has been missing, leaving algorithm and hardware co-design without clear guidance. This paper fills that gap by systematically investigating the trade-offs between FP and INT formats. We reveal a critical performance crossover: while FP excels in coarse-grained quantization, INT consistently surpasses it as the quantization block size shrinks. Our comprehensive comparison demonstrates that for popular fine-grained formats like MX (block size 32), MXINT8 and MXINT4 are superior to their FP counterparts in both algorithmic accuracy and hardware efficiency. We also introduce a symmetric clipping method that resolves gradient bias in fine-grained low-bit INT training, enabling nearly lossless performance for MXINT8 training. These findings challenge the current hardware trajectory and advocate for prioritizing fine-grained INT formats in future AI accelerators to achieve a better balance of accuracy, power, and efficiency. Code is available at https://github.com/ChenMnZ/INT_vs_FP.

The paper examines how granularity changes the balance between accuracy and hardware efficiency.

summary.tldr: The study finds that integer quantization overtakes floating point at smaller block sizes, with MX integer formats improving accuracy and hardware efficiency.

title: INT vs. FP: A Comprehensive Study of Fine-Grained Low-bit Quantization Formats

abstract: We introduce TANGO, a dynamical-systems-inspired framework for graph representation learning that governs node feature evolution through a learned energy landscape and its associated descent dynamics. At the core of our approach is a learnable Lyapunov function over node embeddings, whose gradient defines an energy non-increasing direction that guarantees stability. To enhance flexibility while preserving the benefits of energy-based dynamics, we incorporate a novel tangential component, learned via message passing, that evolves features while maintaining the energy value. This decomposition into orthogonal flows of energy gradient descent and tangential evolution yields a flexible form of graph dynamics, and enables effective signal propagation even in flat or ill-conditioned energy regions, that often appear in graph learning. Our method is designed to help alleviate oversquashing, and is compatible with different graph neural network backbones. Empirically, TANGO achieves strong performance across a diverse set of node and graph classification and regression benchmarks, demonstrating the effectiveness of jointly learned energy functions and tangential flows for graph neural networks.

paragraphs: TANGO treats graph representation learning as a process in which node features evolve through a learned energy landscape. A learnable Lyapunov function assigns energy to the embeddings, and its gradient supplies a direction that does not increase that energy. This gives the feature dynamics a mathematical basis for stability.

Energy descent alone can provide limited movement in flat or poorly conditioned regions. TANGO adds a second component, learned through message passing, that moves features tangentially while preserving the energy value. The two components are orthogonal: one descends the energy landscape, while the other allows additional evolution without undoing that energy behavior.

This decomposition supports flexible dynamics and effective signal propagation in regions where descent is less useful. The framework is designed to help alleviate oversquashing and can work with different graph neural network backbones. Experiments report strong performance across node and graph classification and regression benchmarks. The findings support combining a learned stability structure with energy-preserving movement as a useful design for graph representations.
summary.tldr: TANGO combines stable energy descent with learned energy-preserving flows to improve graph feature evolution and signal propagation.

title: Graph Neural Dynamics via Learned Energy and Tangential Flows

abstract: Geometry is central to PDE-governed systems, motivating shape optimization and inversion. Classical pipelines conduct costly forward simulation with geometry processing, requiring substantial expert effort. Neural surrogates accelerate forward analysis but do not close the loop because gradients from objectives to geometry are often unavailable. Existing differentiable methods either rely on restrictive parameterizations or unstable latent optimization driven by scalar objectives, limiting interpretability and part-wise control. To address these challenges, we propose Geometry-Aware Neural Optimizer (GANO), an end-to-end differentiable framework that unifies geometry representation, field-level prediction, and automated optimization/inversion in a single latent-space loop. GANO encodes shapes with an auto-decoder and stabilizes latent updates via a denoising mechanism, and a geometry-informed surrogate provides a reliable gradient pathway for geometry updates. Moreover, GANO supports part-wise control through null-space projection and uses remeshing-free projection to accelerate geometry processing. We further prove that denoising induces an implicit Jacobian regularization that reduces decoder sensitivity, yielding controlled deformations. Experiments on three benchmarks spanning 2D Helmholtz, 2D airfoil, and 3D vehicles show state-of-the-art accuracy and stable, controllable updates, achieving up to +55.9% lift-to-drag improvement for airfoils and 7% drag reduction for vehicles.

GANO addresses this missing connection by integrating geometry representation, field prediction, and optimization in one differentiable loop.

They report state-of-the-art accuracy alongside stable, controllable updates, including up to 55.9% improvement in airfoil lift-to-drag ratio and 7% vehicle drag reduction. summary.tldr: GANO combines differentiable geometry, physical-field prediction, and denoising to produce stable, controllable shape optimization and inversion.

title: Geometry-Aware Neural Optimizer for Shape Optimization and Inversion

abstract: Proactive Recommender Systems (PRSs) aim to guide user preference shift toward target items by generating paths of intermediate recommendations. Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a principled framework for optimizing such sequential decision tasks, as path rewards can naturally capture both short-term acceptance and long-term guidance effectiveness. However, naively applying policy gradients to PRS results in deficient gradient estimation. We identify two deficiencies: (1) path-level rewards decompose into step-level rewards with positive mean, creating a length-dependent bias that causes gradients to favor path extension over meaningful exploration; (2) weighting each step by the entire path-level reward ignores the decomposition structure, leading to high gradient variance. To rectify these two deficiencies, we propose an effective RL framework ProRL with two novel mechanisms for proactive recommendation. First, Stepwise Reward Centering subtracts expected rewards to neutralize length-dependent bias, ensuring that path extension yields zero expected gradient signal. Second, Position-Specific Advantage Estimation leverages the reward decomposition structure to compute step-dependent baselines, reducing gradient variance. Together, these mechanisms yield policy gradients that precisely target path quality. Our experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that ProRL significantly outperforms state-of-the-art PRSs. Our code is available at https://github.com/hongruhou89/ProRL.

Reinforcement learning can evaluate these paths through short-term acceptance and longer-term guidance. The paper identifies two problems with applying policy gradients directly: an incentive to lengthen paths and noisy credit assignment across individual recommendation steps.

The first problem arises when step rewards have a positive mean, making longer paths attractive independently of their quality. ProRL subtracts expected step rewards so path extension contributes zero expected gradient signal. The second problem comes from weighting every step by the entire path reward. Position-specific advantage estimation uses the reward decomposition to construct step-dependent baselines and reduce variance.

Together, these mechanisms aim the learning signal at path quality while correcting the identified length bias and variance problem. Across three real-world datasets, ProRL significantly outperforms state-of-the-art proactive recommender systems. The results show the value of adapting policy-gradient estimation to the structure of recommendation-path rewards.
summary.tldr: ProRL corrects path-length bias and reduces gradient variance to improve reinforcement learning for proactive recommendation.

title: ProRL: Effective Reinforcement Learning for Proactive Recommendation via Rectified Policy Gradient Estimation

abstract: Resilience against Byzantine attackers and faster convergence on sparse networks are critical for decentralized optimization, yet existing methods fail to achieve both simultaneously. Existing DSGD-based Byzantine-resilient methods suffer from high transient complexity of $\mathcal{O}\left((1-\lambda)^{-6}\right)$, where $1-\lambda$ denotes the spectral gap of the network. While bias-correction methods such as Exact Diffusion can improve topology dependence, directly combining them with robust aggregators can lead to error accumulation. To address this issue, we introduce the scaled dual ascent (SDA) within the augmented Lagrangian framework for decentralized optimization, which mitigates error accumulation by scaling the dual update steps. Based on this, we propose BRED, which integrates Byzantine-robust Exact Diffusion with the SDA framework. We prove that BRED attains linear speedup, and achieves transient complexity of $\mathcal{O}\left((1-\lambda)^{-2}\right)$ when the Byzantine fraction $\delta$ is small. We further propose the momentum variant BRED-M, which reduces the Byzantine-affected transient complexity from $\mathcal{O}\left(\delta^2(1-\lambda)^{-6}\right)$ to $\mathcal{O}\left(\delta^2(1-\lambda)^{-4}\right)$. Empirical results on benchmark datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methods across diverse network topologies.

We further propose the momentum variant BRED-M, which reduces the Byzantine-affected transient complexity from $\mathcal{O}\left(\delta^2(1-\lambda)^{-6}\right)$ to $\mathcal{O}\left(\delta^2(1-\lambda)^{-4}\right)$. Empirical results on benchmark datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methods across diverse network topologies.

paragraphs: Decentralized learning must coordinate updates across a network, sometimes while participants send malicious information. Sparse connectivity makes convergence harder, and combining robust aggregation with bias-correction methods can accumulate errors. This paper addresses that interaction through scaled dual ascent, which adjusts the size of dual updates in an augmented Lagrangian formulation.

The resulting method, BRED, combines this mechanism with Byzantine-robust Exact Diffusion. The authors prove linear speedup and, when the fraction of Byzantine participants is small, improve transient complexity from dependence on the inverse spectral gap to the sixth power to dependence on its square. The spectral gap captures a network property that affects coordination, so this change strengthens the treatment of difficult network topologies.

A momentum extension, BRED-M, further improves the Byzantine-dependent part of transient complexity, reducing its inverse-gap exponent from six to four while retaining the squared dependence on the Byzantine fraction. Benchmark experiments across different network structures support the proposed methods. The strongest stated BRED transient bound specifically depends on a small Byzantine fraction.
summary.tldr: Scaled dual updates improve convergence guarantees for Byzantine-robust decentralized learning, with stronger bounds when the attacker fraction is small.

title: Improving the Robustness-Utility Trade-off in Decentralized Learning over Sparse Networks

abstract: Enabling large language models (LLMs) to solve complex reasoning tasks is a key step toward artificial general intelligence. Recent work augments LLMs with external tools to enable agentic reasoning, achieving high utility and efficiency in a plug-and-play manner. However, the inherent vulnerabilities of such methods to malicious manipulation of the tool-calling process remain largely unexplored. In this work, we identify a tool-specific attack surface and propose Sponge Tool Attack (STA), which disrupts agentic reasoning solely by rewriting the input prompt under a strict query-only access assumption. Without any modification on the underlying model or the external tools, STA converts originally concise and efficient reasoning trajectories into unnecessarily verbose and convoluted ones before arriving at the final answer. This results in substantial computational overhead while remaining stealthy by preserving the original task semantics and user intent. To achieve this, we design STA as an iterative, multi-agent collaborative framework with explicit rewritten policy control, and generates benign-looking prompt rewrites from the original one with high semantic fidelity. Extensive experiments across 6 models (including both open-source models and closed-source APIs), 12 tools, 4 agentic frameworks, and 13 datasets spanning 5 domains validate the effectiveness of STA.

paragraphs: Tool-using language models can solve complex tasks efficiently, but their tool-calling behavior introduces a distinct vulnerability. Sponge Tool Attack studies whether a rewritten prompt can make an otherwise efficient agent consume substantially more computation while still pursuing the same task. The target is the efficiency of the reasoning process.

The attack operates under a strict query-only assumption: it changes the input prompt without modifying the model or its tools. An iterative, multi-agent framework produces benign-looking rewrites with high semantic fidelity and explicit policy control. These prompts turn concise reasoning trajectories into unnecessarily lengthy and complicated ones before the final answer, preserving the original task meaning and user intent.

Experiments cover six models, twelve tools, four agentic frameworks, and thirteen datasets across five domains, including open-source models and closed-source APIs. The reported findings validate the attack’s effectiveness across that tested range. The study shows that preserving the apparent task and eventual answer can coexist with substantial computational overhead, making execution efficiency a meaningful dimension of agent robustness.
summary.tldr: Sponge Tool Attack rewrites prompts to inflate tool-using agents’ computation while preserving the original task’s meaning.

title: Sponge Tool Attack: Stealthy Denial-of-Efficiency against Tool-Augmented Agentic Reasoning

abstract: Zeroth-Order (ZO) optimization is pivotal for scenarios where backpropagation is unavailable, such as memory-constrained on-device learning and black-box optimization. However, existing methods face a stark trade-off: they are either sample-inefficient (e.g., standard finite differences) or suffer from high variance due to randomized estimation (e.g., random subspace methods). In this work, we propose Coherent Coordinate Descent (CoCD), a deterministic, sample-efficient, and budget-aware ZO optimizer. Theoretically, we formalize the notion of gradient coherence and demonstrate that CoCD is equivalent to Block Cyclic Coordinate Descent (BCCD) with “warm starts,” effectively converting historical (stale) gradients from a liability into a computational asset. This mechanism enables $O(1)$ query complexity per step while maintaining global descent directions. Furthermore, we derive error bounds revealing a counter-intuitive insight: larger finite-difference step sizes can induce an implicit smoothing effect on the optimization landscape by reducing the effective smoothness constant, thereby improving convergence stability. Experiments on MLP, CNN, and ResNet architectures (up to 270k parameters) demonstrate that CoCD significantly outperforms BCCD in terms of sample efficiency and convergence loss/accuracy, and exhibits superior stability over randomized ZO methods. Our results suggest that deterministic, structure-aware updates offer a superior alternative to randomization for lightweight ZO optimization.

paragraphs: Zeroth-order optimization improves a model through function evaluations when backpropagation is unavailable. Existing approaches can require many evaluations or suffer from noisy randomized estimates. Coherent Coordinate Descent offers a deterministic, budget-aware alternative that reuses historical gradient information to reduce the evaluation cost of each optimization step.

The theoretical analysis formalizes gradient coherence and connects the method to block cyclic coordinate descent with warm starts. This explains how older gradient estimates can remain useful computational information. The mechanism achieves constant query complexity per step while maintaining global descent directions. Error bounds also show that larger finite-difference steps can smooth the effective optimization landscape and improve convergence stability.

Experiments use MLP, CNN, and ResNet architectures with up to 270,000 parameters. CoCD improves sample efficiency and convergence loss or accuracy over block cyclic coordinate descent, and is more stable than randomized zeroth-order methods. These results support deterministic, structure-aware updates for the lightweight settings studied. The smoothing analysis also shows why a larger finite-difference step can sometimes help, despite appearing to be a coarser local estimate.
summary.tldr: CoCD reuses coherent historical gradients for efficient deterministic zeroth-order optimization and explains how larger finite-difference steps can stabilize learning.

title: Turning Stale Gradients into Stable Gradients: Coherent Coordinate Descent with Implicit Landscape Smoothing for Lightweight Zeroth-Order Optimization

abstract: Large Language Models have achieved strong performance on reasoning tasks with objective answers by generating step-by-step solutions, but diagnosing where a multi-step reasoning trace might fail remains difficult. Confidence estimation offers a natural diagnostic signal, yet existing methods are restricted to final answers or require internal model access. We introduce Stepwise Confidence Attribution (SCA), a framework for closed-source LLMs that assigns step-level confidence based only on generated reasoning traces. SCA applies the Information Bottleneck principle: steps aligning with consensus structures across correct solutions receive high confidence, while deviations are flagged as potentially erroneous. We propose two complementary methods: (1) NIBS, a non-parametric IB approach measuring consistency without graph structures, and (2) GIBS, a graph-based IB model that learns subgraphs through a differentiable mask to capture logical variability. Extensive experiments on mathematical reasoning and multi-hop question answering show that SCA reliably identifies low-confidence steps strongly correlated with reasoning errors. Moreover, using step-level confidence to guide self-correction improves the correction success rate by up to 13.5% over answer-level feedback.

paragraphs: Knowing that a final answer is uncertain does not reveal where a long reasoning process went wrong. Stepwise Confidence Attribution, or SCA, assigns confidence to individual reasoning steps using generated traces, without requiring access to a language model’s internal workings. It is designed to make failures in closed-source models easier to locate.

The framework uses the Information Bottleneck principle to identify useful agreement across correct solutions. Steps that match shared reasoning structures receive higher confidence, while departures are treated as possible errors. NIBS measures consistency without constructing graphs. GIBS instead learns relevant subgraphs through a differentiable mask, allowing the assessment to account for variation in logical structure.

Experiments on mathematical reasoning and multi-hop question answering find that low-confidence steps are strongly associated with reasoning errors. Using these step-level signals to guide self-correction improves correction success by up to 13.5% compared with answer-level feedback. The confidence scores therefore provide a practical diagnostic signal rather than a proof that a particular step is incorrect, and their finer resolution helps direct corrective effort.
summary.tldr: SCA uses agreement across correct reasoning traces to flag uncertain steps and improve self-correction without internal model access.

title: Diagnosing Multi-step Reasoning Failures in Black-box LLMs via Stepwise Confidence Attribution

abstract: High-quality kernel is critical for scalable AI systems, and enabling LLMs to generate such code would advance AI development. However, training LLMs for this task requires sufficient data, a robust environment, and the process is often vulnerable to reward hacking and lazy optimization. In these cases, models may hack training rewards or prioritize trivial correctness over meaningful speedup. In this paper, we systematically study reinforcement learning (RL) for kernel generation. We first design KernelGYM, a robust distributed GPU environment that supports reward hacking check, data collection from multi-turn interactions and long-term RL training. Building on KernelGYM, we investigate effective multi-turn RL methods and identify a biased policy gradient issue caused by self-inclusion in GRPO. To solve this, we propose Turn-level Reinforce-Leave-One-Out (TRLOO) to provide unbiased advantage estimation for multi-turn RL. To alleviate lazy optimization, we incorporate mismatch correction for training stability and introduce Profiling-based Rewards (PR) and Profiling-based Rejection Sampling (PRS) to overcome the issue. The trained model, Dr. Kernel-14B, reach performance competitive with Claude-4.5-Sonnet in Kernelbench. Finally, we study sequential test-time scaling for Dr. Kernel-14B, which even outperforms GPT-5 and Claude-4.5-Sonnet in the Kernelbench level-2 subset.

paragraphs: Dr. Kernel studies how to train language models to generate efficient Triton kernels. The paper highlights two failures in reinforcement learning for this task: exploiting the reward mechanism and settling for correct code without meaningful speed improvements. Its contribution combines a training environment, changes to learning signals, and profiling-based optimization.

KernelGYM provides distributed GPU execution, reward-hacking checks, collection of multi-turn interactions, and support for sustained training. The authors identify bias from self-inclusion in GRPO’s policy-gradient calculation and introduce Turn-level Reinforce-Leave-One-Out for unbiased advantage estimation. They also apply mismatch correction for stability and use profiling-based rewards and rejection sampling to encourage actual optimization rather than correctness alone.

The resulting Dr. Kernel-14B model achieves performance competitive with Claude-4.5-Sonnet on Kernelbench. With sequential test-time scaling, it surpasses GPT-5 and Claude-4.5-Sonnet on the benchmark’s level-2 subset. The latter result is tied to that subset and additional sequential computation. Overall, the findings connect kernel-generation performance to the quality of the execution environment, feedback, and multi-turn reinforcement-learning procedure.
summary.tldr: Dr. Kernel combines robust GPU evaluation, corrected multi-turn learning, and profiling feedback to train models that generate faster Triton kernels.

title: Dr. Kernel: Reinforcement Learning Done Right for Triton Kernel Generations

abstract: Modern large-scale neural networks are often trained and released in multiple sizes to accommodate diverse inference budgets. To improve efficiency, recent work has explored model upscaling: initializing larger models from trained smaller ones to accelerate convergence. However, this method can be sensitive to hyperparameters that need to be tuned at the target upscaled model size, which is prohibitively costly to do directly. It remains unclear whether tuning hyperparameters on smaller models and extrapolating via scaling laws is sound in this setting. We address this with principled approaches to width-based upscaling and efficient hyperparameter tuning in this setting. Motivated by $\mu$P and any-dimensional architectures, we introduce a general upscaling method that, like Net2Net, copies and perturbs weights, but uses theoretically grounded, width-dependent scalings for the perturbation noise and optimizer hyperparameters. First, we prove that under zero perturbation, the upscaled model is functionally equivalent to the base model throughout training. Second, we extend the $\mu$P theory to enable infinite-width limit analysis and establish hyperparameter transfer for upscaled models, greatly reducing the tuning cost. We empirically demonstrate that this method is effective on realistic datasets and architectures.

paragraphs: Initializing a larger neural network from a trained smaller one can accelerate training. However, that benefit becomes less attractive if the enlarged model requires expensive hyperparameter tuning at its final size. This paper develops a principled method for widening trained models and transferring tuning decisions from smaller models.

The method copies existing weights and perturbs them, using theoretically motivated width-dependent scaling for both the perturbations and optimizer hyperparameters. It draws on maximal update parameterization, or μP, and any-dimensional architectures. Under zero perturbation, the authors prove that the enlarged model remains functionally equivalent to the base model throughout training, giving a precise account of that special case.

The paper also extends μP theory to analyze upscaled models in the infinite-width limit and establishes hyperparameter transfer in this setting. This reduces the need to tune directly at the expensive target size. Experiments on realistic datasets and architectures demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The contribution makes warm-starting and tuning part of a common scaling framework, rather than treating enlargement as only a weight-initialization procedure.
summary.tldr: The paper provides theoretically grounded model widening and hyperparameter transfer to make training larger models from smaller ones more efficient.

title: $μ$pscaling small models: Principled warm starts and hyperparameter transfer

abstract: LLM-based multi-agent embodied planning remains impractical due to prohibitively high execution latency. We identify failed actions as the dominant bottleneck, stemming from two core challenges: inaccurate state tracking under partial observability and inefficient coordination that produces redundant or conflicting actions. We introduce Mosaic, a runtime-efficient multi-agent planning framework that addresses both challenges. Mosaic maintains accurate yet lightweight state tracking through agent-centric semantic memory that stores objects in relative coordinates, enabling geometric transformations and coordination. It ensures efficient coordination through Integer Linear Programming that allocates actions at every planning step, enforcing physical feasibility and inter-agent coordination constraints. Across AI2-THOR and search-and-rescue benchmarks, Mosaic achieves 27–32% faster execution, 30–33% fewer LLM calls, 25–31% fewer steps, and 4–10% points higher success rates. These results demonstrate that efficient memory and constraint-guided coordination are critical for scalable, low-latency multi-agent planning.

paragraphs: Teams of language-model-driven embodied agents can spend substantial time attempting actions that fail. This paper identifies two main causes of that bottleneck: inaccurate tracking of a partially observed world and coordination that produces conflicting or redundant actions. Mosaic addresses both causes within a runtime-focused planning framework.

Each agent maintains a lightweight semantic memory that records objects in relative coordinates. This supports geometric transformations and coordination while helping track the state of the environment. At every planning step, an integer linear program allocates actions subject to physical-feasibility and inter-agent coordination constraints. State memory and constrained allocation therefore work together to reduce avoidable execution failures.

Across AI2-THOR and search-and-rescue benchmarks, Mosaic delivers 27–32% faster execution, 30–33% fewer language-model calls, and 25–31% fewer steps. Success rates increase by 4–10 percentage points. These results connect better coordination to both efficiency and task completion: fewer wasted actions reduce runtime while improving the chance of finishing successfully. The findings support treating memory and action allocation as central components of efficient embodied planning.
summary.tldr: Mosaic combines relative-coordinate memory with constrained action allocation to make multi-agent embodied planning faster and more successful.

title: Mosaic: Runtime-Efficient Multi-Agent Embodied Planning

abstract: Training-time privileged information (PI) can enable language models to succeed on tasks they would otherwise fail, making it a powerful tool for reinforcement learning in hard, long-horizon settings. However, transferring capabilities learned with PI to policies that must act without it at inference time remains a fundamental challenge. We study this problem in the context of distilling frontier models for multi-turn agentic environments, where closed-source systems typically hide their internal reasoning and expose only action trajectories. This breaks standard distillation pipelines, since successful behavior is observable but the reasoning process is not. We introduce $\pi$-Distill, a joint teacher–student framework that trains a PI-conditioned teacher and an unconditioned student simultaneously within a single shared-parameter model, enabling the teacher to learn how to use PI while mitigating distribution shift during transfer. We show that $\pi$-Distill effectively distills frontier agents using action-only privileged information, matching or outperforming industry-standard pipelines that assume access to full Chain-of-Thought supervision across multiple agentic benchmarks, models, and forms of PI. We complement our results with extensive analysis that characterize what factors enable effective learning with PI.
