paragraphs: Extra information available during training can help a language-model agent solve difficult, long tasks. The challenge is transferring that capability to an agent that must act without the extra information later. This becomes especially difficult when a frontier model exposes successful action sequences but keeps its internal reasoning private.

The proposed π-Distill framework jointly trains a teacher conditioned on privileged information and a student that does not receive it. Both operate within one shared-parameter model. This arrangement lets the teacher learn how to use the additional information while mitigating the distribution shift involved in transferring its behavior to the student.

Across multiple agent benchmarks, models, and forms of privileged information, π-Distill effectively transfers capabilities using action-only information. It matches or exceeds industry-standard pipelines that assume access to complete chain-of-thought supervision. The results show that observed actions can provide effective training guidance within this joint framework, even when the source agent’s reasoning is unavailable. Further analysis examines factors that enable successful learning with privileged information.
summary.tldr: π-Distill jointly trains a privileged teacher and unconditioned student to transfer agent capabilities from action-only supervision.

title: Privileged Information Distillation for Language Models

abstract: Decision trees and diffusion models are ostensibly disparate model classes, one discrete and hierarchical, the other continuous and dynamic. This work unifies the two by establishing a crisp mathematical correspondence between hierarchical decision trees and diffusion processes in appropriate limiting regimes. Our unification reveals a shared optimization principle: Global Trajectory Score Matching (GTSM), for which gradient boosting (in an idealized version) is asymptotically optimal. We underscore the conceptual value of our work through two key practical instantiations: treeflow, which achieves competitive generation quality on tabular data with higher fidelity and a 2$\times$ computational speedup, and dsmtree, a novel distillation method that transfers hierarchical decision logic into neural networks, matching teacher performance within 2% on many benchmarks.

paragraphs: Decision trees organize computation through discrete hierarchical choices, while diffusion models describe a continuous evolving process. This paper establishes a mathematical correspondence between these seemingly different model classes in appropriate limiting regimes. The connection offers a shared way to understand their behavior rather than treating hierarchy and dynamics as unrelated modeling approaches.

The authors identify a common optimization principle called Global Trajectory Score Matching. Under an idealized formulation, gradient boosting is asymptotically optimal for this principle. Both qualifications matter: the result concerns an idealized version of boosting and its limiting behavior, rather than asserting optimality for every practical boosted-tree implementation.

Two applications demonstrate how the correspondence can inform methods. Treeflow generates tabular data with competitive quality, higher fidelity, and a reported twofold computational speedup. Dsmtree distills hierarchical decision logic into neural networks and comes within 2% of teacher performance on many benchmarks. These results give the theoretical connection practical consequences for both data generation and transferring tree-based decision behavior into neural models.
summary.tldr: A limiting correspondence between decision trees and diffusion yields a shared optimization principle and practical methods for generation and distillation.

title: Trees to Flows and Back: Unifying Decision Trees and Diffusion Models

abstract: Linear bandits traditionally prioritize regret minimization, often overlooking statistical inference of the underlying parameter as a critical objective. In high-stakes settings such as healthcare, precise parameter estimation is indispensable, as it provides fundamental insights into system mechanisms and ensures robust decision-making under covariate shift. We investigate the tripartite balance between regret, inference, and safety, deriving a fundamental minimax lower bound that characterizes the Pareto-optimal frontier of these competing goals. We then propose SERMiSC, a novel algorithm that achieves the optimal trade-off by matching this lower bound while maintaining a near-constant $\tilde{O}(1)$ safety risk. Empirical results demonstrate that SERMiSC effectively navigates the Pareto frontier and outperforms various baselines, thereby validating our theoretical analysis.

paragraphs: A linear bandit algorithm must choose actions while learning an unknown reward relationship. Minimizing regret prioritizes good decisions, but accurately estimating the underlying parameter is a separate objective. This paper studies how those goals interact when actions must also satisfy safety requirements.

The authors derive a fundamental minimax lower bound describing the best attainable trade-off among regret, statistical inference, and safety. This characterizes a Pareto frontier: the boundary of competing outcomes that an algorithm can achieve in the studied setting. The result provides a standard for judging whether an algorithm's balance is optimal, beyond showing good performance on one objective alone.

The proposed algorithm, SERMiSC, matches that lower bound while maintaining a near-constant safety-risk rate expressed as Õ(1). This is a bound on risk, rather than a claim that risk disappears. Empirical comparisons show that SERMiSC navigates the frontier effectively and outperforms the evaluated baselines. Together, the theory and experiments support treating parameter estimation as an explicit objective alongside reward and safety.
summary.tldr: SERMiSC achieves the derived optimal trade-off among regret, parameter inference, and safety in linear stochastic bandits.

title: The Pareto-optimal Trade-off between Regret and Statistical Inference in Linear Stochastic Bandits under Safety Constraints

abstract: This paper presents a state representation framework for Markov decision processes (MDPs) that can be learned solely from state trajectories, requiring neither reward signals nor the actions executed by the agent. We propose learning the $\textit{minimum action distance}$ (MAD), defined as the minimum number of actions required to transition between states, as a fundamental metric that captures the underlying structure of an environment. The MAD naturally enables critical downstream tasks such as goal-conditioned reinforcement learning and reward shaping by providing a dense, geometrically meaningful measure of progress. Our self-supervised learning approach constructs an embedding space where the distances between embedded state pairs correspond to their MAD, accommodating both symmetric and asymmetric approximations. We evaluate the framework on a comprehensive suite of environments with known MAD values, encompassing both deterministic and stochastic transition dynamics, discrete and continuous state spaces, and environments with noisy observations. Empirical results show that the proposed approach learns MAD representations more efficiently than existing methods, produces more accurate estimates of the true MAD, and improves performance on downstream goal-reaching tasks.

paragraphs: Two states can look similar while requiring many actions to move between them. This paper learns a representation based on minimum action distance: the fewest actions needed to transition from one state to another. That distance is intended to capture an environment's transition structure and provide a meaningful measure of progress toward a goal.

The learning procedure uses only sequences of observed states, without rewards or records of the actions performed. It builds an embedding space in which distances between state representations approximate minimum action distance. The framework accommodates both symmetric and asymmetric approximations, allowing its representation of transition distance to account for direction when appropriate.

Evaluation uses environments with known minimum action distances, including deterministic and stochastic dynamics, discrete and continuous states, and noisy observations. The method learns representations more efficiently than existing approaches, estimates the true distances more accurately, and improves downstream goal-reaching performance. These findings connect representation quality with practical usefulness: the learned distances can support goal-conditioned reinforcement learning and reward shaping by providing a dense measure of progress.
summary.tldr: Learning minimum action distances from state trajectories alone yields more accurate representations and improves goal-reaching performance in the evaluated environments.

title: Learning the Minimum Action Distance

abstract: Continual learning enables neural networks to learn tasks sequentially without forgetting previously acquired knowledge. However, neural networks suffer from catastrophic forgetting, where learning new tasks degrades performance on earlier ones. We address this problem with Shapley Neuron Valuation (SNV), a principled framework that quantifies Neuron importance in continual learning, grounded in cooperative game theory. SNV selectively freezes important Neurons while keeping others plastic, enabling buffer-free continual learning without expanding architecture. Experiments on ImageNet-1k show that SNV consistently outperforms existing buffer-free methods. In particular, SNV improves accuracy by +2.88% in the class incremental learning and +6.46% in the task incremental learning scenarios compared to the second baseline.

paragraphs: Learning tasks sequentially can cause a neural network to lose skills acquired earlier, a problem called catastrophic forgetting. Shapley Neuron Valuation addresses this by deciding which neurons should be protected when training moves to a new task. Its aim is to balance preserving existing knowledge with retaining enough flexibility to learn.

The framework grounds neuron importance in cooperative game theory through Shapley valuation. It selectively freezes neurons judged important while allowing the remaining neurons to change. This makes the importance estimate operational: it determines where adaptation is permitted. The resulting continual-learning method uses no replay buffer and does not expand the network architecture.

On ImageNet-1k, SNV consistently outperforms the evaluated buffer-free methods. The abstract reports accuracy improvements of +2.88% in class-incremental learning and +6.46% in task-incremental learning relative to the second baseline. These results support selective preservation of neurons as a way to reduce forgetting within a fixed network. The contribution combines a principled importance framework with a direct training rule and evidence across two continual-learning scenarios.
summary.tldr: Shapley-based neuron importance guides selective freezing to improve continual learning without replay buffers or network expansion.

title: Shapley Neuron Values for Continual Learning: Which Neurons Matter Most?

abstract: Continual Pre-Training (CPT) is essential for enabling Language Models (LMs) to integrate new factual knowledge without erasing old. While classical CPT techniques like data replay have become the standard paradigm, the mechanisms underlying how LMs acquire and retain facts over time, termed as continual Factual Knowledge Acquisition (cFKA), remain unclear. In this work, we present a theoretical framework that characterizes the training dynamics of cFKA using a single-layer Transformer with linear attention, offering a unified explanation for the behavior of popular CPT methods. Our analysis reveals that regularization-based methods merely adjust the convergence rate of parameters without altering the inherent forgetting tendency, whereas data replay methods shift convergence dynamics and stabilize pretrained knowledge. Building on these insights, we propose a novel generative data replay approach, called Selecting Tokens via attentiOn Contribution (STOC), which identifies influential factual snippets to guide replay generation. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets validate our theoretical findings and demonstrate that STOC effectively enhances cFKA by mitigating catastrophic forgetting.

paragraphs: Continual pretraining lets language models acquire new facts, but it can also erase knowledge learned earlier. This paper develops a theoretical account of how factual knowledge is acquired and retained over successive training. The analysis uses a single-layer Transformer with linear attention, providing a simplified setting for examining common continual pretraining methods.

Within that framework, regularization changes how quickly parameters converge without changing their underlying tendency to forget. Data replay changes the convergence dynamics themselves and stabilizes pretrained knowledge. This distinction explains why slowing parameter movement and reintroducing prior information can have different effects, with the theoretical claim grounded in the model studied.

The method connects an explanation of retention dynamics to a concrete strategy for choosing what to replay.

title: Towards Understanding Continual Factual Knowledge Acquisition of Language Models: From Theory to Algorithm

abstract: When a learner faces a new task with few samples, it must leverage any available side information. In practice, this often comes in the form of model evaluations on related tasks in public benchmarks. A key question then is how to model task relatedness such that it is both realistic and the benchmark evaluations lead to provable gains. Empirically, we observe that weak monotonicity is often approximately satisfied: if a model dominates another on many benchmarks, it also tends to outperform on the new task. We explore the statistical complexity of learning under (approximate) weak monotonicity, leveraging it within two learning paradigms: transfer learning and model selection aggregation. We show that not only can we prune the model class based on monotonicity, but we can also further adapt to the geometry of the available trade-offs by hedging on the frontier.

paragraphs: When only a few examples are available for a new task, evaluations on related benchmarks offer potentially useful evidence about which models to trust. The difficulty is deciding what those earlier results actually imply. This paper studies a task-relatedness assumption that can connect benchmark performance to provable benefits on a new task.

The assumption is approximate weak monotonicity: a model that dominates another across many benchmarks tends to perform better on the new task as well. The authors observe this tendency empirically and analyze learning under both weak monotonicity and its approximate form. The relationship is a qualified tendency, so its usefulness depends on how well it describes the tasks being considered.

The analysis covers transfer learning and model selection aggregation. Benchmark information can eliminate parts of the model class, but the authors show that it can also inform adaptation to the geometry of the remaining tradeoffs. Their frontier-based approach therefore uses more than a simple ranking: it exploits the structure of available performance compromises when new-task evidence is scarce.
summary.tldr: Under approximate weak monotonicity, benchmark results can guide few-sample learning through model pruning and adaptation to available performance tradeoffs.

title: Hedging on the Frontier: Learning New Tasks with Few Samples

abstract: Despite the central role of sensor-derived measurements such as imaging traits and plasma biomarkers in biomedical research and clinical practice, existing generative models for disease prediction largely depend on event-level representations from hospital and registry data. Given the multi-factorial nature of human disease, the absence of explicit modeling of social determinants of health (SDoH) limits the capacity for personalized disease modeling and clinical decision support. To address this limitation, we propose a generative model with ICD-coded proxies of SDoH for in silico modeling of disease reasoning, a conditioned latent diffusion framework that establishes the connection between multi-organ sensor data with tokenized healthcare events. Specifically, we introduce a novel geometric diffusion model to characterize the temporal evolution of complex data representation such as brain networks (region-to-region connectivity encoded in a graph), in parallel with diffusion models for tabular data from other organ systems. Together, we integrate the generative model with digitalized SDoH proxies (coined DiffDT) for simulated intervention and reasoning of future disease trajectories. We conduct extensive experiments on the UK Biobank (UKB) dataset, which contains organ-specific imaging traits, including brain (44,834), heart (23,987), liver (28,722), and kidney (32,155), along with nearly 500k medical history sequences (age range: 25$\sim$89 years). Our DiffDT achieves significant improvements over state-of-the-art human disease autoregressive models and imaging trait generative baselines.

paragraphs: Disease progression involves information that hospital-event sequences alone do not capture, including organ measurements and social determinants of health. This paper develops DiffDT to bring these sources into a generative model for simulated disease reasoning. Social determinants enter through ICD-coded proxies, linking their digital representation to healthcare histories and sensor-derived measurements.

The authors report significant improvements over disease autoregressive models and imaging-trait generative baselines. title: Marrying Generative Model of Healthcare Events with Digital Twin of Social Determinants of Health for Disease Reasoning

abstract: Transaction cost optimization (TCO) of online portfolio selection is crucial in computing science, due to the significant impact of transaction costs in practical short-term trading. Moreover, sparsity of portfolio vector is often desired to enhance stability and decrease risk. However, there is a lack of models considering transaction costs and sparsity simultaneously in the literature. In this paper, we first propose a $K$-sparse TCO model that minimizes the negative return and transaction costs while keeping the portfolio vector being $K$-sparse. Noting that the model is NP-hard due to the $K$-sparse constraint, we bypass this difficulty by reformulating the sparse model to a nonsmooth difference of convex (DC) optimization problem. We show that both problems are equivalent by proving that the penalty parameter is large enough. Then, to overcome the difficulty caused by the nonsmoothness and the simplex constraint of the model, we develop a proximal subgradient algorithm (PSGA) to solve the DC problem and apply the alternating direction of multipliers (ADMM) to compute the proximity operator of the corresponding function. Furthermore, we establish the global convergence of the entire sequence generated by PSGA through showing the surrogate function satisfies the Kurdyka-{Ł}ojasiewicz (KL) property. In addition, by showing the KL exponent of the surrogate function is $1/2$, we establish the R-linear convergence rate of PSGA for any arbitrary initiaal point. Finally, we compare our proposed algorithm with other state-of-the-art strategies on four benchmark real-market data sets, with the numerical results showing that the proposed algorithm achieves lower risk while keeping higher return than classical TCO models.

paragraphs: This paper studies portfolio selection when trading costs matter and the investor wants to hold only a limited number of assets. Its model balances returns against transaction costs while imposing a K-sparse constraint: at most K portfolio entries can be nonzero. Combining these goals addresses a gap in models that treat trading costs and sparse holdings separately.

The sparsity constraint makes the problem NP-hard. The authors reformulate it as a nonsmooth difference-of-convex optimization problem and prove equivalence when the penalty parameter is sufficiently large. They develop a proximal subgradient algorithm for this reformulation, using ADMM to compute the proximity operation needed to handle the objective and portfolio constraints.

The theoretical contribution establishes convergence of the entire sequence of iterates and an R-linear convergence rate from any starting point, using properties of a surrogate function. These are convergence guarantees, not a claim that every run finds the global optimum of the original hard problem. Tests on four real-market datasets report lower risk while maintaining higher returns than classical transaction-cost models.
summary.tldr: The paper combines sparse portfolio holdings and transaction costs in an optimization method with proven linear convergence and favorable results on four market datasets.

title: A Linearly Convergent Proximal Subgradient Algorithm for Sparse Portfolio Optimization with Transaction Cost

abstract: Test-time compute (TTC) has become an increasingly prominent paradigm for enhancing large language models (LLMs). Despite the empirical success of methods such as best-of-$n$ (BoN) sampling and sequential revision, their fundamental limits remain unclear. We address this gap by analyzing a mixture-of-reference policy model and proving that standard BoN is inherently suboptimal. To move closer to the optimal frontier, we study reward-filtered sequential inference, a simple procedure that selectively incorporates only high-reward generations into the context. This mechanism concentrates computation on superior policy candidates and suppresses inferior ones. On the theoretical side, we show that reward-filtered sequential inference yields strictly stronger guarantees than standard TTC paradigms. On the empirical side, we evaluate such an inference strategy across diverse benchmarks and observe consistent improvements over widely used approaches, demonstrating the practical effectiveness of our framework.

On the theoretical side, we show that reward-filtered sequential inference yields strictly stronger guarantees than standard TTC paradigms. paragraphs: Spending more computation during inference can improve language-model outputs through methods such as generating many candidates or revising earlier answers. This paper asks what those methods can achieve in principle. Within a mixture-of-reference policy model, the authors prove that standard best-of-n sampling is inherently suboptimal.

They study reward-filtered sequential inference as a way to move closer to the optimal frontier. The procedure selectively adds high-reward generations to the context used for later inference. This allows stronger candidates to influence subsequent computation while suppressing inferior ones. The key design choice is therefore not just how many generations to produce, but which generations should shape the next stage.

The theoretical analysis establishes strictly stronger guarantees for this procedure than for standard test-time-compute paradigms within the studied framework. Experiments across diverse benchmarks also show consistent improvements over widely used approaches. Together, the results support reward-based context filtering as a useful mechanism for allocating inference computation, with both formal and empirical evidence behind the proposed strategy.
summary.tldr: Sequentially retaining high-reward generations improves inference empirically and provides stronger theoretical guarantees within the paper's policy model.

title: On the Limits of Test-Time Compute: Sequential Reward Filtering for Better Inference

abstract: Multimodal alignment can fail under deployment shift because standard objectives entangle cross-modal dependence with marginal-sensitive geometry. Stable Spectral Copula Alignment (SSCA) provides a deployment protocol for copula-stable dependence under approximately coordinate-wise monotone marginal distortions, together with auditable, label-free diagnostics for monitoring and mitigation. SSCA combines (i) clipped soft-rank Gaussianization that suppresses marginal effects while tracking tie and approximation errors, (ii) dependence-weighted sliced Wasserstein hub coupling for globally coherent multiway alignment with cycle auditing, and (iii) diagonal-stabilized block-spectral learning with eigengap-normalized Davis-Kahan diagnostics, yielding an actionable subspace-risk inequality. A calibrated gate maps diagnostic proxies to a reliability signal with a measurable false-alarm/miss trade-off, enabling stability-mode updates, budgeted remediation, and conservative no-update fallback for out-of-scope drift. Evaluations on MOSEI/MELD, MSCOCO, and CC3M-500K show improved performance under perturbation and substantially reduced degradation under controlled monotone distortions, raw-pipeline drifts, and frozen-feature retrieval stress tests.

paragraphs: Multimodal alignment can deteriorate when deployment changes the distributions of individual modalities, even if useful relationships between them persist. SSCA targets dependence that remains stable under approximately coordinate-wise monotone distortions. This is a specific shift setting: the protocol aims to preserve cross-modal relationships while reducing sensitivity to changes in individual feature distributions.

The method first uses clipped soft ranks and Gaussianization to suppress marginal effects while tracking approximation and tie errors. It then couples modalities through a shared hub using dependence-weighted sliced Wasserstein alignment. A stabilized spectral learning stage adds diagnostics for the risk that the learned subspace changes, and cycle auditing checks multiway consistency.

A calibrated gate converts these diagnostics into a reliability signal with measurable false-alarm and miss trade-offs. summary.tldr: SSCA combines shift-resistant multimodal alignment with label-free diagnostics that guide updates and fallback under deployment drift.

title: Stable Spectral Copula Alignment for Robust Multimodal Learning

abstract: In recent years, bilevel optimization (BLO) has attracted significant attention for its broad applications in machine learning. However, most existing works on BLO remain confined to the single-task setting and rely on the lower-level strong convexity assumption, which significantly restricts their applicability to modern machine learning problems of growing complexity. In this paper, we make the first attempt to extend BLO to the multi-task setting under a relaxed lower-level general convexity (LLGC) assumption. To this end, we reformulate the multi-task bilevel learning (MTBL) problem with LLGC into an equality constrained multi-objective optimization (ECMO) problem. However, ECMO itself is a new problem that has not yet been studied in the literature. To address this gap, we first establish a new Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT)-based Pareto stationarity as the convergence criterion for ECMO algorithm design. Based on this foundation, we propose a weighted Chebyshev (WC)-penalty algorithm that achieves a finite-time convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(ST^{-\frac{1}{2}})$ to KKT-based Pareto stationarity in both deterministic and stochastic settings, where $S$ denotes the number of objectives, and $T$ is the total iterations. Moreover, by varying the preference vector over the $S$-dimensional simplex, our WC-penalty method systematically explores the Pareto front. Finally, solutions to the ECMO problem translate directly into solutions for the original MTBL problem, thereby closing the loop between these two foundational optimization frameworks.

paragraphs: Bilevel learning involves an optimization problem whose outcome depends on another optimization problem. Extending this arrangement to several tasks introduces competing objectives. This paper studies that setting while relaxing a common requirement: the lower-level problem needs to be convex, but need not satisfy the stronger condition of strong convexity. That broadens the class of problems covered by the formulation.

The authors convert the multi-task bilevel problem into a multi-objective problem with equality constraints. They then define a convergence criterion using Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions and Pareto stationarity, which describes a stationary tradeoff among objectives. Their weighted Chebyshev penalty algorithm is designed to reach this criterion while handling the equality constraints.

The stated convergence rate is O(S/√T), where S is the number of objectives and T is the iteration count, in both deterministic and stochastic settings. Changing a preference vector lets the method explore the Pareto front. Solutions of the reformulated problem translate back to the original bilevel problem, connecting the algorithmic result to the learning task it was designed to solve.
summary.tldr: The paper connects multi-task bilevel learning to constrained multi-objective optimization and develops an algorithm with a proved rate toward Pareto stationarity.

title: A Tale of Two Problems: Multi-Task Bilevel Learning Meets Equality Constrained Multi-Objective Optimization

abstract: When a neural network estimates someone’s age from a photograph, does it process biometric data? The answer depends on whether identity-discriminative representations arise within the network during inference, a question that may seem trivial to ML researchers but triggers consent requirements under GDPR, statutory damages under BIPA, or high-risk AI classification under the EU AI Act. Yet no regulatory guidance addresses it. This position paper provides empirical evidence: 14 models evaluated across 3 face verification benchmarks show age estimators fall orders of magnitude short of identification thresholds. Age estimation models cannot identify individuals. We call on researchers to provide transparency about what systems store and can do, and on regulators to distinguish transient processing from template storage.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether a network that estimates age from a face also develops internal representations capable of distinguishing individual identities. The authors frame that technical question as central to debates about biometric data: processing a facial photograph and possessing a usable identification capability are different things that need to be examined directly.

The paper supplies empirical evidence from 14 models evaluated on three face verification benchmarks. The tested age estimators performed orders of magnitude below identification thresholds. The authors use these results to support their position that age estimation models cannot identify individuals, grounding the argument in measured identification capability rather than the fact that the input contains a face.

The distinction matters because biometric classifications can carry substantial regulatory consequences. The authors call for researchers to disclose what systems retain and what they can actually do, and for regulators to distinguish temporary computation from storing identifying templates. Their contribution connects an empirical capability assessment to a proposal for more technically informed regulation.
summary.tldr: The authors use face verification evaluations to argue that age estimation should be distinguished from biometric identification.

abstract: In this paper we extend previous results providing a theoretical analysis of a new Monte Carlo ensemble classifier. The framework allows us to characterize the conditions under which the ensemble approach can be expected to outperform the single hypothesis classifier. Moreover, we provide a closed form expression for the distribution of the true ensemble accuracy, as well as of its mean and variance. We then exploit this result in order to analyze the expected error behavior in a particularly interesting case.
originalAbstract: In this paper we extend previous results providing a theoretical analysis of a new Monte Carlo ensemble classifier. The framework allows us to characterize the conditions under which the ensemble approach can be expected to outperform the single hypothesis classifier. Moreover, we provide a closed form expression for the distribution of the true ensemble accuracy, as well as of its mean and variance. We then exploit this result in order to analyze the expected error behavior in a particularly interesting case.

paragraphs: This paper extends a theoretical analysis of a Monte Carlo ensemble classifier. The central question is when combining classifiers can be expected to produce better predictions than using a single hypothesis. The analysis characterizes conditions for such an advantage, so its conclusion concerns when an ensemble helps rather than asserting that combining classifiers always improves accuracy.

The framework also provides a closed-form expression for the distribution of the ensemble's true accuracy. It gives expressions for the mean and variance as well. Together, these quantities describe both the average accuracy and how much accuracy varies within the analyzed framework, providing a fuller account than an average alone.

The authors then use this distributional result to examine expected error behavior in a particular case. The contribution is an analytical basis for understanding ensemble performance: conditions identify when an advantage is expected, and the accuracy distribution supports a more detailed study of the resulting errors. The paper's stated findings are theoretical characterizations of the proposed classifier.
summary.tldr: A theoretical analysis identifies when a Monte Carlo ensemble should outperform a single classifier and derives its accuracy distribution.

abstract: We show how the regularizer of Transductive Support Vector Machines (TSVM) can be trained by stochastic gradient descent for linear models and multi-layer architectures. The resulting methods can be trained online, have vastly superior training and testing speed to existing TSVM algorithms, can encode prior knowledge in the network architecture, and obtain competitive error rates. We then go on to propose a natural generalization of the TSVM loss function that takes into account neighborhood and manifold information directly, unifying the two-stage Low Density Separation method into a single criterion, and leading to state-of-the-art results.

The resulting methods can be trained online, have vastly superior training and testing speed to existing TSVM algorithms, can encode prior knowledge in the network architecture, and obtain competitive error rates. We then go on to propose a natural generalization of the TSVM loss function that takes into account neighborhood and manifold information directly, unifying the two-stage Low Density Separation method into a single criterion, and leading to state-of-the-art results.

paragraphs: This paper tackles the computational cost of transductive support vector machine methods. It shows how to train the TSVM regularizer using stochastic gradient descent for both linear models and multilayer architectures. The resulting procedures can learn online, extending the range of training arrangements available for this form of transductive learning.

The authors report much faster training and testing than existing TSVM algorithms, together with competitive error rates. Multilayer architectures also provide a way to encode prior knowledge in the network's structure. The contribution therefore concerns both computational efficiency and the kinds of models in which the TSVM regularizer can be used.

The paper then generalizes the TSVM loss to incorporate neighborhood and manifold information directly. This combines the two stages of Low Density Separation into one criterion, bringing information about the arrangement of data into the learning objective itself. The authors report state-of-the-art results for this extension. That finding is distinct from the competitive error rates reported for the initial stochastic-gradient formulations.
summary.tldr: Stochastic-gradient TSVM training improves speed, while a generalized loss incorporates neighborhood and manifold information in a single criterion.

title: Large scale manifold transduction

abstract: We study the problem of finding the dominant eigenvector of the sample covariance matrix, under additional constraints on its elements: a cardinality constraint limits the number of non-zero elements, and non-negativity forces the elements to have equal sign. This problem is known as sparse and non-negative principal component analysis (PCA), and has many applications including dimensionality reduction and feature selection. Based on expectation-maximization for probabilistic PCA, we present an algorithm for any combination of these constraints. Its complexity is at most quadratic in the number of dimensions of the data. We demonstrate significant improvements in performance and computational efficiency compared to the state-of-the-art, using large data sets from biology and computer vision.

paragraphs: The paper studies a constrained version of finding the dominant eigenvector of a sample covariance matrix, a central operation in principal component analysis. One constraint limits how many vector entries may be nonzero. Another imposes non-negativity, keeping the entries aligned in sign. These restrictions connect the extracted component with feature selection and dimensionality reduction.

The authors derive an algorithm from expectation-maximization for probabilistic PCA. It handles either constraint individually or both together, providing a common approach to sparse and non-negative variants. The sparsity constraint controls how many original dimensions contribute, while non-negativity restricts the form of their contributions.

The stated computational complexity grows at most quadratically with the number of data dimensions. Experiments on large datasets from biology and computer vision show significant improvements in performance and computational efficiency relative to the compared state-of-the-art methods. The contribution combines flexibility in the allowed constraints with evidence that the resulting optimization method is useful on substantial datasets.
summary.tldr: An expectation-maximization algorithm handles sparse and non-negative PCA constraints with at most quadratic complexity in data dimensionality.

title: Expectation-maximization for sparse and non-negative PCA
